entries.source_text: [Pew] By this definition, both are shorter than the span of the Baby Boomers (19 years) – the only generation officially designated by the U.S. Census Bureau, based on the famous surge in post-WWII births in 1946 and a significant decline in birthrates after 1964. [...] [Wikipedia, Baby boomers] Theirs was a time of economic prosperity and rapid technological progress, and many grew up expecting the world to improve with time. However, young people felt a sense of alienation and sought to assert their own individuality, freedom, and authenticity. [...] [Wikipedia, OK boomer] The phrase has developed into a retort for resistance to technological change, climate change denial, marginalization of members of minority groups, or opposition to younger generations' values more generally. [...] [Wikipedia, Baby boomers] In the West, those born in the years before the actual boom were often the most influential people among boomers. Some of these people were musicians such as The Beatles, Bob Dylan, and The Rolling Stones A significant cultural event of this era was the Woodstock Festival in August 1969, which drew huge crowds despite bad weather and a general lack of facilities. [...] [Word Smarts, 'Everything Is Groovy With This Boomer Slang'] As children and teens during the ’60s and ’70s, boomers came up with some of the grooviest words to boogie down to. While many of these haven’t stood the test of time, other terms remain fresh. Groovy Fashionable and exciting; enjoyable and excellent. [...] [Word Smarts, 'These Slang Terms Reveal Which Generation You Were Born In'] Baby boomers (born between 1946 and 1964) embraced slang on a wider scale, coining sayings such as “boob tube” (“television”), “threads” (“clothing”), and “ticked off” (“annoyed”), to name just a few. Boomers also came up with “dig it” for when you’re really into something, or saying you have to “split” when it’s time to leave. Other slang words from this time include “groovy” (“cool”), “square” (“uncool”), and “moo juice,” to describe a fresh glass of milk. [...] [Babbel, 'Talkin’ ‘Bout The Generations: Baby Boomer Language'] Words and phrases like “groovy” and “boogie” and “space cadet” all reached the heights of mainstream success in those decades, when baby boomers were becoming teen boomers. That also explains why baby boomers are often the people resisting linguistic changes introduced by the younger generations (the overuse of “like,” the non-literal “literally” and vocal fry are all common targets for baby boomers). [...] [Word Smarts, 'How Your Punctuation Habits Reveal Your Age'] millennials have a habit of ending sentences with "lol," while baby boomers might trail off with an ellipsis ("How are you…"). Baby boomers, for example, are known for their love of ellipses. They're everywhere: to end a sentence, to soften the tone, or to indicate trailing thoughts. Less than one-quarter of Gen Z respondents use punctuation in casual communication, while more than half of baby boomers (55%) report always using it while texting or posting online. Meanwhile, only 16% of Gen Z and 28% of millennials consistently use periods at the end of sentences. [...] [Wikipedia, A group where we all pretend to be boomers] A group where we all pretend to be boomers is a Facebook group created in May 2019, for users – the majority of whom are millennials and in Generation Z – to pretend to be baby boomers. Members of the group post in character as a stereotypical baby boomer. The style of speech used in the group has been termed a register called "boomerspeak" by linguist Gretchen McCulloch. Examples of this manner of speech include posts with spelling mistakes, posts written in all capitals, non sequiturs, and the large use of GIFs of Minions. Due to older people more readily sharing fake news on Facebook, many members ironically post fake news in the group, in imitation. [...] [Pew, 'Millennials stand out for their technology use' (2019)] More than nine-in-ten Millennials (93% of those who turn ages 23 to 38 this year) own smartphones, compared with 90% of Gen Xers (those ages 39 to 54 this year), 68% of Baby Boomers (ages 55 to 73) and 40% of the Silent Generation (74 to 91) around three-fourths or more of both Millennials and Gen Xers now report using Facebook (84% vs. 74%, respectively). Boomers and Silents have both increased their Facebook use by double digits since 2015.
entries.nearest_existing: elderly / nostalgic / late_adopter / traditional: elderly is age alone (seventies or beyond); the typed version is a birth cohort (about 62 to 80 in 2026) with the stereotyped postwar optimism, sixties individualism, and resistance to new technology and to younger generations' values.
entries.set_review: Sequence in birth order, v2 with speech and culture. Each draft still opens 'This means being born between <years>' with Pew's years, then two or three markers of the agreed kinds and the v1 portrait traits that fit: boomer = Beatles/Woodstock, 'groovy', Facebook all-caps/ellipses/Minion memes, resistance to change; gen-x = empty house after school, MTV and grunge, eye-rolls and 'as if', independent/skeptical/unconcerned; millennial = AOL Instant Messenger/Myspace/Harry Potter, recession and student debt, avocado toast, 'adulting', confident/tolerant/entitled; gen-z = YouTube/TikTok, smartphone in hand, 'no cap'/'slay', texting without periods, better behaved, open about mental health. Lengths 34 to 36, within the 36 allowance Roger granted for this set. The markers are stereotypes by design and the sources say so (parody group, 'became a stereotype of the millennial generation', 'This type became a stereotype for members of Generation X'); strength mirrored, and the millennial 'entitled' is in by Roger's decision. Caveat on authority: the word-level sources are popular-press slang pieces (Word Smarts, Mental Floss, Babbel) because the dictionary publishers were unreachable; the media habits and touchstones are Wikipedia and Pew. 'Whatever', the Gen X word most often cited, had no reachable cohort-naming source (HowStuffWorks returned an empty bot-check page), so the Gen X phrase is 'as if' (Clueless, 1995), which Word Smarts attributes to Gen X explicitly.
entries.notes: Roger, 2026-10-07: the generation descriptions carry the cohort's stereotyped speech, slang and culture, and voice is wanted here; the 36-word allowance applies to the set. Each v2 draft keeps Pew's birth years and the v1 portrait traits that fit, and adds markers of three kinds: a characteristic word or phrase, a medium or habit of communication, a cultural touchstone. Sources that name the cohort and the words explicitly were preferred; the dictionary publishers were out of reach (Merriam-Webster's slang pages and its 'OK boomer' piece sit behind a bot check, HTTP 403; Dictionary.com's article links redirect to a generic index), so the word-level sources are Word Smarts (three generation-labelled slang pieces and a punctuation piece), Mental Floss and Babbel, with Wikipedia and Pew for the media habits and touchstones. All v1 source pieces are kept; every new piece is checked verbatim against the raw page. Markers: 'the Beatles and Woodstock' from Wikipedia 'Baby boomers' (the most influential people among boomers; the Woodstock Festival as the era's significant cultural event); 'groovy' from Word Smarts' boomer-slang piece, Word Smarts' generations piece and Babbel's boomer piece (all three name boomers and the word); 'posting on Facebook in all caps with ellipses and Minion memes' from Wikipedia's article on the parody group (posts in all capitals, spelling mistakes, non sequiturs, GIFs of Minions, 'boomerspeak') plus Word Smarts' punctuation piece (boomers trail off with an ellipsis, known for their love of ellipses) and Pew 2019 (Boomers' Facebook use up by double digits; 68% own smartphones); 'resisting technological change and younger generations' values' from Wikipedia 'OK boomer', with Babbel's 'resisting linguistic changes introduced by the younger generations' behind it. Dropped from v1 for room: 'growing up in postwar prosperity expecting the world to keep improving' and 'prizing individuality and freedom'. Climate denial and marginalization of minorities (OK boomer list) still left out as the sharpest items. Strength: the Facebook stereotype comes from an article about a parody group that imitates 'a stereotypical internet user from the baby boomer generation', i.e. it is a stereotype by the source's own account; the draft states it as the person's habit, which is the voice Roger asked for. 36 words.

check_result.reasoning: The neg instructions describe someone who embraces new technology, values collective/structural solutions over individualism, sees generational change as progress, adopts digital tools enthusiastically, and rejects older generational standards. This is essentially describing a 'zoomer' (Gen Z) mindset or more broadly a 'millennial' orientation, but as a trait label rather than a generational name, the best descriptors would be 'progressive' or 'tech-savvy' or 'forward-thinking'. However, since the positive label is 'boomer' (a generational identity), the natural opposite generational label would be 'zoomer'. The neg instructions collectively paint a picture of someone who is tech-forward, collectivist, and generationally progressive — the cultural opposite of a boomer. 'Zoomer' is the direct generational antonym, while 'progressive' or 'tech-forward' capture the attitudinal dimension. Since the positive_label is a generational/cultural identity term, 'zoomer' is the most natural symmetric opposite, though 'progressive' captures the ideological dimension well.

entries.source_text: Keywords: gentle, conservative, feeling, nurturing, defensive, contemplative. Sun in Cancer: Sun in Cancer natives have a strong survival instinct. They are protective of those they care about, and of themselves too. They are often quite reticent about sharing their inner selves to the rest of the world, and are often caught up in reminisce. [astrology.com, Cancer page, https://www.astrology.com/zodiac-signs/cancer] "Cancer, the fourth sign of the zodiac, is all about home. Those born under this horoscope sign are 'roots' kinds of people, and take great pleasure in the comforts of home and family."
entries.nearest_existing: nurturing / family_oriented / homebody / sentimental (also guarded): the sign joins the nurturer's care with a defensive, protective reserve and a backward-looking sentimentality; the plain traits each take one of these.
entries.notes: Element water, modality cardinal. Source fallback as for the set (Wikipedia's Cancer (astrology) article has no portrait); cross-check astrology.com/zodiac-signs/cancer: 'all about home', 'maternal, domestic, and love to nurture others', 'prizes family history', 'get emotional about things'; weakness 'hard to let go and make changes'. 'Home' in the draft comes from the cross-check. Strength: keywords mostly gentle, with 'defensive' and 'conservative' as the unflattering side; kept at that level.

check_result.reasoning: The neg instructions collectively describe someone who: (1) makes no special inner circle, treating strangers and friends equally; (2) is forward-looking rather than nostalgic; (3) is emotionally open/transparent rather than guarded; (4) is detached rather than nurturing; and (5) is logic-driven rather than feeling-driven. The opposite of Cancer's cluster (nurturing, protective, private, nostalgic, emotionally guided) points toward someone who is emotionally detached, unsentimental, and indiscriminately open. 'Detached' captures the lack of special bonds and emotional distance. 'Unsentimental' captures the rejection of nostalgia and feeling. 'Aloof' captures the emotional distance but misses the openness aspect. The neg instructions actually describe someone paradoxically both open (shares freely) and detached (no special warmth), which is a complex opposite. 'Detached|unsentimental' best captures the core opposition. The antonym score is moderate-to-strong: Cancer is a specific astrological cluster, and the opposite is a recognizable but somewhat complex pole.

edits.was: This means being ruled by feeling and home: gentle and nurturing toward one's own, protective of them and of oneself, reticent about one's inner life with outsiders, and given to reminiscing.
edits.by: Roger's step-3 decision

Those with Sun in Capricorn have a realistic, grounded approach to life that can be seen no matter how dreamy the rest of the birth chart suggests. These people know how to do things, and to get things done.
entries.nearest_existing: ambitious / self_disciplined / persevering / prudent (also practical, long_term_oriented): the sign is ambition made patient and practical; the plain ambitious wants the top, the typed version climbs toward it one step at a time for years.
entries.notes: Element earth, modality cardinal. Source fallback as for the set (Wikipedia's Capricorn (astrology) article has no portrait); cross-check astrology.com/zodiac-signs/capricorn: 'all about hard work', 'put in a full day at the office', 'one step at a time', 'dedicated to their goals, almost to the point of stubbornness'; weaknesses 'judgmental', 'materialistic, and even miserly', hiding pain 'behind a mask of self-sufficiency'. Strength: Cafe Astrology's keywords for this sign are all flattering or neutral ('conservative' the only non-compliment), so the draft is correspondingly flattering and milder than the cross-check, which carries stubbornness, judgment and miserliness. Flag for Roger: one of three signs whose primary source has no fault side (with Leo and Pisces).

check_result.reasoning: The neg instructions collectively describe someone who is impulsive, lacks follow-through, abandons plans when they get hard, seeks instant gratification, and drifts without direction. The opposite of disciplined/tenacious/prudent/grounded ambition. 'Impulsive' captures the lack of deliberation and acting on whims. 'Fickle' captures the abandonment of commitments. 'Undisciplined' is a direct negation but less natural as a standalone label. 'Impulsive' is probably the strongest single word, but 'fickle' and 'scattered' (used in the neg instructions themselves) are also strong candidates. The antonym score: capricorn as defined is a compound of discipline, tenacity, prudence, and ambition — the neg pole is a compound of impulsivity, fickleness, and recklessness. It's a strong but not perfectly symmetric opposition (capricorn has an ambitious/goal-oriented dimension that the neg doesn't purely negate with just 'impulsive').

entries.source_text: [Table 4.2, Conscientiousness:] Describes socially prescribed impulse control that facilitates task- and goal-directed behavior, such as thinking before acting, delaying gratification, following norms and rules, and planning, organizing, and prioritizing tasks. [Costa & McCrae, NEO-PI-3 Feedback Summary, C domain:] Low scorers are easygoing and not inclined to make plans or schedules. [sample-client text, average range:] You can be sloppy and disorganized, and you are sometimes less dependable and reliable and more likely to bend the rules than you should be. You have limited aspirations and might be considered somewhat lackadaisical or lazy. You sometimes find it difficult to make yourself do what you should, and tend to quit when tasks become too difficult.
entries.nearest_existing: careless (ad-hoc, neg of conscientious): deliberate near-duplicate by rule 5. The ad-hoc file is slapdash work, broken deadlines and promises, inattention to detail; this one adds the deliberation and self-discipline facets (acting on impulse, quitting when it gets hard) and disorder. entries.pair_review: Same scope (order, punctuality, duty and rules, effort, deliberation); 29 and 31 words. The high opens with a two-part gloss ('thinking before acting and putting the task before the pleasure'), the low with a one-part gloss ('acting on the moment'). The high's 'aiming high' (achievement striving) and 'checking the work twice' (competence) answer the low's 'dropping a task once it gets hard' and 'leaving things in a mess' only loosely; 'bending the rules' (from Costa & McCrae's text) has a direct high counterpart in 'honoring every obligation'.
entries.notes: Costa & McCrae's low-C sentence is mild ('easygoing and not inclined to make plans or schedules'); the vice-level wording rests on the marker adjectives and on the sample-client sentences, which are average-range text but low-side in content. Not marked derived for that reason; 'acting on the moment' inverts the definition's 'thinking before acting'. Costa & McCrae's own name for the low pole is 'lack of direction' (per the queue), not 'careless'. Sources as for agreeable (Big Five).
entries.pair_scope_flag: Agree with the writer, and one more scope gap: the high touches seven facets (deliberation and self-discipline in the gloss; order, punctuality, duty, achievement, competence in the list), the low six, and the two it lacks, achievement striving and competence, are in its own source ('limited aspirations', 'Slipshod'), while it spends two clauses on dependability ('showing up late or not at all', 'forgetting promises'). A re-edit could trade 'forgetting promises' for slapdash work or low aims.

check_result.reasoning: The neg instructions describe someone who is thorough, follows through on commitments, meets deadlines, keeps promises, follows rules, plans ahead, and is organized and dependable. The best label is 'conscientious,' though 'diligent' and 'disciplined' are also competitive. 'Conscientious' is the most natural and recognizable label given the Big Five framing. The antonym score is 4 because careless/conscientious are the canonical opposite poles of the same Big Five dimension.

The most natural and recognizable label for this opposite pole is 'open' in the Big Five sense, but 'open-minded' or 'curious' also work well as standalone adjectives. Since this is explicitly the Big Five openness dimension, 'open' is the most precise label. The antonym relationship is essentially perfect — closed vs. open on the same dimension.

entries.source_text: The C (Conscientiousness) style is thoughtful and questioning. This describes people who are analytical, reserved, and precise. [...] Conversely, people with styles that fall toward the bottom of the circle tend to be more moderate-paced and are often described as calm, methodical, and careful. [...] People with DiSC styles that fall toward the left side of the circle are naturally more skeptical in nature and are often described as logic-focused, objective, and challenging.
entries.nearest_existing: conscientious (plain: diligence, thoroughness, attention to detail) / analytical / precise / meticulous / skeptical: the typed version is analytical, precise and reserved with a questioning stance and a moderate pace; plain conscientious is dutifulness and reliability, which the typed version never mentions, so the shared word is misleading (Marston's original factor was compliance).
entries.set_review: Square on the publisher's two dimensions, pace (active, fast-paced vs thoughtful, moderate-paced) by stance (questioning, skeptical vs accepting). Each draft opens 'This means being <pace> and <stance>' so the quadrant is readable off the set, then the style's three descriptors from the publisher's page, a pace clause and a stance clause. 30 to 32 words. The source is a publisher's blurb, uniformly neutral-to-flattering ('no one style is better or worse than the next'), so all four come out milder than their plain corpus neighbours (dominance beside dominant / controlling; conscientiousness beside conscientious / meticulous); mirrored, not sharpened. The stance clause is near-identical for the two members that share a side (i and S both 'people over logic'; D and C both 'logic over people'), which is the axis showing; they differ by pace. Marston 1928 is the system's origin, but his four primary emotions (dominance, inducement, submission, compliance) differ in content from the modern S and C, so he is recorded in notes, not summarised. The publisher's fuller page (discprofile.com) was 403 throughout; see notes.
entries.notes: Primary source is the publisher's (Wiley, Everything DiSC) own page, since the four labels are the publisher's names; the fuller style pages with priorities and motivators (discprofile.com/what-is-disc and its overview-styles PDF) returned HTTP 403 to every fetch, so they are not quoted. A search-engine snippet of that page (unverified, not used in the draft) listed the D style's priorities as getting immediate results, taking action, challenging self and others; i as expressing enthusiasm, taking action, encouraging collaboration; S as giving support, maintaining stability, enjoying collaboration; C as ensuring accuracy, maintaining stability, challenging assumptions. Marston 1928, Emotions of Normal People (public domain; full text at https://archive.org/stream/emotionsofnormal0000mars/emotionsofnormal0000mars_djvu.txt), names the four primary emotions dominance, inducement, submission and compliance on two axes, alliance vs antagonism of the stimulus and superiority vs inferiority of the self's strength; dominance is "chiefly characterized by victory of the motor self over an antagonist of inferior intensity", inducement introspectively "a process of persuading someone, in a friendly way, to perform an act suggested by the subject", submission the bodily attitude of "an obedient child toward a loving mother", compliance that "the subject is moving himself at the dictates of a superior force". Wikipedia's gloss (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DISC_assessment): "Dominance: active use of force to overcome resistance in the environment Inducement: use of charm in order to deal with obstacles Submission: warm and voluntary acceptance of the need to fulfill a request Compliance: fearful adjustment to a superior force." The modern S and C differ from Marston's submission and compliance, so his text is background, not the summarised source. Strength: the publisher's text is neutral and the draft matches it.

check_result.reasoning: The neg instructions collectively describe someone who is fast-moving, gut-driven, emotionally expressive, spontaneous, trusting, and impulsive — the opposite of the analytical, measured, skeptical, reserved conscientiousness described in the positive pole. The best single label capturing this cluster is 'impulsive,' though 'spontaneous' also fits the expressive/fast-moving dimension. 'Impulsive' best captures the gut-trusting, fast-deciding, skip-the-details pattern across all five neg prompts. This is a strong but not perfect antonym to the positive label, since 'conscientiousness_disc' bundles skepticism and precision together, while the neg pole bundles impulsiveness with emotional expressiveness and trust — there's some asymmetry in the constructs.

entries.label: conventional (Kohlberg)
entries.description_draft: This means taking what one's family, group or country expects as right in itself, whatever follows: pleasing others and meaning well, doing one's duty, respecting authority and upholding the social order.
entries.description_notes: Kohlberg's three levels of moral reasoning as a three-corner set (the file says 'three-corner'; 'triangle' is this extraction's reading, a sequence is also conceivable).
entries.description: This means taking what one's family, group or country expects as right in itself, whatever the consequences, and standing loyally by that order: pleasing others, meaning well, doing one's duty, respecting authority.

entries.source_text: 2. Conventional Level. At this level, maintaining the expectations of the individual's family, group or nation is perceived as valuable in its own right, regardless of immediate and obvious consequences. The attitude is not only one of conformity to personal expectations and social order, but of loyalty to it, of actively maintaining, supporting, and justifying the order and of identifying with the persons or group involved in it. [...] Stage 3. The Interpersonal Concordance or "Good Boy - Nice Girl" Orientation. Good behaviour is that which pleases or helps others and is approved by them. [...] "he means well" becomes important for the first time. Stage 4. The Law-and-Order Orientation. [...] Right behaviour consists of doing one's duty, showing respect for authority, and maintaining the given social order for its own sake.
entries.nearest_existing: conventional (plain; already in the corpus, so this is a deliberate standard's near-duplicate, to be said in `source`); conformist and rule_abiding are the behavioral neighbors; this pole is the basis of judgment: the group's expectations held as right in themselves, with loyalty to the order.
entries.set_review: Kohlberg three. The descriptions read as a triangle rather than an ordered sequence. Each names a distinct basis for deciding right and wrong: what the act brings oneself and who has the power (pre), what one's group expects, held as right in itself (conv), principles worked out for oneself and valid apart from any group (post). Nothing in the three texts says earlier/later or less/more adequate, so the developmental order of the source is not readable from them; a reader meets three ways of judging, each contrastable with each other. The pairwise contrasts are all live: pre vs conv is self-interest and power against loyalty to the group; conv vs post is the group's authority against principles above the group; pre vs post is consequences-to-self against self-chosen principle. One caveat for the geometry: pre and post share a feature that a strict line would not predict, both set the group's expectations aside (one for payoff, one for principle), which is the confusion Kohlberg himself warned of between his lowest and highest stages, so the pre-post distance need not be the longest, and a sequence reading (conv in the middle) is not supported by the texts. Grain and shape are matched: each opens 'This means <gerund>' and states the basis of judgment, 30-31 words.
entries.notes: 'Regardless of immediate and obvious consequences' rendered as 'whatever follows'; 'nation' as 'country'; 'frequently judged by intention' as 'meaning well'. No hedge in the level text to carry. Source: Marcus David Feak, 'Moral Development and its Explanation: Kohlberg's Structuralism', MA thesis (Philosophy), McMaster University, August 1979, pp. 3-5, which reproduces Kohlberg's chart 'Definition of Moral Stages' in full and cites it '(1972, 296-297)', i.e. Kohlberg, L., 'Relativity and Indoctrination in Value Education', Zygon 7 (Spring 1972), 285-309, per the thesis bibliography. Kohlberg's own publications of this chart (Zygon 1972; J. Phil. 1973, 630-646; Phi Delta Kappan 1975; Kohlberg & Hersh, Theory Into Practice 1977) are all paywalled, so a quoting scholarly source is used, as the packet allows. The thesis PDF is a scan; its OCR was cleaned for source_text (hyphenation joined; 'ac~!on' -> 'action', 'group pr nation' -> 'group or nation', 'persons or groups or group' -> 'persons or group', 'mora I v1tlues' -> 'moral values', 'tenTIS' -> 'terms', 'Le alistic' -> 'Legalistic', 'Oritntation' -> 'Orientation', 'respect 0 the dig-jljty' -> 'respect for the dignity'; the Stage 3 heading is illegible in the OCR and is supplied from the second reproduction). British spellings ('favours', 'behaviour') are the thesis's. Second reproduction, same chart with an extra Stage 0 and small wording differences ('the individual perceives the maintenance of the expectations of his family...', 'The individual makes a clear effort to define...'): https://xenodochy.org/ex/lists/moraldev.html (Ralph Kenyon, personal site, naming its source as Kohlberg's chapter in M. C. Reynolds (ed.), Psychology and the Process of Schooling in the Next Decade: Alternative Conceptions, c. 1971); a Prince Sultan University handout PDF has the same text. Scholarly paraphrase cross-check: W. C. Crain (1985), Theories of Development, ch. 7, HTML copy at https://www.appstate.edu/~steelekm/classes/psy2664/kohlberg.htm (its Kohlberg quotations are about stages, not levels). Not reachable: the Kohlberg 1976 passage on the three levels as 'three different types of relationships between the self and society's rules and expectations' (Hockenbury textbook table host unreachable; Sage Encyclopedia of Educational Theory and Philosophy paywalled; the SEP 'Moral Psychology: Empirical Approaches' entry does not discuss Kohlberg). Wikipedia 'Lawrence Kohlberg's stages of moral development' paraphrases the levels (citing Kohlberg 1971, 1976 and Colby & Kohlberg 1987) and has no verbatim level text.
review_issues: 'whatever follows:' sits directly before the colon and reads as 'whatever follows the colon', i.e. as introducing the list; the source's 'regardless of immediate and obvious consequences' needs a form such as 'whatever the consequences'.

The level text's defining turn, 'not only one of conformity ... but of loyalty to it, of actively maintaining, supporting, and justifying the order and of identifying with the persons or group', is carried only by 'upholding the social order'; loyalty and identification with the group, the element the source uses to separate this level from plain conformity (and that the writer's own nearest-existing line leans on), are not stated.

Nearest-existing line calls the plain corpus 'conventional' a deliberate near-duplicate; it is not: data/traits/instructions/conventional.json is 'reaching for the standard answer, the template, the way it is usually done' paired with eccentric, a different sense sharing only the word. The file's source note should say homonym with a different scope, not near-duplicate; the content neighbours are conformist, rule_abiding, obedient and deferential.

check_result.reasoning: The neg instructions describe someone who reasons independently from personal principles, defies authority, ignores group norms, and constructs their own moral code — this is the opposite pole of conventional/conformist morality. The best candidates are 'autonomous' (Kohlberg's own term for post-conventional reasoning), 'principled', or 'nonconformist'. Since the instructions explicitly describe someone reasoning from their own conscience and privately constructed principles — which maps closely to Kohlberg's 'post-conventional' or 'autonomous' stage — 'autonomous' is the most technically precise label. However, 'nonconformist' and 'principled' are also strong candidates from a lay perspective. The antonym score is high (3-4) because conventional vs. autonomous/principled is a well-recognized opposition in moral psychology, though 'conventional' in Kohlberg's sense has a specific technical meaning that makes the opposition slightly asymmetric.

The most natural label for this pole in attachment theory is 'securely attached' or more broadly 'anxious attachment,' but the neg instructions don't describe anxiety — they describe comfortable, enthusiastic closeness and interdependence. The best standalone adjective capturing this is 'securely attached' but that's a compound. As a plain adjective, 'interdependent' captures the mutual reliance aspect, while 'emotionally open' or 'attachment-seeking' also fit. In attachment literature, the direct opposite of dismissive-avoidant is often called 'preoccupied' (anxious) or 'secure,' but these prompts most closely describe secure attachment with strong relational orientation. 'Securely attached' is the theoretical opposite, but as a general adjective 'interdependent' or 'emotionally open' work well. Given the emphasis on mutual reliance and welcoming closeness without anxiety, 'securely_attached|interdependent' best captures it. The antonym score is strong (3-4) since dismissive-avoidant and secure/interdependent attachment are well-established opposite poles.

entries.decision: Roger 2026-09-08: definitely add the Big Five and HEXACO by name as standard-named pairs; pairing fixed by the standard, antonym check informational (the ad-hoc twin showing up is expected, not a failure).
entries.section: Part 1: Big Five and HEXACO by name
entries.source_text: Persons with very high scores on the Emotionality scale experience fear of physical dangers, experience anxiety in response to life's stresses, feel a need for emotional support from others, and feel empathy and sentimental attachments with others.
entries.nearest_existing: emotional (ad-hoc, neg non-emotional) is acknowledging and discussing feelings, an expressive style; the name match is the deliberate near-duplicate the packet mentions, but the content differs: this one is the HEXACO factor (fearfulness, anxiety, dependence, sentimentality). Also near: anxious, timid, clingy, dependent, sentimental, empathetic. Not neurotic (Big Five): no anger, depression or impulsiveness; dependence and sentimentality instead.
entries.pair_review: Facet for facet (fearfulness, anxiety, dependence, sentimentality with empathy); 31 and 30 words. The high spends two clauses on the fourth facet ('forming deep, tender attachments', 'feeling their pain as one's own') where the low has one ('holding people at arm's length', which the low's source gives as 'feel emotionally detached from others'; the word 'emotional' was kept out of the low draft because it is the partner's label); the low spends two on dependence ('keeping one's troubles to oneself', 'asking no one for support') where the high has one. Both follow their source sentences, which are uneven the same way.
entries.pair_scope_flag: Agree with the writer on the two-clause facets (sentimentality on the high, dependence on the low; both from the sources). Add: the first clauses are not on the same axis: the high's 'flinching from physical danger' is fear, the low's 'walking toward physical danger without a second thought' is heedless approach (entry issue; the suggested 'pressing on where one could get hurt' puts the low back on fear). 'Staying unworried' is the one negated form on the low side.

check_result.reasoning: The neg instructions collectively describe someone who is physically fearless, emotionally detached from others' suffering, steady under stress, lightly attached in relationships, and generally unmoved by emotional or physical threats. The HEXACO 'Emotionality' factor's opposite pole is typically labeled 'fearless' or 'stoic' in the literature, but the neg instructions emphasize a broader emotional imperviousness — not just fearlessness but also emotional detachment, self-sufficiency under stress, and light attachments. 'Stoic' captures the composure and self-sufficiency well; 'fearless' captures the physical danger aspect; 'resilient' captures the stress-steadiness. However, in HEXACO psycholinguistics, the low-emotionality pole is often called 'fearless' or 'stoic.' Given the breadth of the neg instructions (fearlessness + emotional detachment + stress resilience + light attachment), 'stoic' or 'fearless' are the strongest candidates. 'Stoic' best captures the full cluster. The antonym score is high — these are the defined opposite poles of the same HEXACO dimension.

edits.was: This means flinching from physical danger, worrying hard when life gets stressful, needing a shoulder to lean on, and forming deep, tender attachments to people, feeling their pain as one's own.

entries.description_notes: Low pole of Neuroticism; canonical (Goldberg names the factor Emotional Stability). Paraphrase the NEO-PI-R domain definition (Costa and McCrae 1992; John and Srivastava 1999 has the same content); both poles in the 'This means ...' form; the description does not name the source; US spelling.
entries.description: This means staying calm and even-tempered: expecting things to turn out, slow to anger, quick to shake off gloom, at ease among strangers, passing up temptations, and steady under stress.
entries.decision: Roger 2026-09-08: definitely add the Big Five and HEXACO by name as standard-named pairs; pairing fixed by the standard, antonym check informational (the ad-hoc twin showing up is expected, not a failure).
entries.section: Part 1: Big Five and HEXACO by name
entries.source_text: [Table 4.2, Neuroticism:] Contrasts emotional stability and even-temperedness with negative emotionality, such as feeling anxious, nervous, sad, and tense. [Table 4.4, low-pole markers:] Stable, Calm, Contented. [Table 4.2, behavioral examples, reverse-keyed:] Accept the good and the bad in my life without complaining or bragging (R); Take it easy and relax. (R) [Costa & McCrae, NEO-PI-3 Feedback Summary, N domain:] Traits in the N domain reflect different ways of reacting emotionally to distressing circumstances. Low scorers are resilient, rarely experiencing negative emotions.
entries.nearest_existing: even_tempered (neg temperamental), 'taking either kind of news in stride, with no moods to brace for', is the closest single file; calm, composed, unflappable, placid, resilient and self_assured each take one facet; neurotic's ad-hoc neg is composed. This one is the whole low pole of Neuroticism: the six facets reversed (anxiety, anger, depression, self-consciousness, impulsiveness, vulnerability).
entries.pair_review: Both drafts run the six facets in the same order; 29 and 29 words. The high is all actions ('fretting', 'snapping', 'sinking', 'flushing', 'giving in', 'going to pieces'); the low mixes participles with adjectives ('slow to anger', 'unembarrassed', 'steady'), so the low reads as a state and the high as conduct. The low carries a gloss ('staying calm and even-tempered') the high lacks (cut for length). 'Passing up temptations' answers 'giving in to cravings' almost word for word, the one place the inversion is exact.
entries.notes: Marked derived: the sources give the low pole only as labels ('emotional stability and even-temperedness'), three adjectives (Stable, Calm, Contented), two reverse-keyed items and Costa & McCrae's one sentence ('resilient, rarely experiencing negative emotions'), so the six behaviours are the Neuroticism facets written as their opposites. Goldberg's name for the factor is Emotional Stability (per the queue), which the label follows. Sources as for agreeable (Big Five).
entries.pair_scope_flag: Agree with the writer (actions against states; the low's gloss; 'passing up temptations' the exact inversion). Add: the anxiety facet is where the derivation is weakest: 'fretting over what could go wrong' is worry ahead of events, the low's 'taking bad news in stride' is reaction after them (it comes from the reverse-keyed item), so the low has no 'not worrying ahead' clause; and 'unembarrassed in company' is the one absence-shaped clause in a pole that is meant to be opposite behavior. Both fixable in a re-edit ('expecting things to turn out', 'at ease among strangers').

check_result.reasoning: The neg instructions collectively describe someone who is easily upset, anxious, prone to anger, self-conscious, and impulsive — the classic profile of high neuroticism in Big Five personality theory. The positive label is emotional stability (low neuroticism), and its direct opposite pole in the Big Five is 'neurotic' or 'neuroticism.' However, in everyday language, 'neurotic' captures the anxiety/worry dimension well, while 'emotionally unstable' is the more symmetric structural opposite. 'Neurotic' is the most recognized standalone adjective for this pole. Both 'neurotic' and 'emotionally unstable' are strong candidates.

entries.label: ENFJ (MBTI)
entries.description_draft: This means drawing energy from people, taking in patterns and possibilities, deciding by values, and liking things settled: warm, responsible, highly attuned to others' needs, finding potential in everyone, helping them fulfill it, leading with inspiration.
entries.description_notes: Unpaired type trait (extraverted, intuitive, feeling, judging): state the four preferences plainly and add one or two sentences of the conventional portrait, paraphrasing the Myers & Briggs Foundation's type description; avoid 16personalities nicknames; the description does not name the instrument; negative_label stays the categorical placeholder `non-ENFJ MBTI`.
entries.description: This means drawing energy from people, taking in patterns and possibilities, deciding by values, and liking things settled: warm, responsible, highly attuned to others' needs, finding potential in everyone, helping them fulfill it, leading with inspiration.
entries.decision: Roger 2026-09-08: add the sixteen types as unpaired traits (not roles); the set is the corners of a 4-cube for the derived-dichotomy analysis.
entries.section: Part 1b (definitely): the 16 MBTI types
entries.source_text: Warm, empathetic, responsive, and responsible. Highly attuned to the emotions, needs, and motivations of others. Find potential in everyone, want to help others fulfill their potential. May act as catalysts for individual and group growth. Loyal, responsive to praise and criticism. Sociable, facilitate others in a group, and provide inspiring leadership.
entries.nearest_existing: Preferences touch extroverted / gregarious (E), intuitive / big_picture (N), empathetic / compassionate (F), organized / decisive / closure_seeking (J); the portrait sits nearest inspirational, nurturing, supportive and charismatic.
entries.set_review: V2 UNDER THE RELAXED BAND (Roger, 2026-10-07: cap 40, the extra words only where a type's dropped clauses earn them; 36 stays where one clause restores the hallmark). SHAPE unchanged from v1: 'This means <energy>, <information>, <decisions>, and <outer world>: <portrait>.', one sentence, the eight preference phrases fixed and identical to v1 ('drawing energy from people' / 'from reflection'; 'taking in facts and specifics' / 'patterns and possibilities'; 'deciding by logic' / 'by values'; 'liking things settled' / 'keeping options open'), so each dichotomy is still one phrase swap read off the set and adjacent corners of the cube still differ in exactly one phrase. LENGTH: preamble 18 words in all; portraits 18 to 22; totals 36 to 40 (v1: all 32). Eight at 36: ENFJ, ENTJ, ENTP, ESFP, INFP, INTJ, INTP, ISTJ. Above 36: ENFP 37, ISFP 38, ISTP 38, ESTJ 39, ESTP 39, INFJ 39, ESFJ 40, ISFJ 40. WHY EACH WENT ABOVE 36: ENFP +1 'confidently' (the reviewer's strength point, 'confidently proceed' had been rendered below source); ESFJ +4 'wanting to be appreciated' (a whole source sentence and the type's second hallmark); ESTJ +3 'minding routine details' (the one source sentence otherwise unrepresented, apart from the J-phrase one); ESTP +3 'focused on the here and now' (the type's best-known line, which the reviewer's edit had traded for the problem-solving action; 'pragmatic' and 'at hand' dropped to pay, 'wanting immediate results' carries the pragmatic approach); INFJ +3 'what motivates people' (the first half of the source's second sentence, the type's hallmark, kept in v1 and the reviewer's edit only as 'insightful') plus 'conscientious'; ISFJ +4 'loyal' and 'striving for harmony' (the last source sentence's non-order half; the J phrase carries order, not harmony); ISFP +2 'friendly' and 'loyal' (two source adjectives); ISTP +2 'valuing efficiency' (the last source sentence's one item the T phrase does not carry). KEPT AT 36 because the restored clause is the hallmark and what remains dropped is hedged, preference-carried or flourish: ENFJ ('may act as catalysts', 'responsive to praise and criticism'), ENTJ ('goal setting', 'passing it on to others'), ENTP ('stimulating, alert', 'analyzing them strategically'), ESFP (two 'with others' clauses, E-carried), INFP ('can be catalysts'; 'fulfill their potential' rendered as 'grow'), INTJ ('when committed, organize a job and carry it through', J-carried), INTP ('in their area of interest'), ISTJ ('their work, their home, their life'). GRAIN: all sixteen remain one-sentence lists of adjectives and participial clauses after the colon, five to eleven items; ISFJ (eleven) is the most list-like, as its source paragraph is; no portrait changed shape between 36 and 40. STARTING TEXT: the reviewer's suggested_edit for the eleven 'edit' entries (ISTP uses the reviewer's 36-word version from the set review, since its suggested_edit is the 32-word one), the v1 draft for the five 'ok' entries (ENTP, INFP, ISFJ, ISFP, ISTJ). All five of the reviewer's strength corrections are in (ENFJ 'highly attuned', ENFP 'quickly connecting ... confidently running with them', ESTJ 'following clear standards and expecting the same' for 'holding everyone to', INTJ 'holding oneself and others to high standards', INTP 'whatever interests one' for 'everything'), as are the four faithfulness fixes (ESFJ loyal and follow-through as two items, ESFP common sense and making work fun as two items, INFJ the vision, ISTP the analyze sentence). CLAUSES TAKEN BACK at 36, per type: ENFJ 'helping them fulfill it'; ENFP 'seeking and giving affirmation'; ENTJ 'planning long-term, usually well read' (hedge kept; 'leading readily' for 'quick to lead' pays for it); ENTP 'good at reading people'; ESFJ 'following through even on small matters' whole, plus 'working hard for harmony' back for 'set on harmony' and 'conscientious'; ESFP 'adapting readily to new people' and 'material comforts' ('sensible, making work fun' pays); ESTJ 'forceful in implementing plans'; ESTP 'wanting immediate results'; INFJ 'pursuing a clear vision of the common good'; INFP 'curious' and 'loyal to one's people'; INTJ 'quickly seeing long-range patterns'; INTP 'focusing deeply on problems'; ISFJ 'responsible', 'accurate' and 'those close to one' for 'one's people'; ISFP 'not pushing one's views'; ISTJ 'serious' and 'taking pleasure in making everything orderly'; ISTP 'analyzing what makes things work' with 'flexible' and 'then' kept. NOT FITTED AT 40: ESTP 'material comforts and style', ESFP 'learn best by trying a new skill with other people', ISTP 'get through large amounts of data to isolate the core of practical problems', ISFJ 'at work and at home'; each entry's notes list its remaining drops. STRENGTH: positive and measured as the source; every entry at the source's strength by the reviewer's reading plus the fixes; still markedly milder than the corpus's plain traits in the same regions (dominant, controlling, detached). Hedges kept as plain words, five: INTP 'sometimes', ENFP 'often', ENTP 'apt to', INFP 'unless', ENTJ 'usually'. VERBATIM: INTP 'skeptical, sometimes critical, always analytical' and INFP 'accepting unless a value is threatened' remain quoted whole; the standards rule says paraphrase, the reviewer and I would keep both for the hedges; Roger's call. OTHER POINTS FROM THE REVIEW: 'deciding by values' kept over 'deciding by values and people' (reviewer agrees; cost noted: 'values' alone can be heard as principled rather than people-minded); INFP has 'value(s)' three times in one sentence counting the F phrase, as the source paragraph itself does; preference echoes in the portraits remain (ESTJ 'practical, matter-of-fact', ISTJ 'making everything orderly', ESTP and ISTP 'flexible', ENTJ 'decisive', INTP 'logically ... analytical', INFP 'values', INFJ 'conscientious'); closure_seeking (J) / ambiguity_tolerant (P) added to the J and P facets of all sixteen nearest_existing lines as the reviewer asked; the generator will likely write 'you are an ENFJ' from the injected label, so rule 6's leak check applies to the type code (not a description matter). VOCABULARY: no type code, letters, preference names or instrument name in any description; 'feel' unused; US spelling.
entries.notes: Source of record: the Foundation's single 'The 16 MBTI Personality Types' page. The current myersbriggs.org has no per-type pages (the older URL my-mbti-personality-type/mbti-basics/the-16-mbti-types.htm redirects to this page), so the one paragraph is the whole official text; the page credits it to 'Introduction to Myers-Briggs Type by Isabel Briggs Myers, published by The Myers-Briggs Company'. source_text was taken from the raw page HTML because the fetch tool's summarizer clipped every paragraph. v2 (relaxed band, Roger 2026-10-07) starts from the reviewer's suggested edit ('warm, responsible, highly attuned', restoring the intensifier) and takes back the helping half of 'want to help others fulfill their potential' as 'helping them fulfill it'. Kept at 36: what remains dropped is hedged or secondary: 'May act as catalysts for individual and group growth' (its hedge 'may' goes with the clause), 'Loyal, responsive to praise and criticism', 'Sociable, facilitate others in a group'.

check_result.reasoning: The neg instructions collectively describe someone who is introverted/solitary, coldly logical, emotionally detached, unplanned/spontaneous, and indifferent to others' growth. This is essentially the opposite of ENFJ across all four MBTI dimensions: introverted (vs. extraverted), sensing/thinking (vs. intuitive/feeling), perceiving (vs. judging), and cold/detached (vs. warm/attuned). The closest MBTI opposite would be ISTP, but as a personality trait label rather than MBTI type, the neg instructions most strongly evoke 'detached' or 'cold' as the dominant quality. However, the full picture also includes 'self-focused,' 'emotionally withdrawn,' and 'indifferent.' 'Detached' captures the emotional withdrawal well, while 'cold' captures the logical/unsentimental aspect. Since the neg instructions span multiple dimensions (introversion, cold logic, lack of leadership, indifference to others' potential, emotional detachment), no single adjective perfectly captures all of it. 'Detached' is the strongest single candidate, with 'cold' as a close alternative. The antonym score is moderate because ENFJ is a composite type, not a single trait, so the opposition is real but asymmetric.

entries.label: ENFP (MBTI)
entries.description_draft: This means drawing energy from people, taking in patterns and possibilities, deciding by values, and keeping options open: warmly enthusiastic, imaginative, quickly connecting things and confidently running with them, seeking and giving affirmation, often improvising, verbally fluent.
entries.description_notes: Unpaired type trait (extraverted, intuitive, feeling, perceiving): state the four preferences plainly and add one or two sentences of the conventional portrait, paraphrasing the Myers & Briggs Foundation's type description; avoid 16personalities nicknames; the description does not name the instrument; negative_label stays the categorical placeholder `non-ENFP MBTI`.

entries.source_text: Warmly enthusiastic and imaginative. See life as full of possibilities. Make connections between events and information very quickly, and confidently proceed based on the patterns they see. Want a lot of affirmation from others, and readily give appreciation and support. Spontaneous and flexible, often rely on their ability to improvise and their verbal fluency.
entries.nearest_existing: Preferences touch extroverted (E), intuitive / divergent (N), empathetic (F), spontaneous / improvisational / flexible / ambiguity_tolerant (P); the portrait sits nearest effusive, creative, energetic, encouraging and optimistic.
entries.notes: Same single source page as enfj_mbti (text from the raw HTML). v2 starts from the reviewer's suggested edit ('quickly connecting things and running with them'; 'often improvising, verbally fluent', keeping fluency as its own item) and takes back the affirmation clause as 'seeking and giving affirmation'; at 37, 'confidently' is restored before 'running with them' (the reviewer's strength point). Hedge 'often' kept. Still dropped: 'very', 'a lot of', 'support'; 'See life as full of possibilities' is carried by the N phrase.

check_result.reasoning: The neg instructions collectively describe someone who is introverted (energized by solitude), concrete/practical (sticks to proven facts), sequential and methodical (moves step by step), analytical/logical (cuts feelings from decisions), and reserved/closed (speaks only when certain, commits firmly). This is a strong composite portrait of the ISTJ MBTI type, but as a single adjective label the best fit is 'istj_mbti' — however, since we want a natural adjective rather than an MBTI code, the neg pole is best captured as 'reserved|analytical|introverted'. The most natural single-word label capturing the full opposite cluster (introverted, sensing, thinking, judging) would be something like 'reserved' or 'analytical', but 'reserved' misses the concrete/logical aspects. 'Analytical' misses the introversion and closure. Given the full picture — solitary, concrete, sequential, logical, closed — 'reserved|analytical' surfaces the key ambiguity. The antonym score is high because the neg instructions were clearly designed to oppose ENFP on all four MBTI dimensions (I vs E, S vs N, T vs F, J vs P), making this a strong to near-perfect opposition.

entries.label: Enneagram 1
entries.description_draft: This means living by a strong sense of right and wrong: always striving to improve things, orderly and fastidious, afraid of making a mistake, and slipping into criticism, perfectionism and resentment.
entries.description_notes: Enneagram type; ring (the figure is a circle with wings). Folk system: `source` = the system's name; the description paraphrases the conventional portrait and does not name the system (convention rule 4).
entries.description: This means living by a strong sense of right and wrong: always striving to improve things, orderly and fastidious, afraid of making a mistake, and slipping into criticism, perfectionism and resentment.
entries.decision: Accepted 2026-09-08; write the `arrangement` field at seeding
entries.section: Coverage audit part 4: attitudes, behavior and segmentation (decided 2026-09-08) > Sets and rings (decided 2026-09-08; write the arrangement at seeding)
entries.source_text: The Rational, Idealistic Type: Principled, Purposeful, Self-Controlled, and Perfectionistic. Ones are conscientious and ethical, with a strong sense of right and wrong. They are teachers, crusaders, and advocates for change: always striving to improve things, but afraid of making a mistake. Well-organized, orderly, and fastidious, they try to maintain high standards, but can slip into being critical and perfectionistic. They typically have problems with resentment and impatience. At their Best: wise, discerning, realistic, and noble. Can be morally heroic.
entries.nearest_existing: perfectionist / principled / conscientious (also fastidious, critical): the type is the principled person's ethics driving the perfectionist's standards, with the fear of error and the resentment as the price; the plain traits each carry one piece.
entries.set_review: Nine drafts, 29-32 words, one shape: a gloss of the type's core drive, a colon, then the Institute's own adjectives and 'but can slip into' faults in the order the source gives them. All nine source_texts are the Enneagram Institute's type pages (enneagraminstitute.com/type-N): the one-line summary plus the 'in Brief' paragraph; the overview page (type-descriptions) gives the same one-liners with small adjective differences for types 2, 3, 4 and 7, recorded in those entries' notes. Nicknames (Reformer, Helper, Achiever, Individualist, Investigator, Loyalist, Enthusiast, Challenger, Peacemaker) and the system are unnamed in every draft. One uniform omission: each paragraph ends with an 'At their Best:' sentence describing the type at its healthiest ('wise, discerning, realistic, and noble'; 'unconditional love for others'; ...); it was left out of all nine because it is an aspiration, not the portrait, and would tilt the whole set flattering. The paragraphs themselves are balanced, each pairing virtues with a 'but can also' clause and a 'typically have problems with' sentence, so the drafts sit at about the corpus's plain-trait strength rather than markedly milder; the source's hedges ('sometimes', 'usually', 'tend to be') are rendered as plain words ('at times', 'too readily'), not dropped. The ring is the figure's numbering 1-9 and is readable as such; the drafts also keep the three triads legible without naming them (8-9-1: control, peace, rightness; 2-3-4: being needed, admired, distinct; 5-6-7: knowing, security, experience), the Enneagram's analogue of the zodiac's elements. Distinguishability at 32 words was not a problem; no member needed the 36-word allowance. Where a source item was dropped for length it is named in that entry's notes.
entries.notes: The 'At their Best' sentence is omitted from the draft, uniformly across the nine (see set_review). The Institute's trademarked nickname ('The Reformer') and the system are unnamed. The one-line summary is identical on the overview page and the type page for this type. 'Impatience' from the problems list did not fit at 32 and is the one source item left out.

check_result.reasoning: The neg instructions consistently describe someone who is relaxed about standards, unbothered by imperfection, lets errors slide, and accepts things as they are. This is the classic opposite of perfectionism and moral rigidity. The best single label is 'easygoing' (used explicitly in neg #5), but 'lax' or 'permissive' also capture the moral looseness in neg #2. 'Easygoing' captures the overall gestalt best, though 'lax' captures the standards dimension more precisely. These are genuinely competitive. As an antonym to enneagram type 1's perfectionism/moral rigidity, 'easygoing|lax' surfaces the ambiguity. The opposition is strong but not perfectly symmetric — enneagram 1 has specific features (resentment, moral code, fear of mistakes) that 'easygoing' doesn't fully mirror as a direct opposite label, so I'd score this a 3.

entries.label: Enneagram 2
entries.description_draft: This means being warm-hearted and self-sacrificing: needing to be close to people, helping them so as to be needed, flattering and eager to please, possessive, and slow to admit one's own needs.
entries.description_notes: Enneagram type; ring (the figure is a circle with wings). Folk system: `source` = the system's name; the description paraphrases the conventional portrait and does not name the system (convention rule 4).
entries.description: This means being warm-hearted, generous and self-sacrificing: driven to be close to others, slipping into helping so as to be needed, flattering, eager to please, possessive, and slow to admit one's needs.
entries.decision: Accepted 2026-09-08; write the `arrangement` field at seeding
entries.section: Coverage audit part 4: attitudes, behavior and segmentation (decided 2026-09-08) > Sets and rings (decided 2026-09-08; write the arrangement at seeding)
entries.source_text: The Caring, Interpersonal Type: Generous, Demonstrative, People-Pleasing, and Possessive. Twos are empathetic, sincere, and warm-hearted. They are friendly, generous, and self-sacrificing, but can also be sentimental, flattering, and people-pleasing. They are well-meaning and driven to be close to others, but can slip into doing things for others in order to be needed. They typically have problems with possessiveness and with acknowledging their own needs. At their Best: unselfish and altruistic, they have unconditional love for others.
entries.nearest_existing: helpful / nurturing / clingy / other_focused (also sycophantic for the flattering): the type is helpfulness with a motive, giving in order to be needed, plus possessiveness of the people helped; the plain helpful has no such motive and the plain clingy no such generosity.
entries.notes: 'At their Best' omitted as across the set. Nickname ('The Helper') unnamed. One-liner differs between pages: overview 'Demonstrative, Generous, People-Pleasing, and Possessive', type page 'Generous, Demonstrative, ...'; the type page's order is recorded. Strength: the source's 'can slip into' and 'problems with' clauses are rendered as plain behaviors (helping so as to be needed; possessive; slow to admit one's own needs); 'sentimental' did not fit at 32.
review_issues: Strength: 'helping them so as to be needed' and 'flattering' state flat what the passage hedges ('can slip into doing things for others in order to be needed'; 'can also be sentimental, flattering, and people-pleasing'); neither has flat support in the one-liner ('People-Pleasing' covers 'eager to please', not the motive). The writer's notes say the 'can slip into' clause was deliberately rendered as plain behavior, which is against the strength rule and against the writer's own rendering in type 1 ('slipping into').

Balance: two of the passage's seven virtues are kept ('warm-hearted', 'self-sacrificing') against five of its six faults, the second-harshest ratio in the set; 'generous' fits once 'needing to be close to people' becomes the source's own 'driven to be close to others' and 'one's own needs' loses 'own'.

check_result.reasoning: The neg instructions collectively describe someone who is self-contained, keeps resources for themselves, speaks their mind bluntly without people-pleasing, lets others handle their own problems, maintains loose/detached relationships, and is self-directed in pursuing their own needs. This is the opposite of the warm, other-focused, self-sacrificing Type 2. The best label capturing this pole is 'self-contained' or 'detached' — but more precisely, the neg instructions emphasize self-directedness, autonomy, and lack of other-focus. 'Self-reliant' captures the resource-keeping and self-directed aspects, while 'detached' captures the emotional distance and non-grasping relationship style. 'Autonomous' also fits well. These are moderately strong antonyms — the Type 2 is defined by other-focus and self-effacement, while the neg pole is self-focused and self-directed, making this a strong opposition, though not a perfect mirror (the neg pole isn't necessarily cold or hostile, just non-helping and self-contained).

entries.label: Enneagram 3

entries.source_text: The Success-Oriented, Pragmatic Type: Adaptable, Excelling, Driven, and Image-Conscious. Threes are self-assured, attractive, and charming. Ambitious, competent, and energetic, they can also be status-conscious and highly driven for advancement. They are diplomatic and poised, but can also be overly concerned with their image and what others think of them. They typically have problems with workaholism and competitiveness. At their Best: self-accepting, authentic, everything they seem to be—role models who inspire others.
entries.nearest_existing: ambitious / status_seeking / competitive / performance_oriented (also charismatic): the type is ambition fused with image-management; the plain ambitious wants the achievement, the typed version wants to be seen achieving and adapts itself to be admired.
entries.notes: 'At their Best' omitted as across the set. Nickname ('The Achiever') unnamed. One-liner differs between pages: overview 'Adaptive', type page 'Adaptable'; the type page's is recorded. 'Overly concerned with their image' is rendered as 'preoccupied with one's image', keeping the source's strength; 'workaholism' as 'working without rest'.

check_result.reasoning: The neg instructions describe someone who is indifferent to status, recognition, and others' opinions, doesn't compete, doesn't manage their image, works at an unhurried pace, and feels no drive for achievement or advancement. This is the opposite of the ambitious, image-conscious, status-driven Enneagram 3. The best labels for this pole could be 'unambitious' but a more natural standalone adjective would be 'unassuming' or 'indifferent.' However, 'unassuming' implies modesty rather than pure indifference. 'Indifferent' captures the lack of concern for status and recognition well. 'Laid-back' captures the unhurried, unbothered quality. 'Unambitious' is the most direct antonym to the ambitious/driven quality. Given the combination of traits — no ambition, no image management, no competitive drive — 'unambitious|indifferent' seems most apt. The antonym score is strong (3) because while these are clearly opposite poles, 'unambitious' doesn't fully capture the image-indifference aspect, and the positive label has multiple facets (charm, poise, ambition, status-consciousness) that don't all have a single clean opposite.

entries.source_text: The Sensitive, Introspective Type: Expressive, Dramatic, Self-Absorbed, and Temperamental. Fours are self-aware, sensitive, and reserved. They are emotionally honest, creative, and personal, but can also be moody and self-conscious. Withholding themselves from others due to feeling vulnerable and defective, they can also feel disdainful and exempt from ordinary ways of living. They typically have problems with melancholy, self-indulgence, and self-pity. At their Best: inspired and highly creative, they are able to renew themselves and transform their experiences.
entries.nearest_existing: melancholic / self_absorbed / introspective / self_pitying (also temperamental, self_conscious): the type adds to the melancholic's sadness a sense of being different and exempt from the ordinary, and a creative, emotionally honest expressiveness; no plain trait has the 'exempt' strand.
entries.notes: 'At their Best' omitted as across the set. Nickname ('The Individualist') unnamed. One-liner differs between pages: overview 'The Sensitive, Withdrawn Type', type page 'The Sensitive, Introspective Type'; the type page's is recorded. 'Defective' rendered as 'flawed'; 'typically have problems with' rendered as 'prone to'; 'self-indulgence' from the problems list did not fit at 32 and is the one source item left out.
review_issues: Strength: 'disdainful of ordinary living' states flat what the passage hedges ('they can also feel disdainful and exempt from ordinary ways of living'); no flat support elsewhere ('moody' may stand flat under the one-liner's 'Temperamental'). 'Exempt' is dropped although the writer's nearest-existing line names it as the strand no plain trait has; there is no room for it at 32, so the nearest-existing line overstates what the draft carries (still a fair line).

check_result.reasoning: The neg instructions describe someone who is emotionally stable, content with ordinary life, unselfconscious, outward-focused, and not prone to introspection or melancholy. This is the opposite of the enneagram type 4's sensitivity, moodiness, self-consciousness, and withdrawal. The best labels for this opposite pole are 'well-adjusted' (capturing contentment and ease in ordinary life), 'equanimous' (emotional steadiness), or 'conventional' (acceptance of ordinary living). 'Well-adjusted' captures the overall picture well, but 'equanimous|unselfconscious' also fits. The neg instructions collectively paint a picture of someone grounded, emotionally steady, and comfortable — often called 'well-adjusted' in personality psychology. The opposition to enneagram_4 is strong but not a single clean antonym word, since enneagram_4 is a complex cluster.

entries.source_text: The Intense, Cerebral Type: Perceptive, Innovative, Secretive, and Isolated. Fives are alert, insightful, and curious. They are able to concentrate and focus on developing complex ideas and skills. Independent, innovative, and inventive, they can also become preoccupied with their thoughts and imaginary constructs. They become detached, yet high-strung and intense. They typically have problems with eccentricity, nihilism, and isolation. At their Best: visionary pioneers, often ahead of their time, and able to see the world in an entirely new way.
entries.nearest_existing: cerebral / solitary / detached / curious (also eccentric, isolated): the type is the cerebral person's absorption in ideas with the withdrawal that follows from it, intense rather than cool; the plain detached lacks the intensity and the plain curious the withdrawal.
entries.notes: 'At their Best' omitted as across the set. Nickname ('The Investigator') unnamed. One-liner identical on both pages. 'Nihilism' from the problems list did not fit at 32 and is the one source item left out; 'secretive' from the one-liner is carried only implicitly by 'detached'.

check_result.reasoning: The neg instructions consistently describe someone who is socially engaged, draws energy from others, shares openly, gravitates toward groups, and needs connection to feel whole — the opposite of the withdrawn, mentally self-sufficient, isolated Enneagram 5. The best label for this pole is 'sociable' or 'extroverted.' 'Extroverted' captures the energy-from-others and outward orientation, while 'sociable' captures the people-seeking and connection-needing aspects. Both are strong candidates. The Enneagram 5 is sometimes called 'the Investigator' and its opposite in social terms maps well onto extroversion. The antonym relationship is strong but not perfectly symmetric — Enneagram 5 includes eccentricity and intellectual obsession beyond mere introversion, so the neg pole doesn't fully mirror all aspects.

entries.source_text: The Committed, Security-Oriented Type: Engaging, Responsible, Anxious, and Suspicious. Sixes are reliable, hard-working, responsible, and trustworthy. Excellent 'troubleshooters,' they foresee problems and foster cooperation, but can also become defensive, evasive, and anxious—running on stress while complaining about it. They can be cautious and indecisive, but also reactive, defiant and rebellious. They typically have problems with self-doubt and suspicion. At their Best: internally stable and self-reliant, courageously championing themselves and others.
entries.nearest_existing: anxious / cautious / dependable / paranoid (also loyal, indecisive): the type is dependability powered by anxiety, with the swing between caution and defiance that no plain trait has; the plain anxious is not reliable for it and the plain dependable is not anxious.
entries.notes: 'At their Best' omitted as across the set. Nickname ('The Loyalist') unnamed. One-liner identical on both pages. 'Craving security' in the opening comes from the one-liner's 'Security-Oriented' and the paragraph's thrust; 'trustworthy', 'foster cooperation', 'defensive, evasive' did not fit at 32. The fetched paragraph opens with the one-liner repeated in lower case ('The committed, security-oriented type.'), dropped from source_text as duplicate.

check_result.reasoning: The neg instructions collectively describe someone who is trusting, relaxed, unworried, and spontaneous — they commit quickly, extend trust freely, skip double-checks, make no backup plans, and feel no anxiety. The positive label (enneagram_6) is defined by anxiety, vigilance, suspicion, and indecisiveness. The opposite pole is best captured by 'trusting' (extending trust without suspicion) combined with 'carefree' (no anxiety or worry). 'Trusting' addresses the suspicion/doubt dimension, while 'carefree' addresses the anxiety/vigilance dimension. Both are competitive candidates. 'Carefree' or 'easygoing' captures the relaxed, unguarded, unworried quality well. 'Trusting' captures the opposite of suspicion. Since the neg instructions emphasize both dimensions roughly equally, listing both is appropriate. The opposition is strong but not perfectly symmetric since enneagram_6 is a complex type with multiple facets (anxiety, loyalty, defiance, suspicion), so a single antonym can't capture all of it.

entries.source_text: The Busy, Variety-Seeking Type: Spontaneous, Versatile, Acquisitive, and Scattered. Sevens are extroverted, optimistic, versatile, and spontaneous. Playful, high-spirited, and practical, they can also misapply their many talents, becoming over-extended, scattered, and undisciplined. They constantly seek new and exciting experiences, but can become distracted and exhausted by staying on the go. They typically have problems with impatience and impulsiveness. At their Best: they focus their talents on worthwhile goals, becoming appreciative, joyous, and satisfied.
entries.nearest_existing: restless / distractible / impulsive / hedonistic (also spontaneous, energetic, optimistic): the type is the restless person's hunger for new experience with an optimistic, playful temper and the scattering of talent that follows; the plain hedonistic seeks pleasure, the typed version seeks novelty and stimulation.
entries.notes: 'At their Best' omitted as across the set. Nickname ('The Enthusiast') unnamed. One-liner differs between pages: overview 'The Busy, Fun-Loving Type: Spontaneous, Versatile, Distractible, and Scattered', type page 'The Busy, Variety-Seeking Type: Spontaneous, Versatile, Acquisitive, and Scattered'; the type page's is recorded. 'Extroverted' rendered 'outgoing'; 'over-extended' as 'spreading one's many talents too thin'; 'practical' did not fit at 32.
review_issues: Strength: 'worn out from never stopping' sharpens the passage twice: the hedge 'can become ... exhausted' is dropped and 'staying on the go' becomes 'never stopping'. 'Spreading one's many talents too thin ... undisciplined' states flat the hedged 'can also misapply their many talents, becoming over-extended, scattered, and undisciplined' ('scattered' is in the one-liner and may stand flat). Three words of room exist (29 words), enough for 'apt to' and the source's own 'staying on the go' once one 'and' goes.

check_result.reasoning: The neg instructions describe someone who is focused, disciplined, deliberate, patient, and committed to depth over breadth — staying with one thing, following routines, resisting distraction, thinking before acting, and sitting with difficulty. This is the opposite of the scattered, impulsive, novelty-chasing enneagram 7. The best labels are 'disciplined' or 'focused' or 'deliberate'. 'Disciplined' captures the routine-following, commitment-keeping, distraction-resisting qualities. 'Focused' captures the depth-over-breadth, single-minded quality. 'Deliberate' captures the thoughtful, measured pace. These are all strong candidates. The neg instructions also evoke 'patient' and 'methodical'. Given the full picture — depth over breadth, finishing what's started, resisting novelty — 'disciplined|focused|deliberate' are the top candidates. The antonym relationship is strong but not perfect since enneagram 7 is a complex cluster of traits (optimism, spontaneity, scattered energy) and no single word perfectly opposes all of them.

entries.source_text: The Powerful, Dominating Type: Self-Confident, Decisive, Willful, and Confrontational. Eights are self-confident, strong, and assertive. Protective, resourceful, straight-talking, and decisive, but can also be ego-centric and domineering. Eights feel they must control their environment, especially people, sometimes becoming confrontational and intimidating. Eights typically have problems with their tempers and with allowing themselves to be vulnerable. At their Best: self-mastering, they use their strength to improve others' lives, becoming heroic, magnanimous, and inspiring.
entries.nearest_existing: dominant / controlling / confrontational / self_assured (also blunt): the type is dominance with a protective side and a refusal of vulnerability; the plain dominant takes charge, the typed version must control, and the plain controlling lacks the straight talk and the protectiveness.
entries.notes: 'At their Best' omitted as across the set. Nickname ('The Challenger') unnamed. One-liner identical on both pages. The source's 'sometimes becoming confrontational and intimidating' is rendered as 'confrontational and intimidating at times' (hedge kept as its plain-word equivalent, per the strength rule); 'ego-centric' and 'resourceful' did not fit at 32.
review_issues: Strength: 'unable to let oneself be vulnerable' is a notch above the passage's 'problems with allowing themselves to be vulnerable'; 'loath' is the plain word for it at the same length. The rest mirrors the passage, including 'at times' for 'sometimes' and 'domineering' flat under the title's 'Dominating'.

check_result.reasoning: The neg instructions collectively describe someone who defers to others, avoids confrontation, softens communication, opens up vulnerably, and trusts others to lead and protect themselves. This is the opposite of the domineering, controlling, confrontational Enneagram 8. The best label for this cluster is 'submissive' — someone who yields control, backs down, and lets others lead. 'Meek' or 'deferential' are also strong candidates. 'Submissive' captures the yielding of control and confrontation-avoidance most directly. The antonym relationship is strong but not perfectly symmetric — Enneagram 8 has specific features (protectiveness, hot temper) not fully captured by 'submissive', so a score of 3 is appropriate.

entries.source_text: The Easygoing, Self-Effacing Type: Receptive, Reassuring, Agreeable, and Complacent. Enneagram Type Nines are accepting, trusting, and stable. They are usually creative, optimistic, and supportive, but can also be too willing to go along with others to keep the peace. They want everything to go smoothly and be without conflict, but they can also tend to be complacent, simplifying problems and minimizing anything upsetting. They typically have problems with inertia and stubbornness. At their Best: indomitable and all-embracing, they are able to bring people together and heal conflicts.
entries.nearest_existing: accommodating / conciliatory / placid / passive (also easygoing, agreeable): the type is accommodation for the sake of one's own peace of mind, with inertia and a stubborn core beneath the agreeableness; the plain accommodating has no such inertia and the plain placid no stubbornness.
entries.notes: 'At their Best' omitted as across the set. Nickname ('The Peacemaker') unnamed. The type page's one-liner as fetched read 'Receptive, Reassuring Agreeable, and Complacent' (comma missing, almost certainly a rendering artefact); the overview page's punctuation is recorded. 'Supportive', 'creative', 'optimistic' and 'stable' did not fit at 32; the source's 'too willing' is kept as 'too readily', its 'tend to be complacent' as plain 'complacent', and 'inertia' as 'slow to get moving'.
review_issues: Balance: the passage gives six virtues ('accepting, trusting, and stable', 'usually creative, optimistic, and supportive') and five faults; the draft keeps two virtues and all five faults, so the Nine comes out the harshest of the nine although its passage is as balanced as the others'. 'Supportive' fits if 'whatever is upsetting' becomes 'anything upsetting' (the source's own word) and 'slow to get moving' becomes 'slow to act'. The hedge handling is otherwise right ('too readily' for 'too willing'; 'complacent' flat under the one-liner's 'Complacent').

check_result.reasoning: The neg instructions describe someone who is confrontational, decisive, assertive, and willing to name problems directly rather than smooth them over. They hold firm positions, act without waiting for consensus, and challenge the status quo. The opposite of the peace-seeking, conflict-avoiding, complacent enneagram 9 is best captured by 'assertive' or 'confrontational'. 'Assertive' captures the directness, decisiveness, and willingness to hold positions under pressure. 'Confrontational' captures the willingness to name problems and push through discomfort. These are genuinely competitive candidates. The antonym score is strong but not perfect — enneagram 9 is a complex cluster (accepting + complacent + conflict-avoidant + stubborn), and 'assertive|confrontational' captures the opposite of the conflict-avoidance and passivity aspects well, though 'stubborn' in the positive definition somewhat complicates a clean opposition.
