entries.source_text: Work involves managing, negotiating, marketing, or selling, typically in a business setting, or leading or advising people in political and legal situations. Enterprising occupations are often associated with business initiatives, sales, marketing/advertising, finance, management/administration, professional advising, public speaking, politics, or law.

check_result.reasoning: The neg instructions describe someone who avoids leadership, shrinks from persuasion and negotiation, fears public speaking, prefers being directed rather than directing, and is indifferent to power and influence. This is the opposite of the enterprising/dominant/persuasive pole. The best labels are 'unassuming' (too mild), 'submissive' (captures the deferring/following aspect), 'retiring' (captures withdrawal from public roles), or 'passive' (captures the lack of initiative and avoidance of leadership). 'Submissive' and 'passive' are both strong candidates — 'submissive' captures the yielding in negotiation and deference to others' authority, while 'passive' captures the general withdrawal and indifference to influence. These together map well onto the opposite of enterprising. The antonym score is strong but not perfect because 'enterprising' also has an innovation/initiative connotation beyond just dominance.

entries.source_text: Frank, decisive, assume leadership readily. Quickly see illogical and inefficient procedures and policies, develop and implement comprehensive systems to solve organizational problems. Enjoy long-term planning and goal setting. Usually well informed, well read, enjoy expanding their knowledge and passing it on to others. Forceful in presenting their ideas.
entries.nearest_existing: Preferences touch extroverted (E), intuitive / strategic (N), logical / analytical (T), decisive / organized / closure_seeking (J); the portrait sits nearest dominant, forthright, efficient, confident and bold.
entries.notes: Same single source page as enfj_mbti (text from the raw HTML). v2 starts from the reviewer's suggested edit ('forceful in presenting ideas') and takes back 'Enjoy long-term planning' as 'planning long-term' and 'Usually well informed, well read' as 'usually well read' (the hedge kept as the plain word); 'quick to lead' became 'leading readily' (closer to 'assume leadership readily') to pay for 'usually'. Kept at 36: what remains dropped is secondary: 'goal setting', 'enjoy expanding their knowledge and passing it on to others', 'illogical', 'organizational problems'.

check_result.reasoning: The neg instructions collectively describe someone who: hangs back rather than leads, lives in the present rather than planning long-term, keeps opinions to themselves and avoids friction, keeps options open rather than seeking closure, and is drained by groups rather than energized. This composite portrait maps closely to the INFP or ISFP MBTI types, but as a personality trait label rather than MBTI type, the best descriptors are 'passive' (hanging back, following), 'adaptable|flexible' (improvising, keeping options open), and 'introverted' (drained by groups). However, the most direct opposite of ENTJ across all four dimensions (E vs I, N vs S, T vs F, J vs P) is ISFP. As a trait label rather than MBTI code, the neg instructions most strongly evoke 'passive|reserved|conflict-averse' — but since the positive label is an MBTI type, the natural opposite label would be 'isfp_mbti'. However, the instructions ask for an adjective or short phrase. The neg instructions emphasize passivity, conflict-avoidance, present-focus, and introversion. 'Passive' captures the leadership/initiative dimension, but misses introversion and open-endedness. 'Introverted|passive' or 'passive|conflict-averse' are candidates. Given the full picture — withdrawn, avoids decisions, keeps peace, improvises — 'passive|conflict-averse' seems best, though 'introverted' is also competitive. The antonym score: ENTJ vs its composite opposite is a strong but not perfect antonym relationship as a trait label (not a single clean word), so I'd rate it 3.

entries.source_text: Explorers delight in having the game expose its internal machinations to them. They try progressively esoteric actions in wild, out-of-the-way places, looking for interesting features (ie. bugs) and figuring out how things work. Scoring points may be necessary to enter some next phase of exploration, but it's tedious, and anyone with half a brain can do it. Killing is quicker, and might be a constructive exercise in its own right, but it causes too much hassle in the long run if the deceased return to seek retribution. Socialising can be informative as a source of new ideas to try out, but most of what people say is irrelevant or old hat. The real fun comes only from discovery, and making the most complete set of maps in existence.
entries.nearest_existing: curious / inquisitive / exploratory: the plain traits are interest in topics and probing questions in conversation; the typed version is interest in a game's mechanics, bugs and map, and it actively disdains the scoreboard, which curious does not.
entries.notes: Bartle 1996, 'Hearts, clubs, diamonds, spades: players who suit MUDs', Journal of MUD Research 1(1); the author's own page, fetched raw and quoted from it. Axes in Bartle's words: "The x-axis goes from an emphasis on players (left) to an emphasis on the environment (right); the y-axis goes from acting with (bottom) to acting on (top)." Bartle's quadrant glosses: "Achievers are interested in doing things to the game, ie. in ACTING on the WORLD." and "Explorers are interested in having the game surprise them, ie. in INTERACTING with the WORLD." 'Bugs' is Bartle's own gloss on 'interesting features'. Strength: neutral in the source (mild disdain for points and chatter), neutral in the draft.
review_issues: Record, not description (suggested_edit left null so the draft stands): 'finding points, fights and chatter dull beside discovery' rests for 'fights' on Bartle's sentence about killing for explorers (quicker, but it causes too much hassle in the long run if the deceased return to seek retribution; from memory of the article, the writer should check the fetched page), which the recorded passage elides with '[...]'. Restore that sentence to source_text, dropping the 'anyone with half a brain' clause if the 120-word cap bites. Without it the recorded passage supports points and chatter being dull, not fights.

check_result.reasoning: The neg instructions describe someone who follows established paths, takes things at face value, avoids exploration, focuses on goals/outcomes rather than understanding mechanisms, and has no curiosity about hidden layers. This is the opposite of an explorer who investigates underlying systems. The best label for this pole is 'conformist' in the sense of sticking to prescribed paths, but more precisely these instructions describe someone who is 'goal-oriented' or 'pragmatic' — focused on results rather than discovery. 'Incurious' captures the lack of curiosity well. 'Pragmatic' captures the results-over-understanding orientation. These are genuinely competitive: the neg instructions emphasize both lack of curiosity AND goal/outcome focus. 'Incurious' vs 'pragmatic' are both strong candidates. As an antonym to 'explorer_bartle' (discovery-driven), 'incurious' is perhaps the most direct opposite of the exploratory drive, while 'pragmatic' captures the outcome-focus dimension.

entries.description: This means using one's religion for what it gets one: security and solace, company and distraction, standing and self-justification; the creed itself is held lightly or bent to fit one's other needs.
entries.source: Allport & Ross 1967, JPSP 5(4):432-443, p. 434 (definitions reconstructed from quoting sources; see the queue entry); https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40839-025-00260-9
entries.decision: decided 2026-09-07 (section)
entries.section: Religion (decided 2026-09-07)
entries.source_text: [RECONSTRUCTION of Allport & Ross 1967, p. 434, from secondary sources that quote it verbatim; the paper is closed access and was not read. Sentence-level provenance and agreement counts in roger/chunk4_2026-10-07/allport_reconstruction.json.] Persons with this orientation are disposed to use religion for their own ends. The term is borrowed from axiology, to designate an interest that is held because it serves other, more ultimate interests. Extrinsic values are always instrumental and utilitarian. Persons with this orientation may find religion useful in a variety of ways—to provide security and solace, sociability and distraction, status and self-justification. The embraced creed is lightly held or else selectively shaped to fit more primary needs. In theological terms the extrinsic type turns to God, but without turning away from self. [Summary sentence, p. 434:] The extrinsically motivated person uses his religion, whereas the intrinsically motivated person lives his religion.
entries.nearest_existing: extrinsically_motivated (motivation in general, not religion) and transactional; religious is the affiliation this axis sits inside. Not a near-duplicate: the axis is how religion is held, not whether.
entries.pair_review: The extrinsic draft lists five concrete uses (Allport's own nouns) and ends on how the creed is held; the intrinsic draft is abstract (master motive, other needs fitted around it) and ends on internalizing the creed. Same closing topic, different concreteness: a re-edit could give intrinsic one concrete habit or trim extrinsic's list. Extrinsic also rests on more, shorter fragments than intrinsic. 'uses his religion / lives his religion' is Allport's own antithesis and is deliberately not used in either draft, to avoid naming the partner.
entries.notes: The 1967 paper (J. Pers. Soc. Psychol. 5(4):432-443) is paywalled and no full-text copy could be fetched (the ACU thesis link returned an HTML stub; the UFJF and Brambilla PDFs quote nothing in English), so source_text is assembled from fragments each quoted verbatim by a fetched source, with the quoting source named; nothing bridging them is invented. Quoting sources: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3858239 (Bulbulia, Osborne & Sibley 2013), https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Religious_orientation, https://distantreader.org/stacks/journals/ejop/ejop-397.htm (Flere, Lavrič, Musil & Klanjšek), https://selfdeterminationtheory.org/wp-content/uploads/2014/04/2010_NeyrinckLensetal_JSSR.pdf (Neyrinck, Lens, Vansteenkiste & Soenens 2010). The PMC citation's 'p. 424' lies outside the paper's page range and is probably a typo; left as cited. 'held lightly' comes through Neyrinck's gloss (which also cites Allport 1950), not from a fetched 1967 sentence. Strength: the source is pointed ('always instrumental and utilitarian') and the draft matches it; 'self-justification' kept as Allport's word because the plain alternatives ('a good conscience') soften it.
entries.pair_scope_flag: Agree with the writer: extrinsic lists five concrete payoffs (Allport's own nouns) while intrinsic stays at the level of motive (master motive, other needs fitted around it, creed internalized) and names none of the religious contents the gloss offers (humility, compassion). Both close on how the creed is held, so the closings are parallel; the difference is concreteness, not scope or trigger. A re-edit would either give intrinsic one concrete habit from the gloss or trim extrinsic to three payoffs. Both drafts rest on fragments (the 1967 paper was not fetchable), extrinsic on more and shorter ones; provenance is honestly recorded on both sides.

check_result.reasoning: The neg instructions describe someone who holds religion as an end in itself, with deep conviction, regardless of personal cost — this is precisely Allport's concept of 'intrinsic' religious orientation. The positive label is 'extrinsic_allport,' and its direct theoretical opposite in Allport's framework is 'intrinsic.' The neg instructions perfectly capture intrinsic religiosity: faith as a master motive, not a servant to other needs. The antonym score is 4 because these are the two poles of Allport's well-established extrinsic/intrinsic religiosity dimension — direct, symmetric opposites.

entries.source_text_fragments_2026-10-07: Allport & Ross (1967), as quoted by three fetchable scholarly sources: "Extrinsic values are always instrumental and utilitarian" (cited there as p. 424) and, at the extrinsic end of the continuum, "those who follow religion for personal ends" (Bulbulia, Osborne & Sibley 2013, PLoS ONE); people high in extrinsic orientation use religion "to provide security and solace, sociability and distraction, status and self-justification" (Allport & Ross 1967, p. 434; Wikipedia, Religious orientation); "the extrinsically motivated individual uses his religion, whereas the intrinsically motivated lives his" (p. 434; Flere et al., Europe's Journal of Psychology). Gloss in Neyrinck et al. 2010 (JSSR): "an extrinsically oriented individual approaches religion in a utilitarian or instrumental fashion: it helps one to attain 'self-centered' ends, such as safety, solace, or sociability. Furthermore, religion is lightly held, oversimplified, not reflected upon".

edits.was: This means using one's religion for what it gets one: security and solace, company and distraction, standing and self-justification; the creed itself is held lightly, a means to those ends.

entries.source_text: Fearful - I am somewhat uncomfortable getting close to others. I want emotionally close relationships, but I find it difficult to trust others completely, or to depend on them. I sometimes worry that I will be hurt if I allow myself to become too close to others. [Model: negative self / negative partner; 'the fearful avoidant style of attachment is characterized by high anxiety and high avoidance'.]
entries.nearest_existing: guarded (withholding; this pole wants closeness and fears the hurt, the approach-avoid conflict); also avoidant, insecure, trusting's opposite side.
entries.notes: Hedges kept: 'somewhat', 'sometimes'; 'completely' kept. This is the hedged 1991 wording; the distributed RQ reads 'I am uncomfortable getting close' and 'I worry that I will be hurt' (see below). The mildest of the four, as in the source. Source: Wikipedia, 'Attachment measures', section on Bartholomew and Horowitz, which reproduces the four 1991 prototype paragraphs verbatim under the names Secure / Dismissive / Preoccupied / Fearful and cites Bartholomew, K. & Horowitz, L. M. (1991), 'Attachment styles among young adults: a test of a four-category model', JPSP 61, 226-244. The paper itself is not openly hosted (PubMed 1920064 served only a cookie page; no open PDF found) and Bartholomew's SFU self-report page is a 404, so this reproduction stands in for it. The Wikipedia article 'Attachment in adults', which the packet names, no longer carries the paragraphs: its raw wikitext (fetched today) has only the sentence that its style descriptions are based on the RQ. Second source, the questionnaire as distributed: R. Chris Fraley's measures page (University of Illinois), https://labs.psychology.illinois.edu/~rcfraley/measures/rq.html, styles A-D with no names (psytests.org/ipl/rqen-bl.html has the identical text). The distributed RQ drops some of the paper's hedges: A reads 'It is easy for me' (paper: 'relatively easy'); B reads 'I am uncomfortable getting close' and 'I worry that I will be hurt' (paper: 'somewhat uncomfortable', 'I sometimes worry'). The draft keeps the paper's hedges, as the packet asks. Names: the paper uses secure / fearful / preoccupied / dismissing (so also Cozzarelli et al. 2003, UCSB Close Relationships Lab PDF); Wikipedia 'Attachment measures' uses Secure / Fearful / Preoccupied / Dismissive; the queue's labels are the hybrid names. The two axes: Wikipedia 'Attachment measures' maps model of self to attachment anxiety and model of partner to avoidance: secure low/low, preoccupied high anxiety/low avoidance, dismissive low anxiety/high avoidance, fearful high/high.
review_issues: Minor: in 'finding others hard to trust or depend on completely' the 'completely' now qualifies both verbs; the source puts it on trust only ('difficult to trust others completely, or to depend on them'), so depending on others reads a shade softer than the prototype, where it is difficult outright.

Nearest-existing line leads with guarded, but data/traits/instructions/guarded.json is verbal self-censorship (swallowing the objection and the honest verdict; paired with forthright), not wariness about closeness; the rest of the line (avoidant, insecure, the cynical side of trusting) stands, and none of those is close either, so the pole has no real corpus neighbour.

check_result.reasoning: The neg instructions describe someone who trusts fully, lets others in without reservation, feels secure in deepening bonds, depends on others comfortably, and welcomes being known completely. This is the classic description of 'secure attachment' in attachment theory — the direct opposite pole to fearful-avoidant attachment. The term 'securely attached' is the most precise and recognizable label from the same theoretical framework. However, outside attachment theory jargon, 'trusting' or 'open' could also apply. Since the positive label itself uses attachment theory terminology, 'secure_attachment' is the most natural counterpart. As a standalone adjective, 'secure' or 'trusting' works well. The opposition is strong but not perfectly symmetric in everyday language — fearful-avoidant is a specific clinical/theoretical construct, while 'secure' is its direct theoretical antonym.

entries.description_draft: This means belonging from birth to one's own folk for better or worse, living the familiar, comfortable, exclusive life of kin and home, and staying together in spite of all that separates.
entries.description_notes: Describes a person native to such a society, not a theory of society: someone whose ties are kinship, place and custom, who treats relationships as ends and locates themself in family, village and faith. Diacritics fold to ASCII in the stem, the label keeps them. Durkheim's mechanical solidarity is the same axis seen from the division of labour. entries.description: This means belonging from birth to one's own folk for better or worse, living the familiar, comfortable, exclusive life of kin and home, and staying together in spite of all that separates.
entries.source: Tönnies, Gemeinschaft / Gesellschaft (Durkheim mechanical / organic solidarity is the same axis); https://germanhistory-intersections.org/en/knowledge-and-education/ghis:document-163
entries.decision: decided 2026-09-07
entries.section: Anthropological social structure (decided 2026-09-07)
entries.source_text: All kinds of social co-existence that are familiar, comfortable and exclusive are to be understood as belonging to Gemeinschaft. Gesellschaft means life in the public sphere, in the outside world. In Gemeinschaft we are united from the moment of our birth with our own folk for better or for worse. We go out into Gesellschaft as if into a foreign land. [...] human wills, each one housed in a physical body, are related to one another by descent and kinship; they remain united, or become so out of necessity. [...] In Gemeinschaft they stay together in spite of everything that separates them; in Gesellschaft they remain separate in spite of everything that unites them.
entries.nearest_existing: collectivistic and clannish (group before self; one's own circle), with rooted and family_oriented nearby. Not a near-duplicate: this is a whole way of being bound to people, not a preference.
entries.pair_review: Tönnies' two passages are not equally tempered: Gemeinschaft is described warmly (familiar, comfortable, united for better or worse) and Gesellschaft harshly (out for himself alone, tension against everyone else, gives nothing without an equal trade-off). Under rule 3 both drafts mirror their source, so Gemeinschaft reads as a virtue and Gesellschaft as a vice; that is the source's asymmetry, flagged for Roger rather than evened out. Scope: the Gemeinschaft draft names the institutions (kin, home) while the Gesellschaft draft names none (the fetched passage does not name market, contract or state), which a re-edit could add from the queue notes.
entries.notes: Tönnies' own words in the Harris & Hollis translation (Community and Civil Society, CUP 2001, pp. 17-19, 22-24, 52-54, 257-58), as excerpted on German History Intersections; the excerpt is what was fetched, not the whole book. The excerpt names kinship, descent, mother and child, husband and wife, siblings and the 'domestic community'; it does not mention neighbourhood or the village, so the draft says 'kin and home' rather than the queue note's 'family, village and faith'. Strength: the source is warm and declarative, and the draft keeps that; no hedges to render.
entries.pair_scope_flag: Agree with the writer on both points. Tone: Gemeinschaft warm, Gesellschaft harsh, as in Toennies; kept under the asymmetry rule. Scope: Gemeinschaft names what binds (birth, folk, kin, home); Gesellschaft names only the manner of coexistence and exchange, because the fetched passage names no institution. A re-edit wanting 'market, contract' should fetch a further Toennies passage rather than take them from the queue note, which is not a source. The restored 'peaceably' (entry fix) is Toennies' own qualifier and narrows the tone gap slightly without evening it out.

check_result.reasoning: The neg instructions describe someone who rejects inherited community ties in favor of chosen, contractual, interest-based relationships — a free individual who forms bonds by deliberate choice and merit rather than birth. This maps directly onto Tönnies' own concept of 'Gesellschaft' (society/association), the polar opposite of Gemeinschaft. The best label capturing this is 'gesellschaft' but since we want a natural adjective, 'individualistic' captures much of it, as does 'contractual' or 'cosmopolitan'. However, since the positive label is explicitly Tönnies' Gemeinschaft, the natural antonym in the same theoretical framework is 'gesellschaft_tonnies' or simply 'gesellschaft'. As an adjective, 'individualistic' or 'contractual|transactional' work well. Given the theoretical framing and the neg instructions emphasizing contracts, chosen associations, and rejection of inherited ties, 'gesellschaft' (as the direct Tönnies antonym) or 'individualistic|transactional|cosmopolitan' are all candidates. The antonym score is 4 — this is the textbook direct opposite in Tönnies' own typology.

check_result.reasoning: The neg instructions describe someone who is deep rather than surface-level, consistent rather than changeable, focused rather than scattered, deliberate rather than quick-shifting, and prefers depth over breadth. The positive 'gemini' trait is about superficiality, adaptability, sociability, and constant change. The opposite pole is best captured by 'deep' or 'focused' but more precisely the neg instructions emphasize depth of thought, consistency, and deliberateness — 'deep' captures the intellectual dimension, while 'focused' captures the attentional consistency. 'Deliberate' also fits. However, the most natural single-word antonym to the gemini cluster (skimming, changeable, sociable, witty, surface-level) is 'deep|focused|deliberate'. The strongest candidate is 'deep' as it directly opposes 'skimming the surface,' but 'focused' also strongly opposes the scattered, changeable nature. These are genuinely competitive. The antonym score: gemini is defined by surface-skimming and changeability; the neg pole is depth and consistency — these are clearly opposite but 'gemini' is a somewhat idiosyncratic composite trait, so not a perfect 4.

entries.source_text: [Pew] Generation X (born between 1965 and 1980) [...] [Wikipedia] As children in the 1970s and 1980s, a time of shifting societal values, Gen Xers were sometimes called the "Latchkey Generation", a reference to their returning as children from school to an empty home Xers were dubbed the "MTV Generation" (a reference to the music video channel) and sometimes characterized as slackers, cynical, and disaffected. [...] In 2014, Pew Research provided further insight, describing the cohort as "savvy, skeptical and self-reliant; they're not into preening or pampering, and they just might not give much of a hoot what others think of them. [...] guides regarding managing multiple generations in the workforce describe Gen Xers as: independent, resilient, resourceful, self-managing, adaptable, cynical, pragmatic, skeptical of authority, and as seeking a work-life balance. [...] [Wikipedia, Generation X] Video games, via both arcades and home consoles, were also a major part of childhood entertainment for the first time among Xers. Nirvana singer Kurt Cobain (pictured here in 1992) was called the "voice of Generation X" in the 1990s, playing the same role for this demographic as Bob Dylan and John Lennon played for baby boomers in the 1960s. [...] [Wikipedia, Slacker] "Slacker" became widely used in the 1990s to refer to a type of apathetic youth who were cynical and uninterested in political or social causes. This type became a stereotype for members of Generation X. [...] [Word Smarts, '8 Gnarly Slang Terms Made Popular by Generation X'] Born between baby boomers and millennials, the members of Generation X are marked by unique cultural influences, a rebellious spirit, and distinctive language. This phrase is a great catchall to demonstrate disbelief, skepticism, or dismissiveness, and it works especially well with an eye roll. The 1995 movie Clueless popularized “as if” for the masses, though director Amy Heckerling credits the slang to the LQBTQ+ community Dude For Gen Xers, a dude can be anyone — the word has evolved to be somewhat of a gender-neutral noun. [...] [Word Smarts, 'These Slang Terms Reveal Which Generation You Were Born In'] Generation X includes anyone born from 1965 through 1980. Gen Xers are known for living a somewhat grungier lifestyle than their predecessors, as evidenced by the music that became popular in the late 1980s and early ’90s. This generation popularized terms such as “gnarly” and “phat.” “This rocks” describes something that’s amazing, and slang terms including “dude” and “homeslice” became positive terms of address. [...] [Mental Floss, 'Words Gen X Made Popular'] Gen X, the demographic born between the years 1965 and 1980, was often depicted as relaxed, cynical, and music-loving at their cultural peak in the 1980s and ’90s —and plenty of the slang they used reflects that. [...] [Pew, 'Millennials stand out for their technology use' (2019)] More than nine-in-ten Millennials (93% of those who turn ages 23 to 38 this year) own smartphones, compared with 90% of Gen Xers (those ages 39 to 54 this year), 68% of Baby Boomers (ages 55 to 73) and 40% of the Silent Generation (74 to 91) around three-fourths or more of both Millennials and Gen Xers now report using Facebook (84% vs. 74%, respectively). Boomers and Silents have both increased their Facebook use by double digits since 2015.
entries.nearest_existing: independent / self_reliant / cynical / skeptical: the typed version is the cohort (about 46 to 61 in 2026) with the latchkey childhood and the slacker-skeptic image; plain cynical is distrust of human nature, which the typed version does not claim, and plain self_reliant sees a team as dead weight, which it does not.
entries.notes: Roger, 2026-10-07: the generation descriptions carry the cohort's stereotyped speech, slang and culture, and voice is wanted here; the 36-word allowance applies to the set. Each v2 draft keeps Pew's birth years and the v1 portrait traits that fit, and adds markers of three kinds: a characteristic word or phrase, a medium or habit of communication, a cultural touchstone. Sources that name the cohort and the words explicitly were preferred; the dictionary publishers were out of reach (Merriam-Webster's slang pages and its 'OK boomer' piece sit behind a bot check, HTTP 403; Dictionary.com's article links redirect to a generic index), so the word-level sources are Word Smarts (three generation-labelled slang pieces and a punctuation piece), Mental Floss and Babbel, with Wikipedia and Pew for the media habits and touchstones. All v1 source pieces are kept; every new piece is checked verbatim against the raw page. Markers: 'empty house after school' from Wikipedia 'Generation X' (the latchkey sentence, v1); 'MTV' from the same article's 'MTV Generation' sentence (the channel named, not the nickname); 'grunge' from Wikipedia 'Generation X' (Kurt Cobain called the 'voice of Generation X'; grunge among the genres) and Word Smarts' generations piece ('a somewhat grungier lifestyle'); 'answering with eye-rolls and "as if"' from Word Smarts' Gen X slang piece ('as if' demonstrates disbelief, skepticism, or dismissiveness, 'works especially well with an eye roll', popularized by Clueless, 1995); the portrait traits from v1 (Wikipedia's workforce-guide list and Pew 2014 as quoted there). Not used: 'dude' (Word Smarts, Mental Floss; less specific to the cohort), 'slacker' (Wikipedia 'Slacker': a stereotype for Gen X; the eye-roll clause carries the attitude), arcade and console games (Wikipedia; no room), the French 'Génération Bof' ('bof' = 'whatever'; about France). 'Whatever' itself has no fetched cohort-naming source; if Roger wants it, it would replace 'as if' at equal length. Strength: Mental Floss's 'relaxed, cynical, and music-loving' and Wikipedia's 'slackers, cynical, and disaffected' are the source level; the draft stays there. 36 words.
review_issues: 'turning out independent, skeptical of authority and unconcerned what others think' takes the flattering items (Pew 2014's 'savvy, skeptical and self-reliant', the workforce guides' 'independent') and drops the edge the passage gives twice: 'slackers, cynical, and disaffected' and 'cynical' again in the guides. The writer's note says the kept traits are the ones given twice; cynical is given twice too. Add 'cynical' (replacement given, 32 words). Plain cynical is distrust of human nature, so the overlap stays small, as the nearest-existing line says.

check_result.reasoning: The neg instructions collectively describe someone who defers to authority and institutions, trusts consensus, seeks social approval, embraces enthusiasm without skepticism, and values interdependence over self-reliance. This is the opposite of the cynical, self-reliant, authority-skeptical Gen X persona. The best label capturing this cluster is 'conformist' (deference to authority and social norms) but 'credulous|trusting' also fits the anti-skepticism angle, and 'collectivist' fits the interdependence angle. 'Conformist' best captures the overall opposite pole — deferring to authority, seeking approval, adjusting to consensus. However, 'credulous' captures the anti-cynicism dimension well. 'Conformist' is the strongest single label. The antonym score is 3 rather than 4 because 'gen_x' is a generational identity with multiple dimensions (self-reliance, cynicism, independence, anti-authority), and no single adjective perfectly mirrors all of them in reverse.

entries.label: gen-z
entries.description_draft: This means being born between 1997 and 2012: raised on YouTube and TikTok, smartphone in hand, saying 'no cap' and 'slay', texting without periods, better behaved than earlier teens, and open about mental health.
entries.description_notes: Generational cohort; sequence in birth order. Cohort was folded into age in the first audit; the labels carry speech and culture stereotypes beyond age.
entries.description: This means being born between 1997 and 2012: raised on YouTube and TikTok, smartphone in hand, saying 'no cap' and 'slay', texting without periods, better behaved than earlier teens, and open about mental health.
entries.decision: Accepted 2026-09-08; write the `arrangement` field at seeding

entries.source_text: [Pew] anyone born from 1997 onward is part of a new generation The iPhone launched in 2007, when the oldest Gen Zers were 10. Social media, constant connectivity and on-demand entertainment and communication are innovations Millennials adapted to as they came of age. For those born after 1996, these are largely assumed. [...] [Wikipedia] with the generation typically being defined as people born from 1997 to 2012. Generation Z has been described as "better behaved and less hedonistic" than previous generations. They have fewer teenage pregnancies, consume less alcohol (but not necessarily less of other psychoactive drugs), and are more focused on school and job prospects. [...] There is greater awareness and diagnosis of mental health conditions among Generation Z, and sleep deprivation is more frequently reported. [...] [Wikipedia, Generation Z] Many slang terms of Generations Z and Alpha—such as flex, no cap, slay, or shade—have their roots in African-American vernacular English, and, thanks to the Internet, spread much more rapidly than they otherwise would. At the same time, YouTube has claimed the top spot while Snapchat and Instagram have also made significant gains. During the late 2010s and early 2020s, TikTok exploded in usage among adolescents and has become the second most frequently used platform, surpassing Instagram in 2021. Having a mobile device has become almost universal by the time the first wave of Generation Z reaches adolescence, to such an extent that it is common for them to feel uncomfortable or unsafe without one Speed and reliability are important factors in their choice of social networking platform, and they make frequent use of emojis. [...] [Wikipedia, Glossary of 2020s slang] English-language slang used or popularized in the 2020s, usually by Generation Z or by Generation Alpha, differs from that of earlier generations. cap To lie originating from AAVE. The antonym, "no cap", is typically used after a statement to indicate truthfulness or being genuine. slay To do something well. bussin' Extremely good, excellent. it's giving Used to describe an attitude or connotation. [...] [Word Smarts, 'These Slang Terms Reveal Which Generation You Were Born In'] Gen Zers, also known as “zoomers,” came into the world between 1997 and 2012. For many older adults today, Gen Z slang is enough to make your head spin. But terms such as “cheugy” (“outdated”) and “sus” (“questionable” or “dishonest”) are part of a coded language that these young people share. Another popular series of terms coined by this generation are “cap” (“false”), “no cap” (“true”), and “capping” (“lying”). [...] [Word Smarts, 'How Your Punctuation Habits Reveal Your Age'] Less than one-quarter of Gen Z respondents use punctuation in casual communication, while more than half of baby boomers (55%) report always using it while texting or posting online. Meanwhile, only 16% of Gen Z and 28% of millennials consistently use periods at the end of sentences. [...] [Wikipedia, OK boomer] The phrase first drew widespread attention due to a November 2019 TikTok video in response to an older man, though the phrase had been coined years before that.
entries.nearest_existing: young / plugged_in / well_behaved / risk_averse / health_conscious: young is age alone (teens or twenties); the typed version is the cohort (about 14 to 29 in 2026) with smartphones assumed, the better-behaved-less-hedonistic image, and openness about mental health; plugged_in is on the feeds all day at any age.
entries.notes: Roger, 2026-10-07: the generation descriptions carry the cohort's stereotyped speech, slang and culture, and voice is wanted here; the 36-word allowance applies to the set. Each v2 draft keeps Pew's birth years and the v1 portrait traits that fit, and adds markers of three kinds: a characteristic word or phrase, a medium or habit of communication, a cultural touchstone. Sources that name the cohort and the words explicitly were preferred; the dictionary publishers were out of reach (Merriam-Webster's slang pages and its 'OK boomer' piece sit behind a bot check, HTTP 403; Dictionary.com's article links redirect to a generic index), so the word-level sources are Word Smarts (three generation-labelled slang pieces and a punctuation piece), Mental Floss and Babbel, with Wikipedia and Pew for the media habits and touchstones. All v1 source pieces are kept; every new piece is checked verbatim against the raw page. Markers: 'YouTube and TikTok' from Wikipedia 'Generation Z' (YouTube the top platform, TikTok exploded among adolescents); 'smartphone in hand' from Pew 2019 (the iPhone at 10, constant connectivity 'largely assumed', v1) and Wikipedia (a mobile device almost universal, uncomfortable without one); 'no cap' and 'slay' from Wikipedia 'Generation Z' (slang terms of Generation Z such as flex, no cap, slay, shade, rooted in AAVE), the 'Glossary of 2020s slang' entries, and Word Smarts' generations piece (cap / no cap / capping coined by this generation); 'texting without periods' from Word Smarts' punctuation piece (only 16% of Gen Z consistently use periods; under a quarter use punctuation in casual communication); 'better behaved than earlier teens' and 'open about mental health' from Wikipedia (v1). Not used for room: 'less hedonistic' (v1 wording), 'cheugy', 'sus', 'bussin', 'it's giving' (Word Smarts, the glossary), emojis and Snapchat (Wikipedia), 'OK boomer' as the cohort's retort (Wikipedia 'OK boomer': a November 2019 TikTok video), 'focused on school and work' (v1). Strength: Wikipedia's 'better behaved' is mildly flattering and the draft stays there; the slang is the source's plain list. 34 words.
review_issues: Minor: 'open about mental health' says something the passage does not. Wikipedia has 'greater awareness and diagnosis of mental health conditions' (and more reported sleep deprivation), a statement about awareness and diagnosis, not about talking openly; 'open about' is the popular stereotype imported. 'Attentive to mental health' stays with the passage (replacement given, 32 words).

check_result.reasoning: The neg instructions consistently describe someone who is hedonistic, reckless, heavy-drinking, party-focused, dismissive of mental health, and indifferent to academic/career goals. This maps most naturally onto 'boomer' or 'millennial' generational stereotypes, but as a trait label rather than a generation, the best descriptor is 'hedonistic' — someone who prioritizes pleasure over responsibility and self-care. However, the positive label is 'gen_z' as a generational identity, so the opposite could also be framed as 'boomer' (generationally) or more trait-accurately as 'hedonistic.' Since the definition emphasizes being 'less hedonistic' as a key feature of gen_z, the opposite pole is most cleanly 'hedonistic.' The antonym score is moderate — 'hedonistic' is clearly opposed to the disciplined, wellness-focused, responsible traits of gen_z as defined, but 'gen_z' is a generational label while 'hedonistic' is a personality trait, so it's not a perfect symmetric antonym pair.

entries.label: Gesellschaft (Tönnies)
entries.description_draft: This means living alongside others without being joined to them, out for oneself alone and in tension with everyone else, and giving nothing away except in exchange for at least as much.
entries.description_notes: A person native to a society whose ties are contract, role and interest, who weighs relationships by what they yield and locates themself in profession, market and state. See Gemeinschaft (Tönnies).
entries.description: This means living peaceably alongside others without being joined to them, out for oneself alone and in tension with everyone else, and giving nothing except in exchange for at least as much.
entries.source: Tönnies, Gemeinschaft / Gesellschaft (Durkheim mechanical / organic solidarity is the same axis); https://germanhistory-intersections.org/en/knowledge-and-education/ghis:document-163
entries.decision: decided 2026-09-07
entries.section: Anthropological social structure (decided 2026-09-07)
entries.source_text: The theory of Gesellschaft takes as its starting point a group of people who, as in Gemeinschaft, live peacefully alongside one another, but in this case without being essentially united – indeed, on the contrary, they are here essentially detached. In Gemeinschaft they stay together in spite of everything that separates them; in Gesellschaft they remain separate in spite of everything that unites them. [...] Nothing happens in Gesellschaft that is more important for the individual's wider group than it is for himself. On the contrary, everyone is out for himself alone and living in a state of tension against everyone else. [...] Nobody wants to do anything for anyone else, nobody wants to yield or give anything unless he gets something in return that he regards as at least an equal trade-off.
entries.nearest_existing: transactional (relationships weighed by what they yield) and individualistic; calculating and detached nearby. Not a near-duplicate: transactional is a stance toward dealings, this is the person's whole social world.
entries.notes: Same page and translation as the Gemeinschaft entry, section 'The Theory of Gesellschaft'. Strength: the source is harsh ('out for himself alone', 'tension against everyone else', 'nobody wants to do anything for anyone else') and the draft keeps it at that pitch rather than softening toward 'impersonal' or 'businesslike'; 'live peacefully alongside one another' is rendered as 'living alongside others' (the peacefulness dropped only for length; it qualifies the tension, so a re-edit might restore it). Markedly harsher than the corpus's transactional; noted as the source's doing.
review_issues: Strength, opening clause: Toennies' 'live peacefully alongside one another' is rendered 'living alongside others'; without the qualifier the following 'in tension with everyone else' reads as open hostility, where the source describes the civil, peaceful coexistence of people who are not joined. Restore it (the writer flagged this as a possible re-edit); 'away' trimmed to stay at 32 words.
entries.pair_scope_flag: Agree with the writer on both points. Tone: Gemeinschaft warm, Gesellschaft harsh, as in Toennies; kept under the asymmetry rule. Scope: Gemeinschaft names what binds (birth, folk, kin, home); Gesellschaft names only the manner of coexistence and exchange, because the fetched passage names no institution. A re-edit wanting 'market, contract' should fetch a further Toennies passage rather than take them from the queue note, which is not a source. The restored 'peaceably' (entry fix) is Toennies' own qualifier and narrows the tone gap slightly without evening it out.

check_result.reasoning: The neg instructions describe someone who is communally oriented, selflessly giving, loyal, and bound to others by genuine ties — the opposite of the cold, transactional, self-interested Gesellschaft type. Tönnies himself coined 'Gemeinschaft' as the direct opposite of 'Gesellschaft,' describing exactly this communal, organic solidarity. The best label is 'gemeinschaft_tonnies' to mirror the positive label's naming convention, but as a natural adjective the closest terms are 'communal' or 'altruistic.' Since the positive label uses Tönnies' own terminology, 'gemeinschaft' is the most precise opposite. As a standalone adjective, 'communal' captures the shared-belonging aspect, while 'altruistic' captures the selfless giving. These are genuinely competitive. The antonym score is 4 — Gemeinschaft and Gesellschaft are Tönnies' own paired opposites, making this a perfect conceptual antonym.

entries.label: Gryffindor
entries.description_draft: This means being brave, plucky, daring and determined, with the nerve and chivalry to stand up for the little guy and challenge authority, and a tendency to act first and think later.
entries.description_notes: Hogwarts house; set. Fictional; probably the most LLM-legible personality typology in existence. Folk system: `source` = the system's name; the description paraphrases the conventional portrait and does not name the system (convention rule 4).
entries.description: This means being brave, plucky, daring and determined, with the nerve and chivalry to stand up for the little guy and challenge authority, and a tendency to act first and think later.
entries.decision: Accepted 2026-09-08; write the `arrangement` field at seeding
entries.section: Coverage audit part 4: attitudes, behavior and segmentation (decided 2026-09-08) > Sets and rings (decided 2026-09-08; write the arrangement at seeding)
entries.source_text: Wizarding World, 'What does your Hogwarts house say about you?' (2021-04-28): "Gryffindor house is where you would find the pluckiest and most daring students"; qualities "courage, bravery and determination"; the type of person who "likes to stand up for the little guy, challenges authority, has a tendency to act first and think later". Official fact file: Godric Gryffindor "favoured students who possessed characteristics such as courage, bravery and determination". Wikipedia 'Hogwarts': Gryffindor "values courage, nerve, and chivalry". The Sorting Hat's "dwell the brave at heart" is quoted on the official 'house animal and colours' feature.
entries.nearest_existing: brave / bold / reckless: the typed version is the house portrait, courage plus chivalry (standing up for the little guy) plus the shadow of acting before thinking; brave alone lacks the chivalry and the shadow, reckless lacks the courage's nobility.
entries.set_review: Four members, one grain and shape: the house's virtue list (from the official 2021 feature and fact file, agreeing with Wikipedia's one-line values), then two or three characteristic behaviours from the official feature's 'type of person' list, then the shadow where the source gives one, 31 to 32 words, all 'This means being ...'. Shadows: Gryffindor acts first and thinks later; Slytherin never shows the soft side and minds reputation; Ravenclaw is eccentric and dreamy; Hufflepuff has none in the source (humility is a virtue), so it is the only one without. Strength: all four are flattering by design, markedly more than the corpus's plain traits; Slytherin especially, since the official text ('unfortunate reputation', 'possibly destined for greatness') plays down the villainy the books give the house, and the draft mirrors that rather than the Sorting Hat's 'use any means to achieve their ends', which I could not fetch (Fandom 402; Wikiquote lacks the song). Roger may want Slytherin sharpened toward the book; flagged, not done. The playful list items (best snacks, board games) are omitted as not traits.
entries.notes: Fandom (harrypotter.fandom.com) returns HTTP 402 to this tool and Wikiquote does not carry the Sorting Hat's song, so the song is represented only by the phrases the official site quotes (https://www.harrypotter.com/features/what-your-hogwarts-house-animal-and-colours-could-mean; fact file https://www.harrypotter.com/fact-file/magical-miscellany/gryffindor; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hogwarts). The 2021 feature's jokier items ('class clown', 'takes board games very seriously') are left out. Strength: flattering by design, markedly more so than the corpus's plain brave; the one shadow ('act first and think later') is the source's own.

check_result.reasoning: The neg instructions consistently describe someone who avoids conflict, defers to authority, holds back, keeps their head down, and prioritizes self-preservation over bold action. This is the opposite of brave, daring, and chivalrous. The best labels are 'cowardly' (captures the fear/avoidance aspect) or 'cautious' (captures the risk-aversion) or 'slytherin' (the fictional opposite house, but too niche). 'Cowardly' is the most direct antonym to brave/daring, but the neg instructions also emphasize compliance and deference to authority, which adds a 'submissive' dimension. 'Cautious|cowardly|timid' are all competitive. 'Cowardly' is the strongest antonym to 'gryffindor' as defined, but 'cautious' and 'timid' also fit well. The antonym score is strong but not perfect because 'gryffindor' bundles multiple traits (brave + chivalrous + impulsive) and the neg instructions emphasize caution/compliance more than pure cowardice.

entries.label: high-context (Hall)
entries.description_draft: This means letting the setting and shared history carry most of one's meaning, putting very little into the words themselves, and expecting others to know what is bothering one without being told.
entries.description_notes: Meaning carried by relationship, setting and implication. Expect overlap with blunt / tactful, literal (figurative), circumspect (brash) and enigmatic (straightforward); run the Strategy 1 yield check before judging.
entries.description: This means letting the setting and shared history carry most of one's meaning, putting very little into the words, and expecting others to know what is bothering one without spelling it out.
entries.decision: decided 2026-09-07 (section)
entries.section: Cultural orientation (decided 2026-09-07)
entries.source_text: "A high-context (HC) communication or message is one in which most of the information is either in the physical context or internalized in the person, while very little is in the coded, explicit, transmitted part of the message" (Hall 1976, p. 91). As described by Hall, high-context communication is characteristic of cultures in which people are "deeply involved" with one another and information is widely shared among them (Hall 1976, 39). [...] "When talking about something they have on their minds, a high-context individual will expect others to know what's bothering him, so that he doesn't have to be specific" (Hall 1976, 113).
entries.nearest_existing: cryptic and enigmatic (meaning withheld from the words), with tactful, understated and figurative nearby. Not a near-duplicate: the test is where the meaning sits (setting and shared knowledge), not whether the speaker is being obscure or polite.
entries.pair_review: The high-context draft ends with Hall's sentence about an individual (expects others to know what is bothering him, p. 113); the low-context draft ends with an assumption ('taking for granted that others share little of one's background') built from Hall's remarks about low-context cultures (p. 39: 'highly individualized, somewhat alienated, fragmented') and about encoding (p. 101), not from a sentence about an individual. The two closing clauses therefore rest on unequal sources. The high side also names 'shared history' where the low side mentions only the setting. 'somewhat alienated' was not carried into the low-context draft; a re-edit could render it.
entries.notes: Hall's own definition from Beyond Culture (1976) as quoted with page numbers in Chris Oliver, 'From Class to Culture: Restricted/Elaborated Codes vs. High/Low-context Communication in Basil Bernstein and Edward T. Hall', Sophia University Junior College Division Faculty Journal 37 (2016), 73-83. Wikipedia's article paraphrases Hall but does not quote him; a second handout (https://support.wspa.pl/wp-content/uploads/2020/12/02_Text_Topic-3.2_Cultural-Dimensions-by-E.-T.-Hall.pdf) quotes a variant of the same definition ('already in the person', cited to p. 101) with Hall's twins-versus-lawyers example. Strength: Hall is categorical ('most', 'very little') and the draft keeps those words; 'will expect others to know' rendered as 'expecting others to know'.
review_issues: Strength, closing clause: Hall's 'expect others to know what's bothering him, so that he doesn't have to be specific' is rendered 'without being told', which suggests saying nothing; Hall's person speaks, but not specifically. 'without spelling it out' is the plain equivalent ('themselves' trimmed to stay at 32 words).
entries.pair_scope_flag: Agree with the writer. The closing clauses differ in grain and in source: high-context ends on a specific scenario from Hall's sentence about an individual (what is bothering one); low-context ends on a general assumption assembled from Hall's remarks about low-context cultures and about encoding. High names 'shared history' where low names only the setting. A re-edit could give low-context a matching scenario ('saying outright what is bothering one'), but that would be derived, not sourced, and would need marking as such; the alternative is to leave the asymmetry, which the sources explain. 'somewhat alienated' is rightly not carried on the low side: it is a mood of the culture, and carrying it would add a feelings facet with no high-side counterpart.

check_result.reasoning: The neg instructions consistently describe someone who makes everything explicit in words, states reasons clearly, names problems directly, and leaves nothing for others to infer. This is the classic definition of 'low-context' communication in Hall's framework. The most natural standalone adjective would be 'explicit' or 'direct', but in the context of Hall's cultural communication theory, 'low-context' is the recognized opposite pole. However, as a personality adjective outside the theoretical framework, 'explicit' or 'direct' are strong candidates. Since the positive label itself uses Hall's terminology (high_context_hall), 'low-context' is the most precise and antonymic label. 'Direct' and 'explicit' are also genuinely competitive as standalone descriptors. The antonym score is 4 — these are direct, symmetric opposites in Hall's well-established framework.

entries.label: honest-humble (HEXACO)
entries.description_draft: This means dealing straight with people rather than working them for gain, keeping to the rules even when cheating would pay, caring nothing for riches and luxury, and claiming no special standing.
entries.description_notes: High pole of Honesty-Humility, the genuinely new axis; its low pole is the dark core of the Dark Tetrad literature (line 1617-1619). Paraphrase the two-sided hexaco.org scale description (one sentence for very high scorers, one for very low); the low pole is written from the low-scorer sentence, not as a negation of the high pole; both poles in the 'This means ...' form; the description does not name the source.
entries.description: This means dealing straight with people rather than working them for gain, keeping to the rules even when cheating would pay, caring little for riches and luxury, and claiming no special standing.
entries.source: Ashton & Lee, HEXACO-PI-R, Honesty-Humility scale; https://hexaco.org/scaledescriptions
entries.decision: Roger 2026-09-08: definitely add the Big Five and HEXACO by name as standard-named pairs; pairing fixed by the standard, antonym check informational (the ad-hoc twin showing up is expected, not a failure).
entries.section: Part 1: Big Five and HEXACO by name
entries.source_text: Persons with very high scores on the Honesty-Humility scale avoid manipulating others for personal gain, feel little temptation to break rules, are uninterested in lavish wealth and luxuries, and feel no special entitlement to elevated social status.
entries.nearest_existing: No single corpus trait covers it. Closest: modest ('claiming no special insight or importance'), fair ('refusing any edge gained by cheating'), honest and sincere (truth-telling rather than non-manipulation), and the negatives of greedy and entitled. This is the genuinely new axis: sincerity, fairness, greed avoidance and modesty as one disposition.
entries.pair_review: Facet for facet (sincerity, fairness, greed avoidance, modesty); 32 and 29 words. The high is written as four restraints ('rather than working them', 'even when cheating would pay', 'caring nothing for', 'claiming no'), which follows the source (all four of its clauses are avoidances) but risks reading as an absence beside the low's four active behaviours; the high's sincerity clause also carries a 'rather than' contrast the low has none of. A re-edit could give the high pole positive conduct (paying what is owed, giving credit, living plainly) if Roger wants it to stand on its own.
entries.notes: At the 32-word ceiling.
entries.pair_scope_flag: Agree with the writer (four restraints against four active behaviors; the 'rather than' contrast). Add: 'rather than working them for gain' is the only contrast clause among the 22; rule 5 tolerates it where it picks a sense, and 'dealing straight' can also mean blunt, so it arguably does. The low's 'luxury' is borrowed from the high's source ('lavish wealth and luxuries'), its own saying 'material gain', so the poles share a word their sources do not. If Roger wants positive conduct on the high, 'paying what is owed' or 'living plainly' would do it without changing scope.

check_result.reasoning: The neg instructions collectively describe someone who manipulates others, cheats when advantageous, schemes for more wealth and status, self-aggrandizes, and uses deception and flattery for personal gain. This is the classic profile of someone who is greedy, manipulative, and self-serving. In HEXACO terminology, the opposite of Honesty-Humility is often labeled 'greedy-manipulative' or simply captured by terms like 'manipulative', 'deceitful', or 'self-serving'. The neg instructions emphasize both the manipulative/deceptive dimension and the greed/status-seeking dimension. 'Manipulative' captures the interpersonal deception angle, while 'greedy' captures the acquisitive/status angle. 'Self-serving' captures both reasonably well. These are genuinely competitive candidates. The antonym score is strong (3-4) since these instructions describe the direct opposite pole of the Honesty-Humility factor in HEXACO personality theory.

entries.source_text: Wizarding World (2021-04-28): "Hufflepuff is where you will find the most trustworthy and hardworking students"; "the most humble of all the houses and don't feel the need to shout about their achievements"; the type of person who "has a strong moral compass, always works hard, is the most loyal friend, knows it is the taking part that counts". entries.source_text: The i (Influence) style is active and accepting. This describes people who are outgoing, enthusiastic, and lively. [...] People with DiSC styles at the top of the circle tend to be fast-paced and are often described as assertive, dynamic, and bold. [...] On the other hand, people with styles on the right side of the circle are naturally more receptive in nature and are often described as people-focused, empathizing, and agreeable.
entries.nearest_existing: extroverted / gregarious / energetic / cheerful / charismatic: the typed version is the fast-paced-and-accepting quadrant, extroversion plus agreeableness; plain extroverted lacks the agreeable stance (and is about energy from company), cheerful lacks the pace.
entries.notes: Primary source is the publisher's (Wiley, Everything DiSC) own page, since the four labels are the publisher's names; the fuller style pages with priorities and motivators (discprofile.com/what-is-disc and its overview-styles PDF) returned HTTP 403 to every fetch, so they are not quoted. A search-engine snippet of that page (unverified, not used in the draft) listed the D style's priorities as getting immediate results, taking action, challenging self and others; i as expressing enthusiasm, taking action, encouraging collaboration; S as giving support, maintaining stability, enjoying collaboration; C as ensuring accuracy, maintaining stability, challenging assumptions. Marston 1928, Emotions of Normal People (public domain; full text at https://archive.org/stream/emotionsofnormal0000mars/emotionsofnormal0000mars_djvu.txt), names the four primary emotions dominance, inducement, submission and compliance on two axes, alliance vs antagonism of the stimulus and superiority vs inferiority of the self's strength; dominance is "chiefly characterized by victory of the motor self over an antagonist of inferior intensity", inducement introspectively "a process of persuading someone, in a friendly way, to perform an act suggested by the subject", submission the bodily attitude of "an obedient child toward a loving mother", compliance that "the subject is moving himself at the dictates of a superior force". Wikipedia's gloss (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DISC_assessment): "Dominance: active use of force to overcome resistance in the environment Inducement: use of charm in order to deal with obstacles Submission: warm and voluntary acceptance of the need to fulfill a request Compliance: fearful adjustment to a superior force." The modern S and C differ from Marston's submission and compliance, so his text is background, not the summarised source. Strength: flattering in the source (outgoing, enthusiastic, lively), flattering in the draft.

check_result.reasoning: The neg instructions consistently describe someone who is slow-paced, skeptical, data-driven, emotionally reserved, keeps people at distance, questions enthusiasm, and resists social momentum. The positive label is about being fast-paced, accepting, enthusiastic, people-focused, and agreeable. The opposite pole is best captured by 'reserved|skeptical|cautious' — but looking at the full cluster: reserved captures the interpersonal distance, skeptical captures the questioning stance, and analytical captures the data-over-feelings orientation. The neg instructions emphasize skepticism and deliberateness most strongly. 'Skeptical' is a strong candidate, as is 'reserved|analytical'. Since the positive trait combines social boldness with acceptance/agreeableness, the opposite combines social withdrawal with skepticism. 'Reserved|skeptical' best captures this dual opposition. The antonym score is 3-4: the neg instructions are clearly designed as the opposite pole of this DISC 'Influence' style, making this a strong antonym relationship.

The dominant theme across all five is a lack of independent, strategic, goal-directed thinking — replaced by conformity, impulsivity, and aimlessness. 'Conformist' captures the social deference aspect, while 'scattered|impulsive' captures the lack of focus and planning. 'Dependent' captures the need for external validation. No single word perfectly captures all five dimensions, but 'conformist' vs. 'independent' is the strongest single axis, with 'scattered' also being very relevant. Quoting sources: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3858239, https://tidsskrift.dk/psyke/article/download/8652/7225/27413 (Jan Tønnesvang, 'Religiøsitetens selvobjektfunktionalitet & tilknytningsdimensioner', Psyke & Logos 24 (2003), 778-805, which quotes the English with British spelling 'endeavours'), https://selfdeterminationtheory.org/wp-content/uploads/2014/04/2010_NeyrinckLensetal_JSSR.pdf. 'Other needs, strong as they may be, are regarded as of less ultimate significance' (the usual continuation) was not found verbatim on any fetched page and is not in source_text; 'fitting one's other needs around it' renders Neyrinck's gloss of it. Strength: the source is strong and unhedged ('master motive', 'follow it fully') and so is the draft.
entries.pair_scope_flag: Agree with the writer: extrinsic lists five concrete payoffs (Allport's own nouns) while intrinsic stays at the level of motive (master motive, other needs fitted around it, creed internalized) and names none of the religious contents the gloss offers (humility, compassion). Both close on how the creed is held, so the closings are parallel; the difference is concreteness, not scope or trigger. A re-edit would either give intrinsic one concrete habit from the gloss or trim extrinsic to three payoffs. Both drafts rest on fragments (the 1967 paper was not fetchable), extrinsic on more and shorter ones; provenance is honestly recorded on both sides.

check_result.reasoning: The neg instructions describe someone who uses religion instrumentally — for comfort, social belonging, status, or respectability — rather than as a master motive. This is precisely Allport's concept of 'extrinsic' religious orientation, where religion serves the self rather than the self serving religion. The term 'extrinsic' is the canonical psychological antonym here (from Allport's own framework), but in plain language 'instrumental' also captures it well. Since this is a psycholinguistics dataset referencing Allport's framework, 'extrinsic' is the most natural and recognizable label. These are direct opposites within Allport's own theoretical framework, making this a near-perfect antonym pair.

entries.source_text_fragments_2026-10-07: Allport & Ross (1967), as quoted by fetchable scholarly sources: at the intrinsic end are those who "find their master motive in religion" (p. 434; Bulbulia, Osborne & Sibley 2013, PLoS ONE); "Having embraced a creed the individual endeavours to internalize it and follow it fully. It is in this sense that he lives his religion" (p. 434; Tønnesvang 2003, Psyke & Logos). Gloss in Neyrinck et al. 2010 (JSSR): "An intrinsically oriented person considers religion as an ultimate end in itself; it is a master motive in life. Religious beliefs and values (e.g., humility, compassion, etc.) are internalized 'without reservation,' and other needs and goals are accommodated, reorganized, and brought in harmony with these religious contents. Importantly, an intrinsic religious orientation 'floods the whole life with motivation and meaning' (Allport 1966:455)."

entries.source_text: Killers get their kicks from imposing themselves on others. [...] Much more commonly, people attack other players with a view to killing off their personae (hence the name for this style of play). The more massive the distress caused, the greater the killer's joy at having caused it. Normal points-scoring is usually required so as to become powerful enough to begin causing havoc in earnest, and exploration of a kind is necessary to discover new and ingenious ways to kill people. [...] They're all just means to an end, though; only in the knowledge that a real person, somewhere, is very upset by what you've just done, yet can themselves do nothing about it, is there any true adrenalin-shooting, juicy fun.
entries.nearest_existing: bullying / cruel / ruthless_while_playing / competitive: ruthless_while_playing does for advantage in fiction what it would not do for real; the killer's object is not advantage but the other player's real distress. Bullying and cruel are the real-life cousins; the typed version is confined to play. Competitive wants to win; the killer wants the victim upset.
entries.notes: Bartle 1996, 'Hearts, clubs, diamonds, spades: players who suit MUDs', Journal of MUD Research 1(1); the author's own page, fetched raw and quoted from it. Axes in Bartle's words: "The x-axis goes from an emphasis on players (left) to an emphasis on the environment (right); the y-axis goes from acting with (bottom) to acting on (top)." Bartle's quadrant glosses: "Achievers are interested in doing things to the game, ie. in ACTING on the WORLD." and "Explorers are interested in having the game surprise them, ie. in INTERACTING with the WORLD." The omitted sentence allows a 'nice' busybody variant that Bartle himself dismisses as rare. 'Characters' for Bartle's 'personae'. Strength: Bartle's paragraph is strong (joy at distress, a real person very upset and helpless) and the draft keeps it; the one Bartle member that is a vice.
review_issues: 'the greater the distress caused the better' loses the passage's sharpest point: the joy is in 'a real person, somewhere, is very upset by what you've just done, yet can themselves do nothing about it'. After 'killing their characters' the distress reads as the character's or the game's. The writer's own nearest-existing line makes the real-person point against ruthless_while_playing (where nothing counts for real); the description should make it too (replacement given, 31 words).

check_result.reasoning: The neg instructions describe someone who lifts others up, protects the vulnerable, seeks win-win outcomes, and shows generosity and care rather than predatory dominance. The opposite of a predatory 'killer' player type in Bartle's taxonomy is the 'socializer' who cares about others, but the neg instructions more broadly describe someone who is nurturing, protective, and prosocial. The best label capturing this opposite pole is 'nurturing' or 'prosocial' — but given the gaming context and the explicit focus on protecting/uplifting others rather than crushing them, 'nurturing|prosocial' are both strong candidates. The antonym score is high because the neg instructions are a near-perfect mirror of the pos instructions.

entries.label: loose (Gelfand)
entries.description_draft: This means holding only weak rules of conduct, leaving people to decide for themselves how to behave in most situations, and putting up readily with behavior that steps well outside the usual.
entries.description_notes: Weak norm expectations and tolerance of deviance in others; see tight (Gelfand). [Corrected 2026-10-08: see pair_scope_decision; the distinction from conformist is by content (what one expects of norms and how one lives under them), not by excluding the persona's own conduct.]

entries.decision: decided 2026-09-07 (section)
entries.section: Cultural orientation (decided 2026-09-07)
entries.source_text: With data from 33 nations, we illustrate the differences between cultures that are tight (have many strong norms and a low tolerance of deviant behavior) versus loose (have weak social norms and a high tolerance of deviant behavior). Tightness-looseness is part of a complex, loosely integrated multilevel system that comprises distal ecological and historical threats (e.g., high population density, resource scarcity, a history of territorial conflict, and disease and environmental threats), broad versus narrow socialization in societal institutions (e.g., autocracy, media regulations), the strength of everyday recurring situations, and micro-level psychological affordances (e.g., prevention self-guides, high regulatory strength, need for structure).
entries.nearest_existing: permissive and lenient (what one lets others get away with), with easygoing and laid_back nearby. Not a near-duplicate: permissive is about one's own allowing; this is how strong one expects the rules to be at all.
entries.pair_review: Both drafts come from the same two parentheses, so scope matches on the first and third clauses (strength of rules; tolerance of deviance). The middle clauses differ in origin: tight's 'wanting structure and self-restraint' renders the abstract's micro-level affordances (need for structure, prevention self-guides, regulatory strength), which have no loose-side counterpart in the text; loose's 'leaving people to decide for themselves' renders 'broad socialization', which has no tight-side clause. The tight self-restraint clause also brushes against the queue note's warning that this axis is norm enforcement in others, not one's own compliance (conformist); Roger may want it cut or reworded toward sanctioning others.
entries.notes: Abstract of Gelfand et al., 'Differences between tight and loose cultures: a 33-nation study', Science 332 (2011), 1100-1104 (doi 10.1126/science.1197754), fetched through Europe PMC's REST API; PubMed (cookie wall) and europepmc.org's HTML page (HTTP 403) could not be fetched, and science.org was not tried. Gelfand's lab site (michelegelfand.com) has no definitional text beyond 'more restrictive or permissive norms'. The abstract's definition of each pole is one parenthesis, so the drafts are thin by construction; the loose draft's middle clause renders 'broad socialization' and weak 'everyday recurring situations' as a person's habit. Strength: the source is a flat comparative ('weak', 'high tolerance'); 'only weak' and 'readily' carry that, no sharpening.
entries.pair_scope_flag: Agree with the writer, and would put it more sharply. Tight has four clauses, one of them self-directed ('wanting structure and self-restraint', from the abstract's prevention self-guides and need for structure); loose has three, all about others. The self-directed clause is faithful to the abstract but sits on the conformist side of the line the queue note draws (norm enforcement in others, not own compliance), and loose has no counterpart ('caring little for structure' would be the derived one). A re-edit would either cut tight's fourth clause or add the loose counterpart; this is the one scope question in the sub-chunk that needs Roger's call. Both middle clauses individualise system-level items of the abstract (situational strength; broad socialization) and are where the drafts go furthest beyond the two parentheses; needed for length, since the parentheses alone give about 15 words a side.

check_result.reasoning: The neg instructions describe someone who enforces strict rules, maps out situations in advance, corrects deviations, deliberates carefully, and maintains explicit structure. This is the classic 'tight' pole in Gelfand's tight-loose cultural dimension. The most natural label is 'tight_gelfand' to mirror the positive label, but as a standalone adjective, 'strict' or 'rule-bound' also work. However, since the positive label is 'loose_gelfand', the direct antonym in this framework is 'tight_gelfand'. As a general adjective, 'strict' is the most recognizable standalone word, but 'rigid' also fits. The opposition is essentially perfect within the Gelfand framework — tight vs. loose are defined as direct opposites.
