claims_and_agreement.claim: Lower self-regulatory strength and impulse control; greater impulsivity.
Lower need for structure; comfort with ambiguity, novelty and disorder.

sources.citation: Gelfand, M. J., Raver, J. L., Nishii, L., et al. (2011). Differences between tight and loose cultures: A 33-nation study. Science, 332(6033), 1100-1104. Fetched as the author manuscript on Cornell eCommons (the file the search labelled as the 2006 paper). The Supporting Online Material was NOT fetched: science.org returns a JavaScript challenge page for both the article and the SOM.
used: Accordingly, individuals in nations with high situational constraint will have self-guides that are more prevention-focused (16) and thus will be more cautious (concerned with avoiding mistakes) and dutiful (focused on behaving properly), and will have higher self-regulatory strength (higher impulse control) (17), a higher need for structure (18), and higher self-monitoring ability (19, 20). Put simply, the higher (or lower) degree of social regulation that exists at the societal level is mirrored in the higher (or lower) amount of self-regulation at the individual level in tight and loose nations, respectively.
Weak situations place few external constraints on individuals, afford a wide range of behavioral options, and leave much room for individual discretion.

Hierarchical linear modeling intercept-as-outcomes models showed that higher levels of situational constraint are significantly related to greater prevention self-guides [higher cautiousness ...; higher dutifulness ...], greater self-regulation strength [higher impulse control ...], higher needs for structure [...], and higher self-monitoring [...] (23).

sources.citation: Harrington, J. R., & Gelfand, M. J. (2014). Tightness-looseness across the 50 united states. PNAS, 111(22), 7990-7995. Fetched from PubMed Central.
used: Looseness has previously been linked to greater impulsivity, reduced cautiousness, and decreased self-regulatory strength (15). Study 3 also demonstrated that loose states have lower conscientiousness, a personality variable associated with the ability to delay gratification and engage in deliberate, well-planned behavior (26). Consequently, state-level outcomes that reflect greater behavioral impulsivity and less self-control should be higher in loose compared with tight states.

In contrast, localities with lower threat can afford more unconstrained behavior and more flexible norms, promoting greater openness and less need for conscientiousness, prevention-focus, and impulse control.

sources.citation: Gelfand, M. J., Nishii, L. H., & Raver, J. L. (2006). On the nature and importance of cultural tightness-looseness. Journal of Applied Psychology, 91(6), 1225-1244. Fetched as the pre-publication CAHRS Working Paper WP07-05 (Cornell ILR DigitalCommons) hosted on Gelfand's site; the published JAP text is paywalled and was not fetched.
used: We extend this theory by proposing that individuals in tight societies generally have higher self-regulatory strength than individuals in loose societies. Individuals in tight societies, who have higher felt accountability, engage in more frequent monitoring of their behavior vis-à-vis social norms, are more attentive to discrepancies from norms, and have more intense negative self-reactions when their behavior errs from standards, as compared to individuals in loose societies. Put simply, the high (low) degree of social regulation at the societal level is mirrored in the high (low) amount of self-regulation at the individual level in tight and loose societies, respectively.

Individuals who have a high promotion focus (Crowe & Higgins, 1997; Friedman & Forster, 2001; Levine, Higgins & Choi, 2000), positive attitudes toward errors (Rybowiak, Garst, Frese, & Batinic, 1999), and an openness to experience (George & Zhou, 2001)—all attributes we expect to be cultivated in loose societies—tend to engage in more risk-taking and innovative behavior. Individuals who seek predictability and order, by contrast, tend to avoid ambiguous and novel situations (e.g., Moskowitz, 1993; Neuberg & Newsom, 1993), and are generally less creative (George & Zhou, 2001).

sources.citation: Gelfand, M. J., & Lun, J. (2013). The culture of the situation: The role of situational strength in cultural systems. Asian Journal of Social Psychology (commentary on Bond). Hosted on Gelfand's site; restates the 2011 individual-level findings.
used: individuals who face stronger situations (and, thus, continually experience more limited behavioural options and greater scrutiny and social evaluation of their actions) have self-guides that are more prevention-focused, have higher self-regulatory strength (i.e. higher impulse control), a higher need for structure, and higher self-monitoring ability.

sources.citation: Gelfand, M. J. (2018). Rule Makers, Rule Breakers: How Tight and Loose Cultures Wire Our World. Scribner. The book itself was not fetched; these are Gelfand's own words in a Psychology Today interview about the book (Marianna Pogosyan, 'A Big Picture Look at Social Rules', December 2018).
used: For example, tight cultures have more order, synchrony, uniformity, self-regulation, impulse control and less crime. Loose cultures struggle with this. They are disorganized, have little synchrony and self-regulation. But while tight cultures struggle with openness, loose cultures are much more tolerant of a wide range of people, more open to different ideas and change, more creative.

For example, an individual's mindset (tight vs. loose) can help them fit into strong or weak norms. If you live in a country where there are very loose norms, you need to have a lot of tolerance for ambiguity. In tight cultures, it's the opposite: You need to have strong self-monitoring to detect norms. There is a constellation of personality differences that reinforce and maintain the strength of norms, so personality and culture are intricately connected.

alternatives_not_taken: B: promotion focus ('aiming at gains rather than at avoiding mistakes, and acting on impulse'), 4 primary sources
C: openness to change and low self-monitoring ('open to new ideas and change, and seldom watching one's own conduct')

entries.label: low-context (Hall)
entries.description_draft: This means putting the mass of one's meaning into the explicit words, spelling out whatever the setting does not supply, and taking for granted that others share little of one's background.
entries.description_notes: Meaning carried by explicit words; see high-context (Hall).

entries.decision: decided 2026-09-07 (section)
entries.section: Cultural orientation (decided 2026-09-07)
entries.source_text: "A low-context (LC) communication is just the opposite; i.e., the mass of the information is vested in the explicit code" (Hall 1976, p. 91). [...] low-context communication is said by Hall to be characteristic of "highly individualized, somewhat alienated, fragmented cultures" (Hall 1976, 39). Thus, whereas high-context messages can be verbally abbreviated and compact, low-context messages involve a greater use of explicit code to provide the conveyance of meaning. Precisely because there is less "pre-programmed" information shared between participants in low-context communication, most of the information "must be [encoded] in the transmitted message in order to make up for what is missing in the context" (Hall 1976, 101).
entries.nearest_existing: plain_spoken and literal (meaning in the words as said), with blunt, forthright and clear nearby. Not a near-duplicate: plain_spoken is about manner; this is about where the information is put, whatever the manner.
entries.notes: Same source as high-context (Oliver 2016 quoting Hall 1976, pp. 91, 39, 101); the second and third sentences of source_text are Oliver's connecting prose around Hall's quoted phrases, kept so the quoted fragments are not isolated. Strength: Hall's 'the mass of the information' is kept as 'the mass of one's meaning'; the clause about others sharing little background renders 'highly individualized ... fragmented' and 'what is missing in the context' without the hedge 'somewhat', which is flagged in the pair review.
entries.pair_scope_flag: Agree with the writer. The closing clauses differ in grain and in source: high-context ends on a specific scenario from Hall's sentence about an individual (what is bothering one); low-context ends on a general assumption assembled from Hall's remarks about low-context cultures and about encoding. High names 'shared history' where low names only the setting. A re-edit could give low-context a matching scenario ('saying outright what is bothering one'), but that would be derived, not sourced, and would need marking as such; the alternative is to leave the asymmetry, which the sources explain. 'somewhat alienated' is rightly not carried on the low side: it is a mood of the culture, and carrying it would add a feelings facet with no high-side counterpart.

check_result.reasoning: The neg instructions describe someone who relies on implicit meaning, shared context, unspoken cues, and relational/situational understanding rather than explicit words. This is precisely the concept of 'high-context' communication in Hall's framework. The direct antonym in Hall's own terminology is 'high_context_hall,' but as a natural adjective the best label is 'high-context' or more broadly 'implicit.' Since this is Hall's framework and the positive label uses 'low_context_hall,' the natural opposite pole label is 'high_context_hall' or simply 'implicit|indirect.' The neg instructions emphasize implicitness, indirectness, and reliance on shared context — 'implicit' and 'indirect' are both strong candidates. However, within Hall's framework, 'high-context' is the canonical term. I'll use 'high_context_hall' to mirror the positive label's naming convention, with 'implicit|indirect' as alternatives. The antonym score is 4 — these are direct, symmetric opposites in Hall's communication model.

check_result.reasoning: The neg instructions consistently describe someone who outsources tasks, spends freely, values brand names and status symbols, replaces rather than repairs, and prioritizes convenience and prestige over self-sufficiency and durability. The clearest labels for this opposite pole are 'consumerist' (focused on buying, spending, status goods) or 'status-conscious.' 'Consumerist' captures the outsourcing, spending, and replacement-over-repair behaviors well. 'Status-conscious' captures the brand/prestige dimension. These two are genuinely competitive. The opposition to maker_vals (practical, self-sufficient, DIY, modest) is strong but not perfectly symmetric — 'consumerist' is a fairly direct opposite to the DIY/frugal cluster, though maker_vals also includes a social/relational dimension (close family ties) that consumerist doesn't perfectly mirror.

entries.source_text: [Pew] Anyone born between 1981 and 1996 (ages 23 to 38 in 2019) is considered a Millennial, and anyone born from 1997 onward is part of a new generation. [...] [Wikipedia] elevated familiarity with the Internet and technology in general, and usage of early social media platforms such as AOL Instant Messenger, LiveJournal, and Myspace. [...] Twenge attributes millennials with the traits of confidence and tolerance, but also describes a sense of entitlement and narcissism [...] with many facing high levels of youth unemployment, student debt, and childcare costs in the wake of the Great Recession [...] Across the globe, millennials and subsequent generations have postponed marriage or living together as a couple. [...] [Wikipedia, Millennials] Second-wave millennials are nostalgic for the childhood culture of the early 2000s, such as SpongeBob SquarePants, Samurai Jack, Kim Possible, Pokemon, Lizzie McGuire, the Harry Potter series, and the Game Boy Advance. In 2008, author Ron Alsop called the millennials "Trophy Kids", a term that reflects a trend in competitive sports, as well as many other aspects of life, where mere participation is frequently enough for a reward. Many millennial parents document the childhood and growth of their children on social media platforms such as Instagram and Facebook. [...] [Wikipedia, Avocado toast] In Australia in late 2016, consumption of avocado smashed on toast became a target of criticism after columnist Bernard Salt in The Australian wrote an article about how "young people order smashed avocado with crumbled feta on five-grain toasted bread at $22 a pop and more", arguing that they should be saving to buy a house instead. The article made headlines internationally and became a stereotype of the millennial generation. Tim Gurner, a 35-year-old Australian property developer, stated in May 2017 that millennials should not be buying smashed avocado and $4 lattes in their pursuit of home ownership. [...] [Mental Floss, 'Millennial Slang: 16 Terms You Should Totes Know'] If you still use terms like adulting, doggo, and YOLO, you may be a Millennial. These terms popularized by the generation were inescapable in the 2000s and 2010s. As the youngest millennials entered young adulthood over the next decade , the term exploded in popularity. Though it often appears in a tongue-in-cheek context, it’s been used to reinforce negative stereotypes of Millennials being lazy and immature. [...] [Word Smarts, 'These Slang Terms Reveal Which Generation You Were Born In'] Millennials, the more popular term for Gen Y, are people born from 1981 to 1996. The rise of this generation coincided with the rise of the internet, so many slang terms are the initialisms that developed out of internet culture: “BRB” (“be right back”), “OMG” (“oh my god”), “TBH” (“to be honest”), among others. Millennials are also responsible for coining words such as “bae” (to talk about their significant other) and “slay” (to praise someone doing something exceptionally well). You may also hear a millennial use “adulting” when behaving responsibly, “keeping it 100” when being real and truthful, or “getting swole” when lifting weights at the gym. This generation may also feel serious “FOMO,” which means a “fear of missing out.” [...] [Word Smarts, 'How Your Punctuation Habits Reveal Your Age'] millennials have a habit of ending sentences with "lol," while baby boomers might trail off with an ellipsis ("How are you…"). [...] [Pew, 'Millennials: Confident. Connected. Open to Change' (2010)] They embrace multiple modes of self-expression. Three-quarters have created a profile on a social networking site. One-in-five have posted a video of themselves online. Nearly four-in-ten have a tattoo [...] [Pew, 'Millennials stand out for their technology use' (2019)] Similarly, the vast majority of Millennials (86%) say they use social media, compared with smaller shares among older generations. around three-fourths or more of both Millennials and Gen Xers now report using Facebook (84% vs. 74%, respectively). Boomers and Silents have both increased their Facebook use by double digits since 2015.
entries.nearest_existing: confident / plugged_in / financially_precarious / early_adopter: the typed version is the cohort (about 30 to 45 in 2026) shaped by the internet's arrival and the 2008 recession; plugged_in is on the feeds all day at any age, financially_precarious is a present condition not a cohort history.
entries.notes: Roger, 2026-10-07: the generation descriptions carry the cohort's stereotyped speech, slang and culture, and voice is wanted here; the 36-word allowance applies to the set. Each v2 draft keeps Pew's birth years and the v1 portrait traits that fit, and adds markers of three kinds: a characteristic word or phrase, a medium or habit of communication, a cultural touchstone. Sources that name the cohort and the words explicitly were preferred; the dictionary publishers were out of reach (Merriam-Webster's slang pages and its 'OK boomer' piece sit behind a bot check, HTTP 403; Dictionary.com's article links redirect to a generic index), so the word-level sources are Word Smarts (three generation-labelled slang pieces and a punctuation piece), Mental Floss and Babbel, with Wikipedia and Pew for the media habits and touchstones. All v1 source pieces are kept; every new piece is checked verbatim against the raw page. Markers: 'AOL Instant Messenger, Myspace' from Wikipedia 'Millennials' (early social media platforms, v1 piece); 'Harry Potter' from the same article's nostalgia sentence (second-wave millennials; the Harry Potter series); 'recession with student debt' from Wikipedia and Pew 2019 (v1); 'brunching on avocado toast' from Wikipedia 'Avocado toast' (Salt's column 'became a stereotype of the millennial generation'; Gurner on smashed avocado and $4 lattes); 'calling chores "adulting"' from Mental Floss ('If you still use terms like adulting, doggo, and YOLO, you may be a Millennial') and Word Smarts' generations piece ('adulting' when behaving responsibly); 'confident, tolerant and entitled' from Wikipedia's Twenge sentence, 'entitled' now in by Roger's decision (Mental Floss adds that 'adulting' reinforces the lazy-and-immature stereotype). Not used for room: ending texts with 'lol' (Word Smarts punctuation piece), the initialisms BRB/OMG/TBH, 'bae' and 'FOMO' (Word Smarts), 'Trophy Kids' / participation trophies and Instagram parenting (Wikipedia), social-network profiles and tattoos (Pew 2010). 'AIM' is spelled out as 'AOL Instant Messenger' so a judge or generator knows the medium. Dropped from v1: 'early to social media' (now concrete as the platforms) and 'slow to marry'. Strength: the entitlement claim is contested in the source (Twenge vs. Arnett); stated plainly per Roger. 36 words.
review_issues: 'confident and tolerant' keeps half of Twenge's one clause and drops the other half, 'but also describes a sense of entitlement and narcissism'. The writer's reason is that a critic in the Wikipedia article (outside the recorded passage) contests Twenge; but the critic disputes her reading of the data, which bears on the confident-and-tolerant half as much as on the dropped half, so keeping one half is a one-sided cut, and the queue wants the cohort's stereotype, of which 'entitled' is the best-known item. The description is a portrait; the empirical dispute belongs in notes. Recommend 'entitled' in (replacement given, 32 words). Roger's call, as the writer flagged.

If 'entitled' goes in, add plain entitled (expecting the best table, the exception and other people's time as one's due) to the nearest-existing line: the cohort version is a generation's stereotype, not a personal demand, so the overlap is partial.

check_result.reasoning: The neg instructions consistently describe someone who predates the internet era, values stability and traditional life sequences (job→marriage→house→children), defers to authority, distrusts social media, holds conservative social values, and lived through a stable economy. This profile maps most naturally onto a 'baby boomer' generational identity, though 'traditionalist' also captures the values dimension. The opposition is generational/cohort-based, so 'boomer' is the most direct counterpart to 'millennial' as a generational label. However, since the neg instructions blend generational identity with attitudinal conservatism, 'traditionalist' is also competitive. The antonym score is moderate-to-strong: 'boomer' is a generational opposite but not a perfect semantic antonym in the way 'hot/cold' are — it's a different category member rather than a true polar opposite on a single dimension.

entries.description_draft: This means doing one thing at a time, organizing life around tasks, schedules and procedures, treating time as a thing to be saved, spent, wasted or lost, and keeping to the clock.
entries.description_notes: One thing at a time with schedules binding. Proxies: methodical / improvisational, urgent (relaxed), impatient / patient; yield check first.

entries.section: Cultural orientation (decided 2026-09-07)
entries.source_text: M-time, on the other hand, is oriented to tasks, schedules, and procedures. As anyone who has had experience with our bureaucracies knows, schedules and procedures take on a life all their own without reference to either logic or human needs. ...M-time is also tangible; we speak of it as being saved, spent, wasted, lost, made up, crawling, killed, and running out (pp. 43, 50). [Hall & Hall 1990, p. 15, monochronic actions:] Do one thing at a time; Concentrate on the job; Take time schedules seriously; Are low context and need information; Are committed to the job; Adhere strictly to plans; Are concerned about not disturbing others and follow rules of privacy; Show great respect for private property; rarely borrow or lend; Emphasize promptness; Are accustomed to short-term relationships.
entries.nearest_existing: methodical (one step at a time, in order) and organized; focused, efficient and hurried nearby. Not a near-duplicate: methodical is about how a task is done, this is about how time itself is held (segmented, scheduled, tangible).
entries.pair_review: The polychronic draft is entirely from the 1983 passage; the monochronic draft needed the 1990 table for 'one thing at a time' and 'keeping to the clock' because Hall's M-time paragraph is shorter and partly an aside. Scope differs in one place: polychronic ends with 'hearing people out, schedule or no schedule' (Hall's 'cannot cut them off simply because of a schedule'), to which the M-time text gives no counterpart, and monochronic's 'tangible time' clause has a P-time counterpart ('seldom feeling that time is wasted') that is present. Tone: Hall writes P-time warmly ('if you value people') and M-time drily ('bureaucracies'); the drafts carry a trace of that.
entries.notes: Hall's own words from The Dance of Life (1983), pp. 43 and 50, as quoted on Michael Kearl's Trinity University page 'The Times of Our Lives: Cultural Rhythms' (the first part of source_text, verbatim including the page's ellipses). The bracketed list is Hall & Hall, Understanding Cultural Differences (1990), p. 15, as reproduced in the WSPA handout https://support.wspa.pl/wp-content/uploads/2020/12/02_Text_Topic-3.2_Cultural-Dimensions-by-E.-T.-Hall.pdf ('adapted from Hall and Hall'); it supplies 'one thing at a time' and promptness, which the 1983 passage states only for P-time by contrast. Hall's aside that M-time schedules 'take on a life all their own without reference to either logic or human needs' is about bureaucracies and was not turned into a habit of the person; a re-edit could add it ('even when they serve no one'), which would make the pole harsher. Strength: as the source, matter-of-fact, no hedges.
entries.pair_scope_flag: Agree with the writer. Scope: monochronic is about tasks, schedules and the clock, polychronic about people and the business at hand; that is Hall's own task-versus-people contrast, not an accident. The one unmatched clause is polychronic's 'hearing people out, schedule or no schedule', to which the M-time text gives no counterpart (the 1990 list's 'concerned about not disturbing others' is the nearest and is a different thing). Tone: a trace of Hall's warmth toward P-time and dryness toward M-time, as in the source. Both drafts take 'one thing at a time' / 'many things at once' from the 1990 table, and only the monochronic entry's source_text records its line (see the polychronic entry's notes).

check_result.reasoning: The neg instructions describe someone who does multiple things simultaneously, flows with events rather than the clock, holds plans loosely, and embraces overlap and interruption. This is precisely what Hall called 'polychronic' time orientation — the direct academic opposite of 'monochronic.' The term 'polychronic' is the established antonym in the same theoretical framework. It is a perfect, symmetric opposite within Hall's cultural time model.

entries.description_draft: This means being neither warm nor demanding with one's children: rarely supervising, disciplining or asking maturity of them and, beyond food and shelter, paying little attention to what they feel or do.

entries.description: This means being neither warm nor demanding with one's children: rarely supervising, disciplining or asking maturity of them and, beyond food and shelter, paying little attention to what they feel or do.

entries.source_text: Uninvolved parents are low in both responsiveness and demandingness. In extreme cases, this parenting style might encompass both rejecting-neglecting and neglectful parents, although most parents of this type fall within the normal range. [...] Parental responsiveness (also referred to as parental warmth or supportiveness) refers to "the extent to which parents intentionally foster individuality, self-regulation, and self-assertion by being attuned, supportive, and acquiescent to children's special needs and demands" (Baumrind, 1991, p. 62). Parental demandingness (also referred to as behavioral control) refers to "the claims parents make on children to become integrated into the family whole, by their maturity demands, supervision, disciplinary efforts and willingness to confront the child who disobeys" (Baumrind, 1991, pp. 61-62). [...] [Wikipedia, Parenting styles] They may provide basic necessities such as food, shelter, and clothing, but they do not indulge their children's emotions or opinions.
entries.nearest_existing: neglectful (plain: leaving those in one's care to fend for themselves, no notice of harm) / hands_off / absentee / uncaring: the typed version is the parent low on both warmth and demands, within the normal range per the source, so markedly milder than plain neglectful; plain neglectful is the nurturing pair's vice, this is a quadrant.
entries.notes: Maccoby & Martin 1983 (Handbook of Child Psychology vol. 4) is not open online; quoted as presented in Nancy Darling, 'Parenting Style and Its Correlates', ERIC Digest ED427896 (1999), which attributes the four-fold typology and the uninvolved corner to them ("Categorizing parents according to whether they are high or low on parental demandingness and responsiveness creates a typology of four parenting styles: indulgent, authoritarian, authoritative, and uninvolved (Maccoby & Martin, 1983).") and gives Baumrind 1991's definitions of the two dimensions. The PDF's text layer had no spaces; spaces were restored by hand and the quotes checked against the extracted text with spaces removed. Secondary (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parenting_styles): 'The parent is not responsive and not demanding.' and 'Neglectful parenting, also known as uninvolved, detached, dismissive, or hands-off parenting, is characterized by a lack of warmth and control. Neglectful parents are unaware of what their children are doing, and if they find out, they feel indifferent towards them. They may provide basic necessities such as food, shelter, and clothing, but they do not indulge their children's emotions or opinions.' The draft's 'beyond food and shelter' comes from this. FLAG for Roger: the scholarly source is a placement (low on both) with a hedge ('most parents of this type fall within the normal range'), so the draft is mild, as the strength rule requires; Wikipedia's version is stronger (unaware, indifferent). The draft's 'rarely supervising, disciplining or asking maturity of them' is Baumrind 1991's demandingness list (maturity demands, supervision, disciplinary efforts) negated. The queue's label 'neglectful' is Maccoby & Martin's; Darling's is 'uninvolved'.
review_issues: Record, not description (suggested_edit left null so the draft stands): 'beyond food and shelter' comes from Wikipedia's Parenting styles article ('They may provide basic necessities such as food, shelter, and clothing'), quoted in notes but absent from source_text and source_url. Add that sentence and the URL to the record; the clause is a good concrete particular and should stay.

check_result.reasoning: The neg instructions describe a parent who is both warm/emotionally present AND demanding/structured — monitoring behavior, setting expectations, disciplining, and responding to emotions. In Baumrind's framework, this is the classic 'authoritative' parenting style, which is the direct opposite of neglectful (uninvolved) parenting. 'Authoritative' is the most precise and recognizable label from the same theoretical framework. 'Engaged' is also a strong candidate from everyday language. The opposition is nearly perfect — neglectful parenting is defined by low warmth + low demandingness, while authoritative is high warmth + high demandingness.

The ad-hoc file is anxiety, worry, instability and reactivity in abstract nouns; this one is the six facets as behaviour, adding anger, depression, self-consciousness and impulsiveness. check_result.reasoning: The neg instructions describe someone who is calm under pressure, emotionally stable, resilient to stress, unflappable, and not ruled by impulses or moods. This is the classic opposite pole of neuroticism in Big Five personality theory, which is 'emotional stability.' However, 'resilient' is also a strong candidate. In psycholinguistics and personality research, the standard antonym pole for neuroticism is 'emotionally stable' or simply 'stable.' 'Calm' is also competitive. The most recognized label in personality psychology for the low-neuroticism pole is 'emotionally stable,' but as a single adjective 'stable' or 'resilient' works well. These are genuinely competitive, so I'll list the main candidates. The antonym score is 4 — this is the textbook direct opposite pole of neuroticism.

check_result.reasoning: The neg instructions consistently describe someone who is practical, routine-oriented, conventional, and resistant to new experiences or abstract thinking. They prefer the familiar, trust established customs, dismiss emotions and daydreaming, and only engage with ideas that have concrete utility. The Big Five opposite pole of Openness to Experience is standardly labeled 'closed to experience' or 'conventional.' However, 'conventional' captures the preference for the familiar and established, while 'closed' is the direct technical antonym. 'Practical' also fits strongly given the emphasis on utility over speculation. Since multiple labels are genuinely competitive here, I'll list the strongest candidates.

entries.nearest_existing: open (Big Five) is the twin by design; this one follows the four HEXACO facets (aesthetic appreciation, inquisitiveness, creativity, unconventionality), so it has no feelings or values content and leans to art, nature and oddity. Also near: aesthete, curious, creative, eccentric, absorption_prone.
entries.notes: At the 32-word ceiling.
entries.pair_scope_flag: Agree with the writer. The inquisitiveness facet is where the drafts miss each other: 'wanting to know how everything works' turns breadth across domains of knowledge into mechanism-curiosity, and 'feeling no itch to learn for its own sake' answers motive, not breadth; a re-edit could put both on the source's breadth. The low's 'leaving painting, writing and invention to others' shares its frame with closed (Big Five)'s 'leaving ideas to others'.

check_result.reasoning: The neg instructions consistently describe someone who prefers the familiar, conventional, practical, and mainstream — avoiding strangeness, complexity, and unconventional thinking. The opposite of openness to experience in HEXACO/Big Five is typically labeled 'closed-minded' or 'conventional' or 'unreceptive'. 'Conventional' captures the preference for tradition, routine, and mainstream thinking well. 'Closed-minded' is also a strong candidate as it directly opposes open-mindedness. Both are genuine competitors here. The antonym score is high — openness vs. closedness/conventionality is a well-established personality dimension opposition, essentially a 4.

entries.label: permissive (Baumrind)
entries.description_draft: This means accepting one's children's impulses rather than punishing them: asking little in chores or tidiness, letting them regulate themselves, and being a resource to draw on, not an authority to obey.
entries.description_notes: Baumrind parenting style on warmth × control; square. Suffixed because plain authoritarian is queued in the political sense. (The file's 'authoritarian Baumrind' lacks the parentheses; read as a line-wrap typo.)
entries.description: This means accepting one's children's impulses rather than punishing them: asking little in chores or tidiness, letting them regulate themselves, and being a resource to draw on, not an authority to obey.
entries.decision: Accepted 2026-09-08; write the `arrangement` field at seeding

entries.source_text: The permissive parent attempts to behave in a nonpunitive, acceptant and affirmative manner towards the child's impulses, desires, and actions. She [parent] consults with him [child] about policy decisions and gives explanations for family rules. She makes few demands for household responsibility and orderly behavior. She presents herself to the child as a resource for him to use as he wishes, not as an ideal for him to emulate, nor as an active agent responsible for shaping or altering his ongoing or future behavior. She allows the child to regulate his own activities as much as possible, avoids the exercise of control, and does not encourage him to obey externally defined standards. She attempts to use reason and manipulation, but not overt power to accomplish her ends
entries.nearest_existing: permissive (plain: letting sex, drink, drugs and foul language pass) / lenient / hands_off: the typed version is the parent accepting a child's impulses and making few demands; plain permissive is tolerance of vice, lenient is keeping the bar low for people generally, hands_off is walking away from delegated work.
entries.notes: Baumrind 1966, p. 889, as quoted on the same teaching page. 'A resource to draw on, not an authority to obey' renders 'presents herself to the child as a resource for him to use as he wishes, not as an ideal for him to emulate' and 'does not encourage him to obey externally defined standards'; 'chores or tidiness' renders 'household responsibility and orderly behavior'. Left out at 32 words: 'consults with him about policy decisions' and 'uses reason and manipulation, but not overt power'. Strength: Baumrind's permissive is written neutrally (acceptant, affirmative, few demands) and the draft matches; it is milder than the corpus's lenient.

check_result.reasoning: The neg instructions consistently describe a parent who sets clear rules, enforces standards, assigns chores, disciplines consistently, and expects obedience — this is the authoritarian or strict parenting style in Baumrind's framework. 'Authoritarian' is the most technically precise term from Baumrind's own typology (the direct opposite pole), but 'strict' is also a natural everyday label that captures the same concept. Both are strong candidates. The opposition is very strong — permissive vs. authoritarian are canonical opposites in Baumrind's parenting typology.

entries.source_text: "A person whose primary Love Language® is Physical Touch™ is, not surprisingly, very touchy. Hugs, pats on the back, holding hands, and thoughtful touches on the arm, shoulder, or face – they can all be ways to show excitement, concern, care, and love. Physical presence and accessibility are crucial, while neglect or abuse can be unforgivable and destructive. Physical touch fosters a sense of security and belonging in any relationship."
entries.nearest_existing: flirty / clingy / emotionally_engaged: none is close; the typed version is the channel of affection, touch, with neglect as its wound, and carries no claim of sexuality or dependence.
entries.notes: 'Can be unforgivable' rendered as 'is unforgivable', the plain-word equivalent for the person who feels it. 'Appropriate' touch, which the site's one-liner stresses, is not a trait and is left out. Strength: as the source, warm with one wound.
review_issues: 'very touchy' (the passage's one description of the person's own behaviour: 'is, not surprisingly, very touchy') is dropped; the draft keeps only the receiving side. Restoring it is optional: Roger may prefer the set's uniform receiver-only form.
'neglect or abuse can be unforgivable' rendered as 'neglect is unforgivable': 'abuse' dropped (fine) and Chapman's 'can' rendered flat, as across the set; see the love-languages set review.

check_result.reasoning: The neg instructions consistently describe someone who avoids physical contact, maintains personal space, finds touch unnecessary or uncomfortable, and prefers non-tactile forms of connection. The most natural label for this pole is 'touch-averse' or simply 'distant.' 'Touch-averse' captures the specific discomfort with physical contact, while 'distant' is broader. Since the positive trait is specifically about physical touch as a love language, 'touch-averse' is the most precise opposite. However, 'physically distant' or 'non-tactile' are also reasonable. The antonym relationship is strong and direct — one pole craves touch, the other avoids it.

entries.source_text: Keywords: intuitive, dreamy, artistic, humane, sympathetic, sensitive, compassionate, perceptive, tender, impressionable. Sun in Pisces: As the twelfth and last sign of the zodiac, Pisces contains within itself a little experience of all the signs. This gives Pisces Suns the ability to identify with people from all walks of life—from all backgrounds—in some way. These individuals are not only changeable and adaptable, but they also have open minds and tremendous understanding. [astrology.com, Pisces page, https://www.astrology.com/zodiac-signs/pisces] "They may take certain comments too much to heart and get easily wounded emotionally"
entries.nearest_existing: empathetic / sentimental / intuitive / thin_skinned (also ethereal, compassionate, mystical): the sign is empathy as porousness, taking on others' moods and identifying with anyone, dreamy rather than practical; the plain empathetic understands others without dissolving into them.
entries.notes: Element water, modality mutable. Source fallback as for the set (Wikipedia's Pisces (astrology) article has no portrait); cross-check astrology.com/zodiac-signs/pisces: 'selfless, spiritual, and very focused on their inner journey', 'intuition ... highly evolved', 'dreams and secrets', 'illusory world'; weaknesses 'get easily wounded emotionally', 'escapism, self-medication, and avoidance', 'codependent'. 'Easily wounded' comes from the cross-check and from the keyword 'impressionable' (also rendered 'taking on the moods around one'); 'spiritual' and 'escapism' did not fit at 32. Strength: Cafe Astrology's keywords are all flattering or neutral ('impressionable' the only soft fault), so the draft is gentle and milder than the cross-check's escapism and codependence; flag for Roger (with Capricorn and Leo).

check_result.reasoning: The neg instructions consistently describe someone who is rational, fact-based, emotionally detached, thick-skinned, concrete-minded, and quick to judge — the opposite of the dreamy, empathic, permeable, open Pisces archetype. The best single label capturing this cluster is 'rational' or 'analytical,' but the emotional detachment and impermeability are equally central, making 'detached' and 'hard-headed' competitive. 'Rational|analytical|detached' captures the main poles. As an antonym to Pisces (dreamy, intuitive, empathic, open), this is a strong but not perfectly symmetric opposition — Pisces is a composite trait and the neg pole hits most but not all dimensions cleanly.

entries.description_draft: This means doing many things at once, putting people and the business at hand before a preset schedule, seldom feeling that time is wasted, and hearing people out, schedule or no schedule.
entries.description_notes: Several things at once with relationships ahead of appointments; see monochronic (Hall).

entries.decision: decided 2026-09-07 (section)
entries.section: Cultural orientation (decided 2026-09-07)
entries.source_text: P-time stresses involvement of people and completion of transactions rather than adherence to preset schedules. ... For polychronic people, time is seldom experienced as "wasted," and is apt to be considered a point rather than a ribbon or a road, but that point is often sacred. ...Polychronic cultures are by their very nature oriented to people. Any human being who is naturally drawn to other human beings and who lives in a world dominated by human relationships will be either pushed or pulled toward the polychronic end of the time spectrum. If you value people, you must hear them out and cannot cut them off simply because of a schedule. [Hall & Hall 1990, p. 15, monochronic actions:] Do one thing at a time; Concentrate on the job; Take time schedules seriously; Are low context and need information; Are committed to the job; Adhere strictly to plans; Are concerned about not disturbing others and follow rules of privacy; Show great respect for private property; rarely borrow or lend; Emphasize promptness; Are accustomed to short-term relationships.
entries.nearest_existing: improvisational (plans changed as one goes) and distractible; unhurried, spontaneous and other_focused nearby. Not a near-duplicate: improvisational is about method; this is about several things and several people held at once, with the schedule yielding to them.
entries.notes: Hall's own words, The Dance of Life (1983), pp. 43 and 50, as quoted on the Trinity page (verbatim, with the page's ellipses). 'Doing many things at once' is from the Hall & Hall 1990 table ('Do many things at once'; see the monochronic entry's notes), since the 1983 passage names involvement and completion rather than simultaneity. Strength: 'seldom' kept as 'seldom'; 'you must hear them out and cannot cut them off' rendered as 'hearing people out, schedule or no schedule', the same strength in plain words; 'often sacred' not carried (length). [2026-10-07: the Hall & Hall 1990 table line behind 'doing many things at once' appended from the monochronic entry's record, per the reviewer.]
entries.pair_scope_flag: Agree with the writer. Scope: monochronic is about tasks, schedules and the clock, polychronic about people and the business at hand; that is Hall's own task-versus-people contrast, not an accident. The one unmatched clause is polychronic's 'hearing people out, schedule or no schedule', to which the M-time text gives no counterpart (the 1990 list's 'concerned about not disturbing others' is the nearest and is a different thing). Tone: a trace of Hall's warmth toward P-time and dryness toward M-time, as in the source. Both drafts take 'one thing at a time' / 'many things at once' from the 1990 table, and only the monochronic entry's source_text records its line (see the polychronic entry's notes).

check_result.reasoning: The neg instructions describe someone who works sequentially (one thing at a time), guards their schedule strictly, cuts conversations when time is up, and treats interruptions as disruptions. This is the classic 'monochronic' orientation in Hall's time theory — the direct theoretical opposite of polychronic. The term 'monochronic' is the established antonym in the same framework. It could also be described as 'sequential' or 'schedule-driven', but 'monochronic' is the precise theoretical counterpart. Since the positive label itself uses Hall's terminology (polychronic_hall), monochronic is the perfect paired opposite.

entries.label: postconventional (Kohlberg)
entries.description_draft: This means working out for oneself the principles of rights and justice one judges by, and holding them valid apart from any group's authority and from one's loyalty to that group.
entries.description_notes: Kohlberg's three levels of moral reasoning as a three-corner set (the file says 'three-corner'; 'triangle' is this extraction's reading, a sequence is also conceivable).
entries.description: This means working out for oneself the principles of rights and justice one judges by, and holding them valid apart from any group's authority and from one's loyalty to that group.
entries.decision: Optional three-corner set, accepted 2026-09-08, low priority

entries.source_text: 3. Postconventional, Autonomous, or Principled Level. At this level, there is a clear effort to define moral values and principles which have validity and application apart from the authority of the groups or persons holding these principles and apart from the individual's own identification with these groups. [...] Stage 5. The Social Contract Legalistic Orientation. [...] Right action tends to be defined in terms of general individual rights and in terms of standards which have been critically examined and agreed upon by the whole society. [...] Stage 6. The Universal Ethical Principle Orientation. Right is defined by the decision of conscience in accord with self-chosen ethical principles [...]. At heart, these are universal principles of justice [...] and of respect for the dignity of human beings as individual persons.
entries.nearest_existing: principled (holds to principles; this pole is where the principles come from and that they stand above any group's authority); also moral_universalist, autonomy_respecting, deontological, utilitarian, nonconformist.
entries.notes: 'Rights and justice' summarizes the two stages' content (individual rights and critically examined standards; universal principles of justice and human dignity); 'the individual's own identification with these groups' rendered as 'one's loyalty to that group'. The stage-5 hedge 'tends to be defined' is not carried because the level sentence, which the draft follows, has none. Source: Marcus David Feak, 'Moral Development and its Explanation: Kohlberg's Structuralism', MA thesis (Philosophy), McMaster University, August 1979, pp. 3-5, which reproduces Kohlberg's chart 'Definition of Moral Stages' in full and cites it '(1972, 296-297)', i.e. Kohlberg, L., 'Relativity and Indoctrination in Value Education', Zygon 7 (Spring 1972), 285-309, per the thesis bibliography. Kohlberg's own publications of this chart (Zygon 1972; J. Phil. 1973, 630-646; Phi Delta Kappan 1975; Kohlberg & Hersh, Theory Into Practice 1977) are all paywalled, so a quoting scholarly source is used, as the packet allows. The thesis PDF is a scan; its OCR was cleaned for source_text (hyphenation joined; 'ac~!on' -> 'action', 'group pr nation' -> 'group or nation', 'persons or groups or group' -> 'persons or group', 'mora I v1tlues' -> 'moral values', 'tenTIS' -> 'terms', 'Le alistic' -> 'Legalistic', 'Oritntation' -> 'Orientation', 'respect 0 the dig-jljty' -> 'respect for the dignity'; the Stage 3 heading is illegible in the OCR and is supplied from the second reproduction). British spellings ('favours', 'behaviour') are the thesis's. Second reproduction, same chart with an extra Stage 0 and small wording differences ('the individual perceives the maintenance of the expectations of his family...', 'The individual makes a clear effort to define...'): https://xenodochy.org/ex/lists/moraldev.html (Ralph Kenyon, personal site, naming its source as Kohlberg's chapter in M. C. Reynolds (ed.), Psychology and the Process of Schooling in the Next Decade: Alternative Conceptions, c. 1971); a Prince Sultan University handout PDF has the same text. Scholarly paraphrase cross-check: W. C. Crain (1985), Theories of Development, ch. 7, HTML copy at https://www.appstate.edu/~steelekm/classes/psy2664/kohlberg.htm (its Kohlberg quotations are about stages, not levels). Not reachable: the Kohlberg 1976 passage on the three levels as 'three different types of relationships between the self and society's rules and expectations' (Hockenbury textbook table host unreachable; Sage Encyclopedia of Educational Theory and Philosophy paywalled; the SEP 'Moral Psychology: Empirical Approaches' entry does not discuss Kohlberg). Wikipedia 'Lawrence Kohlberg's stages of moral development' paraphrases the levels (citing Kohlberg 1971, 1976 and Colby & Kohlberg 1987) and has no verbatim level text.

check_result.reasoning: The neg instructions describe someone who derives moral standards from group membership, defers to community consensus, and views departing from group norms as presumptuous or disloyal. This is the hallmark of Kohlberg's 'conventional' stage of moral reasoning, where right and wrong are defined by group loyalty, social norms, and institutional authority. The best label for this is 'conventional' in the Kohlberg sense, but as a standalone adjective it could also be called 'conformist' or 'group-conforming'. 'Conventional' is the most technically precise antonym within Kohlberg's framework, while 'conformist' is the most natural everyday adjective. These are genuinely competitive candidates. The antonym score is very high — postconventional vs. conventional (or conformist) is a direct, well-defined opposition within the same theoretical framework.

entries.source_text: 1. Preconventional Level. At this level the child is responsive to cultural rules and labels of good and bad, right or wrong, but interprets these labels in terms of either the physical or hedonistic consequences of action (punishment, reward, exchange of favours) or in terms of the physical power of those who enunciate the rules and labels. [...] Stage 1. The Punishment and Obedience Orientation. [...] Stage 2. The Instrumental Relativist Orientation. Right action consists of that which instrumentally satisfies one's own needs and occasionally the needs of others. Human relations are viewed in terms like those of the market place. [...] Reciprocity is a matter of "you scratch my back and I'll scratch yours", not of loyalty, gratitude or justice.
entries.nearest_existing: expedient and transactional (self-interested conduct and dealing; this pole is a basis of moral judgment: right is what pays or what the powerful demand); also selfish, amoral, gain_seeking, obedient (deference to power).
entries.notes: The source says 'the child'; the trait is any person reasoning this way, so the draft drops the age. 'Physical or hedonistic consequences (punishment, reward, exchange of favors)' rendered as 'what it brings oneself, whether punishment, reward or a favor returned'; 'the physical power of those who enunciate the rules' as 'the power of whoever lays down the rule'. check_result.reasoning: The neg instructions describe someone who acts on principle regardless of personal cost, follows rules because they are right, treats others fairly without expectation of return, and holds consistent standards in public and private. This is the opposite of preconventional (self-interested, punishment/reward-based) moral reasoning. The best label for this pole is 'principled' or 'postconventional' in Kohlberg's framework, but as a natural adjective the neg instructions most clearly describe someone who is 'principled' — acting from internalized moral principles rather than self-interest. entries.source_text: Secure - It is relatively easy for me to become emotionally close to others. I am comfortable depending on others and having others depend on me. I don't worry about being alone or having others not accept me. [Model: positive self / positive partner; 'The secure style of attachment is characterized by low anxiety and low avoidance'.]
entries.nearest_existing: trusting (trusts what people say; this pole is comfort with closeness and mutual dependence, and no worry about being left or unaccepted); also self_assured, happily_partnered (a status, not a style), emotionally_engaged.
entries.notes: Hedge kept: 'relatively' (the distributed RQ drops it: 'It is easy for me'). Source: Wikipedia, 'Attachment measures', section on Bartholomew and Horowitz, which reproduces the four 1991 prototype paragraphs verbatim under the names Secure / Dismissive / Preoccupied / Fearful and cites Bartholomew, K. & Horowitz, L. M. (1991), 'Attachment styles among young adults: a test of a four-category model', JPSP 61, 226-244. The paper itself is not openly hosted (PubMed 1920064 served only a cookie page; no open PDF found) and Bartholomew's SFU self-report page is a 404, so this reproduction stands in for it. The Wikipedia article 'Attachment in adults', which the packet names, no longer carries the paragraphs: its raw wikitext (fetched today) has only the sentence that its style descriptions are based on the RQ. Second source, the questionnaire as distributed: R. Chris Fraley's measures page (University of Illinois), https://labs.psychology.illinois.edu/~rcfraley/measures/rq.html, styles A-D with no names (psytests.org/ipl/rqen-bl.html has the identical text). The distributed RQ drops some of the paper's hedges: A reads 'It is easy for me' (paper: 'relatively easy'); B reads 'I am uncomfortable getting close' and 'I worry that I will be hurt' (paper: 'somewhat uncomfortable', 'I sometimes worry'). The draft keeps the paper's hedges, as the packet asks. Names: the paper uses secure / fearful / preoccupied / dismissing (so also Cozzarelli et al. 2003, UCSB Close Relationships Lab PDF); Wikipedia 'Attachment measures' uses Secure / Fearful / Preoccupied / Dismissive; the queue's labels are the hybrid names. The two axes: Wikipedia 'Attachment measures' maps model of self to attachment anxiety and model of partner to avoidance: secure low/low, preoccupied high anxiety/low avoidance, dismissive low anxiety/high avoidance, fearful high/high.

check_result.reasoning: The neg instructions describe two somewhat distinct patterns: instructions 1, 3 describe avoidant attachment (keeping distance, resisting closeness, treating intimacy as a trap), while instructions 2, 4, 5 describe anxious/preoccupied attachment (fear of rejection, clinginess, need for reassurance, feeling unwanted). These are the two classic insecure attachment styles. The overarching label that covers both is 'insecure_attachment,' but since we need a single adjective or short phrase, 'insecure' captures the opposite pole well. However, the neg instructions are split between avoidant and anxious patterns, so 'anxious|avoidant' could also be listed as the two poles. The best single-word antonym to 'secure_attachment' is 'insecure' — this is the standard psycholinguistic opposite used in attachment theory. The antonym score is very high since secure vs. insecure attachment are the canonical opposites in attachment theory.

entries.description_draft: This means giving high priority to protecting the environment, accepting foreigners, gays and lesbians, treating women and men as equals, and demanding a say in economic and political decisions.

entries.source_text: Self-expression values give high priority to environmental protection, growing tolerance of foreigners, gays and lesbians and gender equality, and rising demands for participation in decision-making in economic and political life.
entries.nearest_existing: progressive (the nearest single trait), with environmental, inclusive, egalitarian, feminist, gay_affirming and pro_immigration each covering one clause. Not a deliberate duplicate: this bundles four commitments the corpus holds separately, as the instrument does.
entries.pair_review: The two sources are not mirror images: self-expression lists four commitments (environment, tolerance of foreigners and gays and lesbians, gender equality, participation); survival has three (economic and physical security, an ethnocentric outlook, low trust and tolerance), and only tolerance appears on both sides. The survival draft also carries two hedges ('somewhat', 'little') where the self-expression draft has none, because the WVS writes 'relatively ethnocentric' and 'low levels'; survival thus reads milder and vaguer than self-expression. A re-edit could not add security to self-expression or the environment to survival without going beyond the source.
entries.notes: Same WVS page as the other Inglehart-Welzel entries. Strength: 'high priority' kept; 'growing tolerance' rendered 'accepting' (tolerance is the source's word, and 'welcoming' would sharpen it); 'rising demands for participation' rendered 'demanding a say'. No hedges in the source and none in the draft. The queue note treats postmaterialism as identical to this pole; the WVS text does not use the word, so nothing was added for it.
entries.pair_scope_flag: Agree with the writer: the two WVS sentences are not mirror images (four commitments against three attitudes, only tolerance on both sides); survival carries the hedges 'somewhat' and 'little' because the source does, and reads milder and vaguer. Nothing can be added to either side from the source. Added: survival's ethnocentric clause is unclear as written (entry fix); with it clarified, the pair's remaining asymmetry is the source's. Lengths 29 vs 24 follow the sources.

check_result.reasoning: The neg instructions consistently describe someone focused on physical/economic security, deference to authority, suspicion of outsiders, conformity to traditional norms, and distrust of participation — this is precisely the 'survival values' pole in Inglehart & Welzel's framework, directly opposed to 'self-expression values.' The most natural label is 'survival-oriented' or simply 'survivalist,' but in the Inglehart-Welzel framework the canonical term is 'survival values.' As an adjective, 'survival-oriented' or 'authoritarian|traditional' also fit. The neg instructions blend traditionalism, authoritarianism, and survival orientation. The best standalone adjective capturing the opposite pole is 'survival-oriented,' though 'traditional|authoritarian' are also competitive. The antonym score is 4 because this is the direct, canonical opposite pole in the same theoretical framework.

entries.description_draft: This means flattering people to get what one wants, breaking a rule whenever it pays, chasing money and luxury, and carrying oneself as someone who matters more than others.
entries.description_notes: Low pole of Honesty-Humility, from the authors' low adjectives: sly, deceitful, greedy, pretentious, hypocritical, boastful, pompous. Paraphrase the two-sided hexaco.org scale description (one sentence for very high scorers, one for very low); the low pole is written from the low-scorer sentence, not as a negation of the high pole; both poles in the 'This means ...' form; the description does not name the source.
entries.description: This means flattering people to get what one wants, ready to break a rule when it pays, out for whatever one can gain, and acting as if one matters more than others.
entries.source: Ashton & Lee, HEXACO-PI-R, Honesty-Humility scale; https://hexaco.org/scaledescriptions
entries.decision: Roger 2026-09-08: definitely add the Big Five and HEXACO by name as standard-named pairs; pairing fixed by the standard, antonym check informational (the ad-hoc twin showing up is expected, not a failure).
entries.alternatives: deceitful (HEXACO), self-serving (HEXACO)
entries.section: Part 1: Big Five and HEXACO by name
entries.source_text: Conversely, persons with very low scores on this scale will flatter others to get what they want, are inclined to break rules for personal profit, are motivated by material gain, and feel a strong sense of self-importance.
entries.nearest_existing: manipulative, scheming and deceitful are the sincerity facet; rule_breaking and unfair the fairness facet; greedy and materialistic the greed facet; arrogant, grandiose, entitled and self_aggrandizing the modesty facet. No single file has the four together; this is the dark core the queue describes. 'Sly' is the first of Ashton & Lee's low adjectives; the description carries the whole pole, not cunning alone.
entries.notes: The source's 'are inclined to' and 'are motivated by' are rendered as outright behaviour ('breaking a rule whenever it pays', 'chasing money and luxury'), per the vice rule.
entries.pair_scope_flag: Agree with the writer (four restraints against four active behaviors; the 'rather than' contrast). Add: 'rather than working them for gain' is the only contrast clause among the 22; rule 5 tolerates it where it picks a sense, and 'dealing straight' can also mean blunt, so it arguably does. The low's 'luxury' is borrowed from the high's source ('lavish wealth and luxuries'), its own saying 'material gain', so the poles share a word their sources do not. If Roger wants positive conduct on the high, 'paying what is owed' or 'living plainly' would do it without changing scope.

check_result.reasoning: The neg instructions describe someone who is honest and plain-spoken (not flattering), rule-abiding even when unobserved, indifferent to wealth/status, treats others as equals, and is straightforward rather than manipulative. This is the opposite of the sly/Machiavellian/manipulative pole. The best labels are 'sincere' (capturing the honesty and non-flattering aspect), 'honest', or 'principled' (capturing rule-following and integrity). 'Sincere' maps well against the flattery/manipulation dimension. However, 'principled' captures the rule-following and integrity aspects. The HEXACO construct being opposed here is the H factor (Honesty-Humility) — the positive pole of that factor. The neg instructions collectively describe someone who is honest, humble, and non-greedy. 'Honest' or 'sincere|principled' are strong candidates. Given the breadth (honesty, humility, fairness, integrity), 'sincere|principled' captures it well. The antonym score: sly vs. sincere/principled is a strong opposition — these are clearly opposite poles of the Honesty-Humility dimension.

entries.description_draft: This means being ambitious, shrewd, cunning and proud, always one step ahead and using any means to achieve one's ends, minding one's reputation, and never letting anyone see one's soft side.
entries.description_notes: Hogwarts house; set. Fictional; probably the most LLM-legible personality typology in existence. Folk system: `source` = the system's name; the description paraphrases the conventional portrait and does not name the system (convention rule 4).
entries.description: This means being ambitious, shrewd, cunning and proud, always one step ahead and using any means to achieve one's ends, minding one's reputation, and never letting anyone see one's soft side.
entries.decision: Accepted 2026-09-08; write the `arrangement` field at seeding
entries.section: Coverage audit part 4: attitudes, behavior and segmentation (decided 2026-09-08) > Sets and rings (decided 2026-09-08; write the arrangement at seeding)
entries.source_text: Sorting Hat's song (Philosopher's Stone, ch. 7), quoted in Wizarding World's 'The Wizarding Songbook' (2015-12-09, https://www.harrypotter.com/features/the-wizarding-songbook-hogwarts-greatest-hits): "Or perhaps in Slytherin / You'll make your real friends, / Those cunning folk use any means / To achieve their ends." Goblet of Fire song, quoted by the Harry Potter Lexicon (https://www.hp-lexicon.org/thing/sorting-hat-songs/, 'Harry's Fourth Year'): "And power-hungry Slytherin / loved those of great ambition". Wizarding World house feature (2021-04-28): "ambitious, shrewd and possibly destined for greatness"; "is always one step ahead, has a dark sense of humour, thinks reputation is important, takes pride in their appearance and doesn't let anyone see their soft side". Official fact file: "characters defined by cunning, pride and ambition". Wikipedia: "values ambition, cunning, leadership, and resourcefulness."
entries.nearest_existing: ambitious / ends_justify_means / calculating / scheming / guarded: the typed version is the house portrait, ambition and cunning worn with pride and a guarded front, and the Hat's 'any means' now puts it beside ends_justify_means and calculating; it differs in being a whole character (reputation, pride, the hidden soft side, the 'real friends' of one's own house) rather than a single moral stance, and the source still does not call it villainy.
entries.notes: Sharpened toward the books at Roger's request (2026-10-07): the Hat's 'use any means to achieve their ends' is now in the description, displacing the 2021 feature's 'dark sense of humour' and 'pride in appearance' for length; 'possibly destined for greatness' is still dropped. The Hat's line was found on the official site's 2015 songbook feature and on the Harry Potter Lexicon's songs page (whose transcription reads 'cunning folks', plural; the official site has 'cunning folk', which is used); Wikipedia's Hogwarts article (and its Slytherin redirect), the 'Magical objects in Harry Potter' article and Wikiquote's Philosopher's Stone, Goblet of Fire and Order of the Phoenix pages carry no Sorting Hat lines; Fandom returns 402. The Goblet of Fire line is recorded from the Lexicon only, since the official page does not carry it. Strength: now at the books' level, markedly less flattering than the other three houses' drafts, which stay at the official site's level; the set keeps its shape (virtues, behaviours, shadow) but Slytherin now carries two shadows (any means; hidden soft side). Supersedes the 'flagged, not done' remark in the Hogwarts set_review on gryffindor in drafts_d3_sets.json. The other three houses are unchanged. 31 words. US spelling throughout (no 'humour' remains in the draft).
review_issues: Faithful to the recorded official passage, and that is the problem: the packet names the Sorting Hat's descriptions first for this folk system, and the Hat's 'Those cunning folk use any means / To achieve their ends' (Philosopher's Stone, ch. 7; Goblet of Fire's song adds 'power-hungry Slytherin loved those of great ambition') is the canonical popular portrait and the most LLM-legible line about the house. Without it the draft is a flattering 'ambitious, shrewd' type that sits on top of the corpus's ambitious plus guarded, and its shadows (minds reputation, hides the soft side) weigh less than Gryffindor's 'act first and think later'. Recommend sharpening: 'This means being ambitious, shrewd, cunning and proud, always one step ahead and using any means to achieve one's ends, minding one's reputation, and never letting anyone see one's soft side.' (31 words; 'dark sense of humor' and 'appearance' give way.)

The Hat's line must first be recorded in source_text from a fetchable page (the writer could not: Fandom 402, Wikiquote lacks the song); Wikipedia's 'Hogwarts' article, already a recorded source, may carry it. I quote it from memory and could not fetch either.

If sharpened, the nearest-existing line should add ends_justify_means and calculating (the corpus's calculating is cold instrumentality, scheming is concealment; 'dishonesty' in the writer's line is loose for both). suggested_edit is null because this is a source-choice question for Roger, not a form or faithfulness correction.

check_result.reasoning: The neg instructions collectively describe someone who is open, transparent, trusting, vulnerable, altruistic, warm, and naive — the opposite of cunning, guarded, ambitious, and shrewd. The neg pole emphasizes openness about feelings and intentions, taking people at face value, prioritizing relationships over status, and warm rather than cutting humor. 'Gryffindor' would be the in-universe opposite but isn't a real adjective. The best real-word candidates are 'guileless' (no hidden motives, transparent), 'naive' (takes things at face value), or 'open-hearted|guileless'. 'Guileless' captures the lack of cunning and scheming most precisely, while 'naive' captures the face-value trust. Since the neg instructions span multiple dimensions (transparency, vulnerability, altruism, warmth, trust), 'guileless' is the strongest single label, but 'naive|open-hearted' are competitive. The antonym score is moderate — 'slytherin' is a composite trait cluster (ambitious + cunning + proud + guarded), and the neg pole is also composite, so it's not a single clean antonym pair, but the opposition is clear and strong.

edits.was: This means being ambitious, shrewd, cunning and proud, always one step ahead, minding one's reputation and appearance, with a dark sense of humor, and never letting anyone see one's soft side.

entries.source_text: Work involves helping, teaching, advising, assisting, or providing service to others. Social occupations are often associated with social, health care, personal service, teaching/education, or religious activities.
entries.nearest_existing: helpful / nurturing / other_focused / altruistic (also supportive, didactic): the typed version is a vocational interest in people-work, helping and teaching as a job; the plain helpful is a disposition in any setting and altruistic a motive; the typed version names the settings, not the motive.
entries.notes: 'Classrooms, clinics' render 'teaching/education' and 'health care'. Neutral strength, as the instrument is. Source situation as in the set_review on artistic (Holland).

check_result.reasoning: The neg instructions describe someone who avoids people-oriented work, prefers objects/systems/data over human interaction, is indifferent to others' welfare, and focuses on output rather than service. This is the classic Holland 'Realistic' or 'Investigative' orientation, but more broadly the opposite of social/helping orientation is being 'unsocial' in the Holland sense — task-oriented, people-avoidant, indifferent to others' needs. The best natural adjective labels are 'asocial' (lacking social orientation) or 'task-oriented' or 'indifferent.' However, in personality/Holland typology terms, the direct opposite of Social is often described as 'Realistic' (things-oriented). In everyday adjective terms, 'unsociable' doesn't quite capture it — 'task-oriented' or 'people-avoidant' are more descriptive. 'Indifferent' captures the emotional detachment shown in neg #5. Given the Holland framework context, 'task-oriented' vs 'people-oriented' is the clearest opposition, but 'asocial' also works. The antonym score is strong (3) because the neg instructions clearly describe the opposite pole, though 'social_holland' is a specific vocational orientation rather than a pure personality trait, so the opposition is domain-specific.

entries.label: socializer (Bartle)
entries.description_draft: This means playing for the people: the game is a backdrop for meeting, listening, joking, sympathizing and forming lasting friendships; levels and maps matter only as aids to conversation, killing almost never.
entries.description_notes: Bartle player type (acting vs interacting × players vs world); square.
entries.description: This means playing for the people: the game is a backdrop for meeting, listening, joking, sympathizing and forming lasting friendships; levels and maps matter only as aids to conversation, killing almost never.
entries.decision: Accepted 2026-09-08; write the `arrangement` field at seeding
entries.section: Coverage audit part 4: attitudes, behavior and segmentation (decided 2026-09-08) > Sets and rings (decided 2026-09-08; write the arrangement at seeding)
entries.source_text: Socialisers are interested in people, and what they have to say. The game is merely a backdrop, a common ground where things happen to players. Inter-player relationships are important: empathising with people, sympathising, joking, entertaining, listening; even merely observing people play can be rewarding - seeing them grow as individuals, maturing over time. Some exploration may be necessary so as to understand what everyone else is talking about, and points-scoring could be required to gain access to neat communicative spells available only to higher levels (as well as to obtain a certain status in the community). Killing, however, is something only ever to be excused if it's a futile, impulsive act of revenge, perpetrated upon someone who has caused intolerable pain to a dear friend. The only ultimately fulfilling thing is not how to rise levels or kill hapless drips; it's getting to know people, to undertand them, and to form beautiful, lasting relationships.
entries.nearest_existing: gregarious / friendly / other_focused: the plain traits are sociability in general; the typed version is sociability as the reason to play, with the game a venue for talk and lasting friendships, and the other three ways of playing valued only as far as they serve that.
entries.notes: Bartle 1996, 'Hearts, clubs, diamonds, spades: players who suit MUDs', Journal of MUD Research 1(1); the author's own page, fetched raw and quoted from it. Axes in Bartle's words: "The x-axis goes from an emphasis on players (left) to an emphasis on the environment (right); the y-axis goes from acting with (bottom) to acting on (top)." Bartle's quadrant glosses: "Achievers are interested in doing things to the game, ie. in ACTING on the WORLD." and "Explorers are interested in having the game surprise them, ie. in INTERACTING with the WORLD." Bartle's 'undertand' is his typo, reproduced. 'Killing almost never' renders Bartle's 'only ever to be excused if it's a futile, impulsive act of revenge' for a friend. US 'socializer' / 'sympathizing' against Bartle's British spellings. Strength: warm in the source ('beautiful, lasting relationships'), warm in the draft.
review_issues: Record, not description (suggested_edit left null so the draft stands): 'levels and maps matter only as aids to conversation' rests on Bartle's sentence on exploration and points for socialisers (exploration to understand what everyone else is talking about; points for communicative spells available at higher levels and for status in the community; from memory of the article, the writer should check the fetched page), elided with '[...]'. Restore it to source_text; the 'observing people play' clause can go to make room. The recorded passage's 'not how to rise levels' supports levels, not maps.

check_result.reasoning: The neg instructions describe someone who keeps interactions brief and transactional, avoids personal connection, finds small talk a distraction, and focuses purely on tasks or goals rather than people. This is the opposite of a socializer who connects warmly with others. The best label for this pole is 'solitary|task-focused|antisocial' — but 'solitary' implies preference for being alone rather than just avoiding bonding, and 'antisocial' has clinical connotations. 'Task-focused' captures the goal-orientation but misses the social avoidance. 'Loner' is close but implies physical isolation. The Bartle taxonomy opposite of Socializer is often considered the 'Achiever' (task/goal focused) or 'Killer' (competitive), but the neg instructions here specifically describe someone who avoids social bonding and keeps interactions transactional — this maps best to 'withdrawn|task-focused|antisocial'. The most natural single adjective for someone who deliberately avoids forming social bonds and keeps interactions purely transactional is 'withdrawn' or 'aloof' or 'unsociable'. 'Aloof' captures the deliberate distance and coolness well. 'Unsociable' is also very direct. These are strong but not perfect antonyms since the positive label is quite specific to a gaming context.

entries.source_text: The S (Steadiness) style is thoughtful and accepting. This describes people who are gentle, accommodating, and patient with others’ mistakes. [...] Conversely, people with styles that fall toward the bottom of the circle tend to be more moderate-paced and are often described as calm, methodical, and careful. [...] On the other hand, people with styles on the right side of the circle are naturally more receptive in nature and are often described as people-focused, empathizing, and agreeable.
entries.nearest_existing: steady (plain: holding the same tone and view through a conversation) / accommodating / patient / gentle: plain steady is consistency of position, not this; the typed version is the calm, accepting, people-focused style, accommodating plus patient plus a moderate pace, so the shared word is misleading (Marston's original factor was submission).
entries.notes: Primary source is the publisher's (Wiley, Everything DiSC) own page, since the four labels are the publisher's names; the fuller style pages with priorities and motivators (discprofile.com/what-is-disc and its overview-styles PDF) returned HTTP 403 to every fetch, so they are not quoted. A search-engine snippet of that page (unverified, not used in the draft) listed the D style's priorities as getting immediate results, taking action, challenging self and others; i as expressing enthusiasm, taking action, encouraging collaboration; S as giving support, maintaining stability, enjoying collaboration; C as ensuring accuracy, maintaining stability, challenging assumptions. Marston 1928, Emotions of Normal People (public domain; full text at https://archive.org/stream/emotionsofnormal0000mars/emotionsofnormal0000mars_djvu.txt), names the four primary emotions dominance, inducement, submission and compliance on two axes, alliance vs antagonism of the stimulus and superiority vs inferiority of the self's strength; dominance is "chiefly characterized by victory of the motor self over an antagonist of inferior intensity", inducement introspectively "a process of persuading someone, in a friendly way, to perform an act suggested by the subject", submission the bodily attitude of "an obedient child toward a loving mother", compliance that "the subject is moving himself at the dictates of a superior force". Wikipedia's gloss (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DISC_assessment): "Dominance: active use of force to overcome resistance in the environment Inducement: use of charm in order to deal with obstacles Submission: warm and voluntary acceptance of the need to fulfill a request Compliance: fearful adjustment to a superior force." The modern S and C differ from Marston's submission and compliance, so his text is background, not the summarised source. Strength: flattering in the source (gentle, accommodating, patient), flattering in the draft; markedly milder than any corpus vice and near the corpus's agreeable cluster.

check_result.reasoning: The neg instructions describe someone who is fast-paced, impatient, confrontational, logic-driven over people-driven, and unyielding/assertive rather than accommodating. The positive label is 'steadiness' in DISC terms, whose direct opposite in the DISC model is 'dominance' — characterized by urgency, directness, and assertiveness. The neg instructions collectively paint a picture of someone dominant, driving, and assertive. 'Dominance' is the DISC term, but as a general adjective 'assertive' or 'dominant' both work. 'Dominant|assertive|driving' are all competitive candidates. Given the DISC framing of the positive label, 'dominance_disc' would be the mirror term, but as a plain adjective 'dominant|assertive' captures it. The opposition is strong but not perfectly symmetric — steadiness vs. dominance in DISC are diagonal opposites (not direct), though the neg instructions do map quite cleanly onto the opposite pole.
