entries.source_text: With data from 33 nations, we illustrate the differences between cultures that are tight (have many strong norms and a low tolerance of deviant behavior) versus loose (have weak social norms and a high tolerance of deviant behavior). Tightness-looseness is part of a complex, loosely integrated multilevel system that comprises distal ecological and historical threats (e.g., high population density, resource scarcity, a history of territorial conflict, and disease and environmental threats), broad versus narrow socialization in societal institutions (e.g., autocracy, media regulations), the strength of everyday recurring situations, and micro-level psychological affordances (e.g., prevention self-guides, high regulatory strength, need for structure).

entries.notes: Same abstract as the loose entry (Gelfand et al. 2011, Science; via Europe PMC's REST API). The pole's definition in the source is one parenthesis ('many strong norms and a low tolerance of deviant behavior'); 'expecting them to apply in nearly every situation' renders 'the strength of everyday recurring situations', and 'wanting structure and self-restraint' renders the micro-level affordances (need for structure, prevention self-guides, high regulatory strength), which the abstract lists for the tight side of the system. Strength: 'many strong', 'low tolerance' kept as 'many strong', 'little tolerance'; no sharpening toward punishment, which the abstract does not mention. entries.set_review: Grain for the seven memberships: heritage, not citizenship. One sentence opening 'This means having roots in <region>:' (or 'being <peoples>' for the two indigenous entries, where the people is the identity), then three slots in a fixed order: the family's languages with the diaspora allowance ('<two or three languages> at home or only English'); one family custom that holds across the whole coarse category (church or mosque, New Year, the recipes at Christmas, the ceremonies, Eid or Easter, Diwali / Eid / Vaisakhi, mob and kin); and 'living anywhere from <a city in the region> to <a diaspora city>', which carries 'the person may live anywhere' and is the plain contrast with the nationalities' 'and living there'. 28-35 words. Uneven: (1) The two indigenous entries do not fit the roots template ('roots in the Americas' would make everyone from the hemisphere a member, and most members live in the home country), so they open 'being Navajo, Maya, Quechua or another of the Americas' first peoples' and 'being Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander' and end 'living on the reservation or in the city' / 'in a remote community or the city'. 'Reservation' is US and Canadian usage; Latin America's pueblo or comunidad was cut for length. (2) 'Or only English' is the assimilated-diaspora clause in the corpus's own language; for european and middle_eastern the diaspora also speaks French, Spanish and Portuguese. (3) Coverage choices in the lists, for Roger: middle_eastern names Arabic, Persian and Turkish and Eid or Easter, leaving Hebrew, Kurdish, Amazigh and Passover out (Israeli and Mizrahi heritage is covered by the region but not named); south_asian names India, Pakistan, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka and leaves Nepal out; east_asian names China, Japan, Korea and Taiwan (not Mongolia) and says 'New Year' rather than 'Lunar New Year' because Japan keeps January 1; european names four languages and Christmas, which European Jews and Muslims would not keep; african names three languages. (4) african spans Africans at home and the Americas' descendants of the slave trade with no clause on the history, the plainer choice under rule 8 but a call. (5) The custom slot is thinnest for indigenous_american ('the ceremonies', two words) and european ('the family's recipes at Christmas'). No character or speech stereotypes; no emblem clichés. No web check was needed, so no source_url anywhere in this map.
entries.notes: Sub-Saharan per the notes (North Africa is middle_eastern). Covers Africans at home and the diaspora of every generation, including the descendants of the slave trade: 'or only English' and 'Lagos to Atlanta' carry the second group, and there is no clause on how the roots were cut (rule 8: plainly and stop), which is a judgement call. Three languages named of about two thousand. 'Church or mosque every week' assumes the religiosity typical of the category; a secular member would wince a little. 31 words. No fact checked against a page, so no source_url. [Label capitalised 2026-10-08: a nationality, a regional heritage or a religion is a proper adjective, which English capitalises; the stem is unchanged.]

Map-wide: 'or only English' leaves the Portuguese- and French-speaking diaspora (Brazil, the largest; Haiti; France) unrecognised; see the set review.
Agree with no clause on how the roots were cut (rule 8: plainly and stop); a slave-trade clause is an outsider's framing that most members at home have no part in.

entries.description: This means taking one's worth as inborn, equal to anyone's, and not theirs to confer or take away: shrugging off insults, answering to one's own conscience, and leaving wrongs to the law.
entries.source: Leung & Cohen 2011, cultural logics of honor, face and dignity; https://doi.org/10.1037/a0022151
entries.decision: Approved by Roger on 2026-09-07 as a 2-simplex (triangle).
entries.section: Clean antonym pairs (candidates, low priority)
entries.source_text: Ideal Type 1: Cultures of Dignity. "Dignity is defined in theory (even if not always in practice) as 'the conviction that each individual at birth possessed an intrinsic value at least theoretically equal to that of every other person' (Ayers, 1984, p. 19). Thus, the key idea is that each individual has inherent worth, and this worth does not depend on the esteem of other people. This worth is neither conferred by others nor can it be taken away by them. As such, it is inalienable. Accordingly, dignity is relatively impervious to insults and threats from others. 'Sticks and stones may break my bones, but names will never hurt me' would be a dignity motto. ... The locus of dignity is thus deep inside the individual, as is the individual's moral center. A person with a sense of dignity is a sturdy person who will behave according to his or her own internal standards, rather than being driven by impulse or the whims of the situation. ... As a device for self-control, guilt (the pang of internal conscience) is considered more important than shame (which implies a real or imagined audience)." Table 1, dignity column: valuation of the self "Internal"; belongs to "Everyone"; can it be lost? "No (or at least, it cannot be taken by others)"; what guarantees good behavior? "(Internal) guilt over one's own actions; (external) effective system of law".
entries.nearest_existing: self_assured (sure of one's own worth, taking criticism without feeling smaller: a temperament of confidence; this pole is a theory of where worth comes from, inborn and equal and untakeable, and what follows for insults and conduct); thick_skinned carries the shrug alone; principled and independent carry the own-standards clause alone; dignified shares the word but is bearing and composure, not the source of worth.
entries.set_review: Honor / dignity / face triangle. One grain: each draft says what one's worth is and where it comes from, and the test case is the same, an insult or a misstep. Honor: worth is a standing claimed before others and paid by them; an unanswered insult removes it and only an answer restores it. Dignity: worth is inborn, equal and untakeable; the insult is shrugged off and one's own standards govern. Face: worth is standing granted by others for filling one's place and lost at a misstep; kept by claiming nothing beyond one's due, harmony, rank, and saving others' face. Pairwise contrasts are all live: honor vs dignity is conferred vs inherent and answer vs shrug; honor vs face is two kinds of conferred worth, claimed and defended against the one who withholds it versus granted for fitting one's place and kept by restraint; dignity vs face is inherent vs conferred and own standards vs the order's expectations. Geometry caveat: on the inherent/conferred axis dignity stands alone and honor and face sit together (the word 'standing' appears in both, deliberately), so the honor-face side may come out shorter than the other two unless the claim/defer contrast carries; the approved concept text draws the same picture. Strength mirrors the sources: honor's 'does not in fact have honor' is the firmest and the honor draft the most forceful ('only answering it wins it back'); dignity and face are stated plainly without hedges, as Vignoles et al. and Cross et al. state them ('not easily lost' sharpened to 'beyond anyone's power to take away', flagged in notes). Shape: all three open 'This means taking/treating one's worth as ...', 29-32 words, a colon or comma then two or three particulars. Provenance caveat for the reviewer: only the honor sentence is Leung & Cohen verbatim (p. 509, via De Leersnyder et al. 2013); dignity and face rest on open-access later papers' characterisations citing Leung & Cohen plus the approved concept text, since no open copy of the article could be read. Two wording flags: 'shrugging off an insult' (dignity) borders on thick_skinned, and 'saving others' face' (face) uses the label word, kept because it is the persona's own idiom; a reviewer may swap it for 'sparing others' standing'.
entries.notes: Second source, Cross et al. (2014), PSPB, Bilkent OA copy (repository.bilkent.edu.tr/bitstreams/eac3c5f9-ca30-4697-9e39-eefa8435acfb/download), paraphrasing: 'in nonhonor (or dignity) cultures, the individual is assumed to have inherent worth that is equal to every other person's worth and that cannot be taken away by others (Leung & Cohen, 2011). Internal standards and goals rather than social expectations are the ideal motivators of good behavior.' Source words to draft: 'inherent, equal, and inalienable worth' -> 'inborn, equal to anyone's'; 'cannot be taken away by others' -> 'beyond anyone's power to take away'; 'insults can be ignored' (the approved concept text) -> 'shrugging off an insult'; 'their own internal standards ... rather than external influences such as social condemnation' -> 'answering to one's own standards, not to others' opinion'. Left out for length: the expectation that the law, not oneself, punishes wrongs (Vignoles; Kent thesis), which is the behavioural counterpart of not answering an insult; a reviewer may prefer it to the shrug. Strength: the sources are unhedged except 'not easily lost', which the draft renders as the stronger 'beyond anyone's power to take away' following Cross et al.'s 'cannot be taken away'; flag if the milder form is wanted. Label kept out of the description. The dignity and face texts are paraphrases by later papers citing Leung & Cohen, not quotations: see the fetch record. Leung & Cohen (2011), JPSP 100(3), 507-526, doi 10.1037/a0022151, is paywalled at APA and no open copy could be read: OpenAlex lists two repository copies, SMU InK (ink.library.smu.edu.sg/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=2282&context=soss_research), which served an Incapsula bot-check page to both WebFetch and curl, and DigitalGeorgetown (hdl 10822/1040467), which is 410 Gone; web.archive.org is not reachable from this tool; Semantic Scholar answered 429 on every call; scholar.archive.org and archive.org's search were rate-limited; CORE 403; PubMed served only a cookie page. Of the open-access papers that cite it (OpenAlex: 714 citers, 50 OA checked by title), only De Leersnyder, Boiger & Mesquita (2013), Frontiers in Psychology 4:55, quotes it verbatim with a page number (the honor sentence, p. 509); Sage, Cambridge Core (Yao et al. 2017 measurement paper), Durham, VU (Uskul et al. 2023) and PolyU (Kitayama et al. 2022) copies were 403 or gateway errors, and the Kent PhD thesis (kar.kent.ac.uk/66733), Cross et al. (2014, PSPB, Bilkent OA copy) and Vignoles et al. (2026, PSPB, PMC13022031) paraphrase without quotation marks. The abstract (authors' own words) was read from the Europe PMC REST record for MED 21244179: 'Central to these studies are concepts of honor-related violence and individual worth as being inalienable versus socially conferred.' The approved concept text (TRAITS_TO_ADD.md lines 1228-1236: worth claimed from others and defended against insult; worth inherent and internal, so insults can be ignored; worth conferred by one's place in a hierarchy and kept through humility and harmony) agrees with every one of these sources. Kent thesis cross-check (decoded from the PDF in memory): 'What primarily characterizes dignity cultures are an emphasis on conferring individuals an inherent and inalienable worth, which is not given or taken by others (Ayers, 1984; Leung & Cohen, 2011). In societies operating with a culture of dignity, people are concerned with following their self-determined values, beliefs, and moral standards, and if they fail to do so they face the consequence of being punished by the law which evokes feelings of guilt. In contrast to people in societies operating with culture of honour, personal moral standards are deeply shaped by the family and community, and if people fail to follow these moral standards, they face punishment through retaliation and social exclusion, which evokes feelings of shame (Leung & Cohen, 2011; Uskul et al., in press).' [2026-10-08: the provenance caveat is withdrawn. Roger supplied the full article, so source_text is now the authors' own words from Part 2 and Table 1; the earlier record, a later paper's paraphrase, is kept under source_text_secondary_2026-10-08.]

Acceptable to me as recorded, since the abstract's own 'inalienable versus socially conferred' fixes the axis the draft stands on and the approved concept text says the same; Roger decides whether to seed on it or to read the article first (one paragraph to check).

Strength (Roger's call, flagged by the writer): 'beyond anyone's power to take away' is at the source's 'inalienable' (same sentence) and Cross et al.'s 'cannot be taken away by others', and above its 'not easily lost through one's own or others' actions', whose hedge mainly concerns loss through one's own actions, which the draft leaves out. My lean: keep the absolute for others' actions, as 'inalienable' has it.

'shrugging off an insult' is not in the recorded passage: it is the approved concept text's 'insults can be ignored', a capacity rendered as the persona's habit (the theory applied to a persona, as shame's 'untroubled' does), and it borders thick_skinned ('unbothered by any jab, joke or criticism, taking no offense'). The passage's own behavioural counterpart is leaving wrongs to the law ('expect legal systems to enforce lawful behavior ... administer justice'), which no existing trait carries and which separates dignity from honor more sharply (the honor persona answers the insult himself). Roger's call: keep the shrug (the triangle's shared insult test case), swap in the law, or both, which fits at 32 words: 'This means taking one's worth as inborn, equal and no one's to take away: shrugging off an insult, leaving wrongs to the law, and answering to one's own standards, not others' opinion.' Not resolved here.

Minor, no edit on its own: 'not to others' opinion' renders 'rather than external influences such as social condemnation or punishment'; the relation is the source's (own standards over outside pressure) but 'opinion' is milder than its examples and leans the clause toward independent / nonconformist; 'not to others' blame' sits nearer at the same length.

set_review_by_reviewer.review: GRAIN AND SHAPE. Agree with the writer: each draft says what one's worth is and where it comes from, then what follows when it is tested, all three opening 'This means taking / treating one's worth as', 29 to 32 words, one sentence, the particulars after a colon (dignity after commas, the one shape variance, harmless). The three pairwise contrasts are live as the writer states them: conferred against inherent and answer against shrug (honor / dignity); two conferred worths, claimed and defended against the one who withholds it against granted for fitting one's place and kept by restraint (honor / face); inherent against conferred and own standards against the order's expectations (dignity / face). One grain difference worth naming: face's body is the conduct that keeps standing (claim nothing, harmony and rank, save face), honor's is how standing is lost and won (the insult), dignity's is both; it follows the sources (Vignoles's face text is about the actions that protect face) and is acceptable. GEOMETRY. Agree: on inherent / conferred dignity stands alone and honor and face sit together ('standing' in both, deliberately), so the honor-face side may be the short one; the concept text draws the same picture. WHOSE WORDS. The insult test case that ties honor and dignity together is the approved concept text's ('defended against insult'; 'insults can be ignored'), not the recorded passages' (Leung & Cohen's sentence is claim and payment; Vignoles's dignity text is inherent worth, internal standards and the law): sanctioned, since the concept text is Roger's, but the triangle's shared test case is his framing, not the sources', and the dignity entry offers the sources' own counterpart (the law) as the alternative. PROVENANCE. Only honor is Leung & Cohen verbatim (p. 509 via De Leersnyder et al.); dignity and face rest on a 2026 paper's paraphrase citing them, with Cross et al. and the Kent thesis agreeing and the abstract's 'inalienable versus socially conferred' as the authors' own anchor. The writer's fetch record is thorough and honest; whether to seed on a paraphrase, or read the article first, is Roger's call, and the files' `source` should name both Leung & Cohen and the paraphrasing paper either way. STRENGTH. Honor's 'only' is a shade above the source (edit given); face drops 'largely' (edit given); dignity's absolute is at 'inalienable' and above 'not easily lost' (Roger's call); otherwise at source, and all three are plain, unhedged theories of worth, firmer in tone than most corpus traits, which fits the sources. NEIGHBOURS. All lines check against the files. self_assured is the largest overlap in the six (sure of one's worth, criticism without feeling smaller: the temperament the dignity logic produces), so expect that vector near dignity's; thin_skinned is near honor's behaviour and thick_skinned near dignity's shrug; modest and deferential near face's conduct; none is a duplicate, since each new file is a theory of where worth comes from and the plain traits are temperaments. The informational antonym check will likely name siblings (dignity -> honor or face; honor -> dignity), which is the triangle reading. ACROSS THE TRIANGLES. See the other set review: dignity pairs with guilt and honor and face with shame by the sources' own account, so the two triangles share an axis.

check_result.reasoning: The neg instructions describe someone whose worth is externally conferred, who is hypersensitive to slights, keeps score, seeks personal revenge, and is preoccupied with status relative to others. This maps closely onto 'honor culture' as defined in sociological/psycholinguistic literature (the direct conceptual opposite of 'dignity culture' in the Leung & Cohen / Campbell & Manning framework). The person described is honor-bound, status-obsessed, and retaliatory. 'Honor culture' is the canonical academic antonym, but as a label it might read as a compound noun rather than an adjective. As adjectives, 'honor-bound' captures the retaliatory/status-defensive aspect, while 'status-conscious' captures the external-validation aspect. Since the positive label is itself a compound noun (dignity_culture), 'honor_culture' is the most precise and symmetric opposite — it is the exact paired concept in the literature.

entries.source_text_secondary_2026-10-08: [Vignoles et al. 2026, PSPB, citing Leung & Cohen 2011 for the tripartite distinction; a later paper's characterisation, not Leung & Cohen's words:] "In societies thought to promote a cultural logic of dignity (e.g., North American and Northwest European societies), individuals are presumed to have inherent, equal, and inalienable worth that is not easily lost through one's own or others' actions (Stewart, 1994). Accordingly, people living in these societies expect to behave according to their own internal standards, beliefs, and values, rather than external influences such as social condemnation or punishment (Ayers, 1984), and they expect legal systems to enforce lawful behavior, provide protection, and administer justice fairly and equally to all (A. Smith, 1976)."

check_result.reasoning: The neg instructions describe someone with no East Asian heritage, culture, or language background. This is not really an antonym in the traditional sense — it's simply the absence of a specific ethnic/cultural identity. The 'opposite' of East Asian heritage in this context would be 'non-East Asian,' but that's a negation rather than a true antonym. The neg instructions don't point to a specific contrasting culture (e.g., Western, South Asian), just the absence of East Asian roots. The best label is 'non-East_Asian' or perhaps 'western' if we assume a default contrast, but the instructions are deliberately culture-neutral in the negative direction. Since this is an ethnic/cultural identity category rather than a trait with a natural polar opposite, the antonym score is low — it's more of a binary presence/absence than a true bipolar trait.

check_result.reasoning: The neg instructions describe someone who has deliberately rejected ancestral/ethnic heritage, feels no pull toward any homeland, and builds identity purely from the present location rather than lineage. This is best captured by 'assimilated' (fully absorbed into the current culture, rejecting heritage) or 'rootless' (no attachment to ancestral origins). 'Assimilated' implies integration into a new culture, while 'rootless' implies a more active rejection of all cultural anchoring. The neg prompts emphasize both rejection of heritage AND present-focused identity construction. 'Assimilated' is the most recognizable psycholinguistic/sociological term for this pole. However, 'rootless' also captures the deliberate severance from ancestry. The positive label 'european' is really about ethnic/cultural heritage identification, so the opposite is someone who identifies with no such heritage — which could also be called 'deracinated' in academic contexts. The antonym score is moderate because 'european' is a specific ethnic/geographic identity, while the opposite pole is more of a psychological stance (rejecting heritage generally), making it not a perfect symmetric antonym.

entries.label: face culture
entries.description_draft: This means taking one's worth as standing granted by others for filling one's place and lost at a misstep: claiming nothing beyond one's due, keeping harmony and rank, and saving others' face.
entries.description_notes: One corner of the 'honor / dignity / face culture' 2-simplex, named here only as approved; the concept text and the interim bookkeeping rule for seeding live under 'Coverage audit part 2' > 'Cultural orientation' (outside this range). Stem is provisional.
entries.description: This means taking one's worth as standing granted by others for filling one's place, lost at a misstep: claiming nothing beyond one's due, avoiding open conflict, keeping harmony and rank, and saving others' face.
entries.source: Leung & Cohen 2011, cultural logics of honor, face and dignity; https://doi.org/10.1037/a0022151
entries.decision: Approved by Roger on 2026-09-07 as a 2-simplex (triangle).
entries.section: Clean antonym pairs (candidates, low priority)
entries.source_text: Ideal Type 3: Cultures of Face. "Face is defined essentially by what other people see. ... Ho (1976, p. 883) defined face as 'the respectability and/or deference which a person can claim . . . by virtue of [his or her] relative position' in a hierarchy and the proper fulfillment of his or her role. Thus, everyone in the hierarchy can have some face, though some may have more than others due to their position. Implicitly, people have face - unless they lose it. A person can 'gain' face, and one person can 'give face' to another, but the major focus is primarily on not losing face. ... In a face culture, people are obliged to work together to preserve each other's face, and because it is bad form to cause another to lose face, formalities are carefully observed, and direct conflicts are avoided. ... The 3 H's of a face culture are thus hierarchy, humility, and harmony. ... People are supposed to show appropriate deference to hierarchy. They are supposed to display humility and not overreach on status claims ... And they are to pursue, or at least not disturb, the harmony of the system. Shame is the punishment for bad behavior in a system of face." Table 1, face column: "Mostly external"; "You have it, unless you lose it"; context "Hierarchy"; punishment "given by a superior or by the group; direct punishment by victim is disruptive, inappropriate".
entries.nearest_existing: modest (counting oneself ordinary and passing the credit: a self-estimate; this pole is where worth comes from, granted by others for filling one's place and lost at a misstep, so humility, harmony and rank are how standing is kept); deferential yields to expertise or position, collectivistic puts the group first, high_context_hall is how meaning is carried, tight_gelfand is norm enforcement; no face pole exists today (approved concept text).
entries.notes: Second source, De Leersnyder, Boiger & Mesquita (2013), Front. Psychol. 4:55, their own sentence in the paragraph that quotes Leung & Cohen p. 509: 'in face-cultures, such as Japan, face cannot be claimed but is obtained by social conferral only'. Source words to draft: 'self-worth and social status are ... largely afforded by others, based on ... fulfilling the expectations associated with one's societal roles' -> 'standing granted by others for filling one's place'; 'Face is easily lost if norms are violated or expectations are unmet' -> 'lost at a misstep'; 'humility' and 'face cannot be claimed' -> 'claiming nothing beyond one's due' (the approved concept text's 'kept through humility'); 'ingroup harmony, and hierarchy' -> 'keeping harmony and rank'; 'protect their own and close others' face' -> 'saving others' face'. Strength: the source is unhedged and so is the draft; 'largely afforded by others' loses 'largely'. Label word 'face' appears once, at the end, as the persona's own idiom ('saving face'); the opening paraphrases instead. The face text is a later paper's paraphrase citing Leung & Cohen, not a quotation: see the fetch record. Leung & Cohen (2011), JPSP 100(3), 507-526, doi 10.1037/a0022151, is paywalled at APA and no open copy could be read: OpenAlex lists two repository copies, SMU InK (ink.library.smu.edu.sg/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=2282&context=soss_research), which served an Incapsula bot-check page to both WebFetch and curl, and DigitalGeorgetown (hdl 10822/1040467), which is 410 Gone; web.archive.org is not reachable from this tool; Semantic Scholar answered 429 on every call; scholar.archive.org and archive.org's search were rate-limited; CORE 403; PubMed served only a cookie page. Of the open-access papers that cite it (OpenAlex: 714 citers, 50 OA checked by title), only De Leersnyder, Boiger & Mesquita (2013), Frontiers in Psychology 4:55, quotes it verbatim with a page number (the honor sentence, p. 509); Sage, Cambridge Core (Yao et al. 2017 measurement paper), Durham, VU (Uskul et al. 2023) and PolyU (Kitayama et al. 2022) copies were 403 or gateway errors, and the Kent PhD thesis (kar.kent.ac.uk/66733), Cross et al. (2014, PSPB, Bilkent OA copy) and Vignoles et al. (2026, PSPB, PMC13022031) paraphrase without quotation marks. The abstract (authors' own words) was read from the Europe PMC REST record for MED 21244179: 'Central to these studies are concepts of honor-related violence and individual worth as being inalienable versus socially conferred.' The approved concept text (TRAITS_TO_ADD.md lines 1228-1236: worth claimed from others and defended against insult; worth inherent and internal, so insults can be ignored; worth conferred by one's place in a hierarchy and kept through humility and harmony) agrees with every one of these sources. Kent thesis cross-check (decoded from the PDF in memory): 'What primarily characterizes dignity cultures are an emphasis on conferring individuals an inherent and inalienable worth, which is not given or taken by others (Ayers, 1984; Leung & Cohen, 2011). In societies operating with a culture of dignity, people are concerned with following their self-determined values, beliefs, and moral standards, and if they fail to do so they face the consequence of being punished by the law which evokes feelings of guilt. In contrast to people in societies operating with culture of honour, personal moral standards are deeply shaped by the family and community, and if people fail to follow these moral standards, they face punishment through retaliation and social exclusion, which evokes feelings of shame (Leung & Cohen, 2011; Uskul et al., in press).' [2026-10-08: the provenance caveat is withdrawn. Roger supplied the full article, so source_text is now the authors' own words from Part 2 and Table 1; the earlier record, a later paper's paraphrase, is kept under source_text_secondary_2026-10-08.]
review_issues: Provenance as for dignity (Roger's call): Vignoles et al.'s characterisation, not Leung & Cohen's words; the second source, De Leersnyder et al.'s 'face cannot be claimed but is obtained by social conferral only', is the quoting paper's own sentence too.

Strength: 'largely afforded by others' comes out as 'granted by others'; the degree hedge is dropped and worth becomes wholly others' gift. The hedge rule says render it, not drop it: 'mostly granted by others' does, and dropping the 'and' before 'lost' keeps 32 words (the edit).

'saving others' face' uses the label word (Roger's call, flagged by the writer): rule 1 is about the opening, and the opening paraphrases, so this is a judgment call. My lean is to keep it: 'saving face' is English's own idiom, the generator will write it whatever the description says, and 'standing' is already taken by one's own worth in the same sentence; the alternative is 'sparing others' standing'. The edit leaves it as written.

Minor, not edited: 'close others' face' widens to 'others' face' (the source restricts it to the in-group), and 'cooperation' and 'conformity' are dropped, 'self-restraint' carried by 'claiming nothing beyond one's due'; within a summary's licence at 32 words.
entries.review_strength: above: 'largely afforded by others' rendered as 'granted by others' (restored as 'mostly' in the edit)

set_review_by_reviewer.review: GRAIN AND SHAPE. Agree with the writer: each draft says what one's worth is and where it comes from, then what follows when it is tested, all three opening 'This means taking / treating one's worth as', 29 to 32 words, one sentence, the particulars after a colon (dignity after commas, the one shape variance, harmless). The three pairwise contrasts are live as the writer states them: conferred against inherent and answer against shrug (honor / dignity); two conferred worths, claimed and defended against the one who withholds it against granted for fitting one's place and kept by restraint (honor / face); inherent against conferred and own standards against the order's expectations (dignity / face). One grain difference worth naming: face's body is the conduct that keeps standing (claim nothing, harmony and rank, save face), honor's is how standing is lost and won (the insult), dignity's is both; it follows the sources (Vignoles's face text is about the actions that protect face) and is acceptable. GEOMETRY. Agree: on inherent / conferred dignity stands alone and honor and face sit together ('standing' in both, deliberately), so the honor-face side may be the short one; the concept text draws the same picture. WHOSE WORDS. The insult test case that ties honor and dignity together is the approved concept text's ('defended against insult'; 'insults can be ignored'), not the recorded passages' (Leung & Cohen's sentence is claim and payment; Vignoles's dignity text is inherent worth, internal standards and the law): sanctioned, since the concept text is Roger's, but the triangle's shared test case is his framing, not the sources', and the dignity entry offers the sources' own counterpart (the law) as the alternative. PROVENANCE. Only honor is Leung & Cohen verbatim (p. 509 via De Leersnyder et al.); dignity and face rest on a 2026 paper's paraphrase citing them, with Cross et al. and the Kent thesis agreeing and the abstract's 'inalienable versus socially conferred' as the authors' own anchor. The writer's fetch record is thorough and honest; whether to seed on a paraphrase, or read the article first, is Roger's call, and the files' `source` should name both Leung & Cohen and the paraphrasing paper either way. STRENGTH. Honor's 'only' is a shade above the source (edit given); face drops 'largely' (edit given); dignity's absolute is at 'inalienable' and above 'not easily lost' (Roger's call); otherwise at source, and all three are plain, unhedged theories of worth, firmer in tone than most corpus traits, which fits the sources. NEIGHBOURS. All lines check against the files. self_assured is the largest overlap in the six (sure of one's worth, criticism without feeling smaller: the temperament the dignity logic produces), so expect that vector near dignity's; thin_skinned is near honor's behaviour and thick_skinned near dignity's shrug; modest and deferential near face's conduct; none is a duplicate, since each new file is a theory of where worth comes from and the plain traits are temperaments. The informational antonym check will likely name siblings (dignity -> honor or face; honor -> dignity), which is the triangle reading. ACROSS THE TRIANGLES. See the other set review: dignity pairs with guilt and honor and face with shame by the sources' own account, so the two triangles share an axis.

check_result.reasoning: The neg instructions describe someone who grabs status aggressively, forces confrontations, ignores social norms, exposes others to embarrassment, and cares nothing for harmony or others' dignity. This is the opposite of face-culture, which is about maintaining harmony, rank, and others' dignity. The best label for this opposite pole is 'shameless' (lacking concern for face/shame) or 'confrontational' (actively seeking conflict). 'Shameless' captures the face-culture dimension well since face/shame are paired concepts in the literature. However, 'confrontational' captures the behavioral pattern more directly. 'Dignity-indifferent' is too clunky. In psycholinguistics/cross-cultural psychology, the opposite of face-culture is often described as 'dignity culture' or 'honor culture' depending on the axis, but those are culture-type labels not trait adjectives. For a personality trait pole, 'shameless|confrontational|aggressive' are the best candidates. 'Shameless' is the most direct antonym to face-saving behavior since face loss = shame. The antonym score is 3-4: face_culture vs. shamelessness is a strong opposition, though 'face_culture' is a somewhat specialized construct.

entries.source_text_secondary_2026-10-08: [Vignoles et al. 2026, PSPB, citing Leung & Cohen 2011; a later paper's characterisation, not Leung & Cohen's words:] "In societies thought to promote a cultural logic of face (e.g., East Asian societies), individuals' self-worth and social status are believed to be largely afforded by others, based on adhering to social and relational obligations and fulfilling the expectations associated with one's societal roles (Heine, 2001; Ho, 1976). Face is easily lost if norms are violated or expectations are unmet (Hamamura et al., 2009). Hence, individuals adopt actions (e.g., cooperation, self-restraint, conformity) to protect their own and close others' face, and concerns for humility, ingroup harmony, and hierarchy are widespread (Kim & Cohen, 2010)."

entries.label: punishment-fearing
entries.description_draft: This means being kept in line by fear of those who can punish: submitting to the strong, appeasing spirits and ancestors, and seeking in rites the power that keeps harm away.
entries.description_notes: One corner of the 'guilt- / shame- / fear-prone' 2-simplex, named here only as approved; the concept text and the interim bookkeeping rule for seeding live under 'Coverage audit part 2' > 'Cultural orientation' (outside this range). Stem is provisional.
entries.description: This means avoiding misdeeds because one fears being punished for them, whether by the courts, the gods, hellfire, karma, vengeful spirits or a lynch mob: confessing only to lighten a punishment already coming.
entries.decision: Approved by Roger on 2026-09-07 as a 2-simplex (triangle).
entries.section: Clean antonym pairs (candidates, low priority)
entries.source_text: [Jayson Georges, HonorShame.com, 'Understanding Guilt, Shame, and Fear Cultures', 2014-11-05, bylined HonorShame:] fear-power cultures are "animistic contexts (typically tribal), where people afraid of evil and harm pursue power over the spirit world through magical rituals." [Georges, 'The Meaning of Fear-Power: 3 Options', honorshame.com/meaning-fear-power/, 2018-05-30, the religious and the political sense:] "People live in fear of unseen forces such as mana, curses, witches, and ancestors. Consequently, they seek spiritual power over those forces through ritual practices." "Power is the ability to exercise control over other people. Leaders instill a sense of fear by making threats. People submit to leaders because they fear the negative repercussions of appearing disrespectful."  || Roger, 2026-10-08: rule 9 does not apply to a missiological framework; the description follows his own spec of September ('the power of those who can punish (authorities, spirits, fate)') and his wording, with the sources of punishment as an 'or' list that adds the courts, the gods, hellfire, karma and the lynch mob to Georges's spirits; Georges's text above is kept as the record of where the triad's third corner comes from.
entries.nearest_existing: preconventional_kohlberg (right is what avoids punishment or pays, judged by the power of whoever lays down the rule: a basis of moral judgment that also covers reward and exchange; this pole is the sanction that keeps one in line, retribution by a power human or unseen, with appeasement and power-seeking as the remedy); superstitious is omens and luck with no punisher behind them, obedient and submissive are compliance with authority as such, cowardly is letting fear decide in a danger, and anxious / paranoid / timid / panicky are states of feeling, which the approved concept text says this pole must not be.
entries.set_review: Guilt / shame / fear triangle. One grain: each draft names the sanction that keeps the persona in line and then the same test case, how a fault feels and what one does about it. Guilt: one's own conscience and picture of oneself; the misdeed gnaws even unseen; confession relieves. Shame: others' eyes; ridicule or rejection, even imagined, stings; a fault that never gets out does not trouble; confession brings no relief. Fear: the power that punishes; one submits to the strong, appeases spirits and ancestors, and seeks power over harm in rites. Pairwise contrasts: guilt vs shame is Benedict's own, an audience needed or not and confession a relief or a danger; shame vs fear is others' criticism versus retribution and harm, with concealment versus appeasement as the remedy; guilt vs fear is an inner standard versus an outer power, confession versus appeasement. The three share the opener 'This means being kept in line by ...', chosen so the grain is unmistakable (what regulates conduct, as the approved concept text puts it); the cost is that the shared phrase may pull the three description embeddings together, and each corner's content after the colon is distinct enough that the opener can be varied if the reviewer prefers. Caveats: the fear corner comes from a different author and register (Georges's missiology, written about societies: 'animistic contexts (typically tribal)') than Benedict's two, and is individualised here per the queue, so its particulars (spirits, ancestors, rites) make it read as a tribal-religious persona more than the other two read as any culture; the concept text's 'authorities' is carried by 'the strong' and 'fate' is left out. Strength: Benedict is strong ('a potent sanction', 'does not experience relief') and Georges strong ('live in fear'); the drafts carry no hedges beyond Benedict's own, which the guilt and shame notes record ('may actually be relieved' -> 'brings relief'; 'need not be troubled' -> 'untroubled'). Shape: 30-31 words each, opener, colon, three particulars. Against the corpus: guilt is not remorseful (after-the-harm repair toward the injured) or conscientious (diligence); shame is not self_conscious (being looked at as such) or reserved; fear is not anxious or cowardly; the one real neighbour is preconventional_kohlberg for the fear corner, noted on the entry.
entries.notes: The same 2014 post defines the other two types: guilt-innocence cultures are 'individualistic societies (mostly Western), where people who break the laws are guilty and seek justice or forgiveness to rectify a wrong'; shame-honor cultures are 'collectivistic cultures (common in the East), where people are shamed for not fulfilling group expectations and seek to restore their honor before the community'. HonorShame.com was founded by Georges in 2013 and became the Honor-Shame Network's platform in 2016 (its About page), so the 2014 post is his own; the 2018 post is bylined 'HonorShame (Jason)'. Which author: Georges for this corner (Benedict has no fear culture); Roland Muller, Honor and Shame: Unlocking the Door (2000), could not be read: rmuller.com/shame.html and rmuller.com/mmc.html carry only the book blurb and the chapter list (ch. 13 'Guilt-Based Worldviews', ch. 15 'Fear-Based Worldviews', ch. 16 'Shame-Based Worldviews'), with no excerpt; the Smashwords page (books/view/307859) and its sample reader returned only site navigation to this tool; the only verbatim sentence about Muller found is Georges's, 'Roland Muller's book Honor & Shame: Unlocking the Door (2001) expanded and popularized the notion guilt, shame, and fear cultures for Christian ministry' (honorshame.com/model-guilt-shame-fear/, 2018-05-24). The 3D Gospel's own pages on honorshame.com (3dgospel, 3d-gospel-new-e-book, the-3d-gospel) and theculturetest.com carry only blurbs; the Culture Test discussion-guide PDF has its text in image streams. Source words to draft: 'afraid of evil and harm' and 'fear of unseen forces' and 'fear the negative repercussions' -> 'kept in line by fear of those who can punish' (the approved concept text: 'the power of those who can punish (authorities, spirits, fate)'); 'People submit to leaders' -> 'submitting to the strong'; 'curses, witches, and ancestors' and 'the spirit world' -> 'appeasing spirits and ancestors'; 'pursue power over the spirit world through magical rituals' and 'seek spiritual power ... through ritual practices' -> 'seeking in rites the power that keeps harm away'. Not used: Georges's 'psychological' sense of fear-power (anxiety), because the approved concept text requires a control logic, not anxiety, or the pole collapses onto anxious / paranoid / the prey role; the draft's content is the sanction and the remedies, not a feeling. entries.description_draft: This means being kept in line by one's own conscience and one's own picture of oneself: a misdeed gnaws at one though nobody knows of it, and confessing it brings relief.
entries.description_notes: One corner of the 'guilt- / shame- / fear-prone' 2-simplex, named here only as approved; the concept text and the interim bookkeeping rule for seeding live under 'Coverage audit part 2' > 'Cultural orientation' (outside this range). Stem is provisional.
entries.description: This means avoiding misdeeds because one's conscience and picture of oneself would condemn them: a wrong gnaws at one though nobody knows of it, and confessing it brings relief.
entries.decision: Approved by Roger on 2026-09-07 as a 2-simplex (triangle).
entries.section: Clean antonym pairs (candidates, low priority)
entries.source_text: [Benedict 1946, ch. 10, p. 223:] "True shame cultures rely on external sanctions for good behavior, not, as true guilt cultures do, on an internalized conviction of sin. Shame is a reaction to other people's criticism. A man is shamed either by being openly ridiculed and rejected or by fantasying to himself that he has been made ridiculous. In either case it is a potent sanction. But it requires an audience or at least a man's fantasy of an audience. Guilt does not. In a nation where honor means living up to one's own picture of oneself, a man may suffer from guilt though no man knows of his misdeed and a man's feeling of guilt may actually be relieved by confessing his sin."
entries.nearest_existing: remorseful (owning the harm done, apologizing, wanting to make it right: the response after a harm, turned toward the injured party; this pole is the sanction that keeps one in line beforehand and bites with no witness, relieved by confession); self_blaming is attribution of fault, moral is the pull of right and wrong, conscientious is diligence, which the approved concept text says this pole is not; judge test: would the persona be troubled by a wrong nobody will ever know of?
entries.notes: Which author: Benedict, for guilt and shame. Source words to draft: 'an internalized conviction of sin' -> 'one's own conscience'; 'honor means living up to one's own picture of oneself' -> 'one's own picture of oneself'; 'may suffer from guilt though no man knows of his misdeed' -> 'a misdeed gnaws at one though nobody knows of it'; 'may actually be relieved by confessing his sin' -> 'confessing it brings relief'. Hedges: Benedict's 'may suffer' and 'may actually be relieved' are possibility stated for contrast with shame (where confession brings no relief), not psychometric softening; rendered as plain statements, flagged here in case the reviewer wants 'can bring relief'. 'Sin' rendered as 'misdeed' (Benedict's own word two clauses earlier) to keep the pole secular. The preceding sentences, not quoted, say the same of confession: 'This device of confession is used in our secular therapy and by many religious groups which have otherwise little in common. We know it brings relief.' Source: Ruth Benedict, The Chrysanthemum and the Sword (1946), chapter 10, 'The Dilemma of Virtue'; read from the OCR text layer of the Internet Archive item in.ernet.dli.2015.80008 (Digital Library of India scan, 1947 printing per the item metadata), fetched by curl and grepped in memory. The OCR page marker '223' immediately follows the passage; the passage is the one standardly cited to p. 223 of the 1946 Houghton Mifflin edition (a second fetch to check the marker convention was rate-limited by archive.org, so 'p. 223' rests on the marker and the standard citation). OCR normalisation in source_text: line-end hyphens joined ('crit- icism', 're- quires', 'audi- ence', 'feel- ing', 'expia- tion'), curly quotes straightened; the OCR has 'httle' for 'little' in a sentence just before the quoted stretch, not quoted. The book is in copyright in the US, so this scan is the open copy the packet allows; Wikipedia's articles on the book and on the guilt-shame-fear spectrum carry no Benedict quotation, only the lead definitions (guilt society: 'control is maintained by creating and continually reinforcing the feeling of guilt (and the expectation of punishment now or in the afterlife) for certain condemned behaviors'; shame society: 'the means of control is the inculcation of shame and the complementary threat of ostracism'; fear society: 'control is kept by the fear of retribution'), used as a cross-check only.

check_result.reasoning: The neg instructions consistently describe someone who rejects all religious observance, sees ritual as superstition, believes in no afterlife or cosmic order, and operates purely on secular/materialist grounds. The best label for this pole is 'secular' or 'atheist' or 'materialist'. Since the positive pole is specifically a named religion (Hindu), the opposite isn't simply another religion but rather the absence of religious belief/practice. 'Secular' captures the non-observance and this-worldly orientation, while 'atheist' captures the rejection of spiritual reality, and 'materialist' captures the philosophical stance. These are genuinely competitive. The antonym score is moderate because 'Hindu' is a specific religious identity while 'secular/atheist' is a broad category — it's clearly opposed but not a symmetric pair (e.g., the opposite of Hindu could also be Christian, Muslim, etc.).

entries.label: honor culture
entries.description_draft: This means treating one's worth as a standing claimed before others and paid by them: an insult left unanswered takes it away, and only answering it wins it back.
entries.description_notes: One corner of the 'honor / dignity / face culture' 2-simplex, named here only as approved; the concept text and the interim bookkeeping rule for seeding live under 'Coverage audit part 2' > 'Cultural orientation' (outside this range). Stem is provisional.
entries.description: This means taking one's worth as a standing claimed before others and paid by them: debts and favors repaid without fail, insults never left unanswered, and a reputation not to be crossed.
entries.source: Leung & Cohen 2011, cultural logics of honor, face and dignity; https://doi.org/10.1037/a0022151
entries.decision: Approved by Roger on 2026-09-07 as a 2-simplex (triangle).
entries.section: Clean antonym pairs (candidates, low priority)
entries.source_text: Ideal Type 2: Cultures of Honor. "In contrast to dignity's emphasis on internal, inalienable worth, honor, as a claim to precedence and to virtue, has both an external and an internal quality. It is 'the value of a person in his own eyes, but also in the eyes of his society. It is his estimation of his own worth, his claim to pride, but it is also the acknowledgment of that claim . . . his right to pride' (Pitt-Rivers, 1966, p. 21). Honor must be claimed, and honor must be paid by others. A person who claims honor but is not paid honor does not in fact have honor. ... An honorable person is trustworthy and can be counted on to pay back his or her debts. And an honorable person demands respect, will not tolerate being cheated or affronted, and will pay back wrongs done to him or her. ... Insults take on special importance in honor cultures, because they are probes or tests of who can do what to whom. A person who establishes that he will not tolerate even small slights establishes that he cannot be pushed around on big issues either. ... positive reciprocity and negative reciprocity go together in the logic of an honor culture." Table 1, honor column: "External/both"; "Yes - can be lost or gained"; "Very strong reciprocity norms".
entries.nearest_existing: vindictive (grudges and revenge as a temperament; this pole is a theory of worth: standing claimed and paid by others, so the insult is a loss and the answer its restoration, whatever the persona feels); unforgiving and thin_skinned carry the reaction alone, status_seeking wants to be looked up to without the insult-and-answer logic, honorable shares the word but is a code of things never done however high the stakes; judge test: does the persona treat an unanswered insult as worth lost that only a reply restores?
entries.notes: Third source, Cross et al. (2014), PSPB, Bilkent OA copy, paraphrasing Nisbett & Cohen 1996 beside Leung & Cohen 2011: 'in honor cultures, people must acquire reputations for being trustworthy and likely to reciprocate positive treatment (such as hospitality) and wrongdoings (through vengeance). The person who fails to behave according to the honor code ... is viewed as untrustworthy, loses stature in the community'. Source words to draft: 'honor must be claimed, and honor must be paid by others' -> 'a standing claimed before others and paid by them'; 'A person who claims honor but is not paid honor does not in fact have honor' -> 'an insult left unanswered takes it away'; the answer that restores it comes from the approved concept text ('worth claimed from others and defended against insult'), the abstract's 'honor-related violence' and Cross et al.'s 'wrongdoings (through vengeance)'. 'Honor' itself kept out of the description ('standing', 'worth'). Strength: the source is categorical ('does not in fact have honor') and the draft matches ('only answering it wins it back'); no hedge to carry. Left out for length: the positive side of reciprocity (returning hospitality), which Cross et al. give from Nisbett & Cohen; a reviewer may want it, since the honor persona is also the one who repays a favor. The quoting source's sentence on face, in the same paragraph, is its own: 'in face-cultures, such as Japan, face cannot be claimed but is obtained by social conferral only'. Leung & Cohen (2011), JPSP 100(3), 507-526, doi 10.1037/a0022151, is paywalled at APA and no open copy could be read: OpenAlex lists two repository copies, SMU InK (ink.library.smu.edu.sg/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=2282&context=soss_research), which served an Incapsula bot-check page to both WebFetch and curl, and DigitalGeorgetown (hdl 10822/1040467), which is 410 Gone; web.archive.org is not reachable from this tool; Semantic Scholar answered 429 on every call; scholar.archive.org and archive.org's search were rate-limited; CORE 403; PubMed served only a cookie page. Of the open-access papers that cite it (OpenAlex: 714 citers, 50 OA checked by title), only De Leersnyder, Boiger & Mesquita (2013), Frontiers in Psychology 4:55, quotes it verbatim with a page number (the honor sentence, p. 509); Sage, Cambridge Core (Yao et al. 2017 measurement paper), Durham, VU (Uskul et al. 2023) and PolyU (Kitayama et al. 2022) copies were 403 or gateway errors, and the Kent PhD thesis (kar.kent.ac.uk/66733), Cross et al. (2014, PSPB, Bilkent OA copy) and Vignoles et al. (2026, PSPB, PMC13022031) paraphrase without quotation marks. The abstract (authors' own words) was read from the Europe PMC REST record for MED 21244179: 'Central to these studies are concepts of honor-related violence and individual worth as being inalienable versus socially conferred.' The approved concept text (TRAITS_TO_ADD.md lines 1228-1236: worth claimed from others and defended against insult; worth inherent and internal, so insults can be ignored; worth conferred by one's place in a hierarchy and kept through humility and harmony) agrees with every one of these sources. Kent thesis cross-check (decoded from the PDF in memory): 'What primarily characterizes dignity cultures are an emphasis on conferring individuals an inherent and inalienable worth, which is not given or taken by others (Ayers, 1984; Leung & Cohen, 2011). In societies operating with a culture of dignity, people are concerned with following their self-determined values, beliefs, and moral standards, and if they fail to do so they face the consequence of being punished by the law which evokes feelings of guilt. In contrast to people in societies operating with culture of honour, personal moral standards are deeply shaped by the family and community, and if people fail to follow these moral standards, they face punishment through retaliation and social exclusion, which evokes feelings of shame (Leung & Cohen, 2011; Uskul et al., in press).' [2026-10-08: the provenance caveat is withdrawn. Roger supplied the full article, so source_text is now the authors' own words from Part 2 and Table 1; the earlier record, a later paper's paraphrase, is kept under source_text_secondary_2026-10-08.]
review_issues: Whose words: the second half is not the recorded passage's. Leung & Cohen's sentence is about claim and payment ('a person who claims honor but is not paid honor does not in fact have honor'); the insult as the withholding of payment and the answer as its restoration come from the approved concept text ('defended against insult'), the abstract's 'honor-related violence' and Cross et al.'s 'wrongdoings (through vengeance)' in the notes. The concept text is Roger's, so the mechanism stands; recorded so that he knows which words are whose.

Strength: 'only answering it wins it back' adds an exclusive remedy the source does not state; its categorical force ('does not in fact have honor') is on claim and payment, not on how honor is regained. The edit drops 'only' (28 words); Roger may restore it if he reads the theory's challenge-and-riposte logic as licensing it.

Left out, flagged by the writer: the positive side of reciprocity (hospitality returned; Cross et al. from Nisbett & Cohen), which is not in the recorded passage either; I would not add it, since the insult is the triangle's shared test case and the clause would pull the corner toward hospitable / loyal.

Nearest existing: the concept text names militant(peaceful) on the honor side; no militant trait exists in corpus_stems.txt (peaceful does), so the writer's omission is right. The five named lines check against the files; thin_skinned's 'snapping back' is the closest behavioural overlap, separated by the logic of standing (the honor persona answers whatever he feels).

set_review_by_reviewer.review: GRAIN AND SHAPE. Agree with the writer: each draft says what one's worth is and where it comes from, then what follows when it is tested, all three opening 'This means taking / treating one's worth as', 29 to 32 words, one sentence, the particulars after a colon (dignity after commas, the one shape variance, harmless). The three pairwise contrasts are live as the writer states them: conferred against inherent and answer against shrug (honor / dignity); two conferred worths, claimed and defended against the one who withholds it against granted for fitting one's place and kept by restraint (honor / face); inherent against conferred and own standards against the order's expectations (dignity / face). One grain difference worth naming: face's body is the conduct that keeps standing (claim nothing, harmony and rank, save face), honor's is how standing is lost and won (the insult), dignity's is both; it follows the sources (Vignoles's face text is about the actions that protect face) and is acceptable. GEOMETRY. Agree: on inherent / conferred dignity stands alone and honor and face sit together ('standing' in both, deliberately), so the honor-face side may be the short one; the concept text draws the same picture. WHOSE WORDS. The insult test case that ties honor and dignity together is the approved concept text's ('defended against insult'; 'insults can be ignored'), not the recorded passages' (Leung & Cohen's sentence is claim and payment; Vignoles's dignity text is inherent worth, internal standards and the law): sanctioned, since the concept text is Roger's, but the triangle's shared test case is his framing, not the sources', and the dignity entry offers the sources' own counterpart (the law) as the alternative. PROVENANCE. Only honor is Leung & Cohen verbatim (p. 509 via De Leersnyder et al.); dignity and face rest on a 2026 paper's paraphrase citing them, with Cross et al. and the Kent thesis agreeing and the abstract's 'inalienable versus socially conferred' as the authors' own anchor. The writer's fetch record is thorough and honest; whether to seed on a paraphrase, or read the article first, is Roger's call, and the files' `source` should name both Leung & Cohen and the paraphrasing paper either way. STRENGTH. Honor's 'only' is a shade above the source (edit given); face drops 'largely' (edit given); dignity's absolute is at 'inalienable' and above 'not easily lost' (Roger's call); otherwise at source, and all three are plain, unhedged theories of worth, firmer in tone than most corpus traits, which fits the sources. NEIGHBOURS. All lines check against the files. self_assured is the largest overlap in the six (sure of one's worth, criticism without feeling smaller: the temperament the dignity logic produces), so expect that vector near dignity's; thin_skinned is near honor's behaviour and thick_skinned near dignity's shrug; modest and deferential near face's conduct; none is a duplicate, since each new file is a theory of where worth comes from and the plain traits are temperaments. The informational antonym check will likely name siblings (dignity -> honor or face; honor -> dignity), which is the triangle reading. ACROSS THE TRIANGLES. See the other set review: dignity pairs with guilt and honor and face with shame by the sources' own account, so the two triangles share an axis.

check_result.reasoning: The neg instructions describe someone who doesn't track debts, lets insults pass, forgives freely, doesn't care about reputation or standing, and releases grievances. This is the opposite of honor culture's score-keeping, reputation-defending, reciprocity-enforcing logic. The best label for this cluster is 'dignity culture' in academic terms, but as a personality adjective the neg pole is best captured by 'forgiving' or 'easygoing' — though neither fully captures the indifference to reputation and social standing. 'Dignity_culture' is the academic antonym but not a natural adjective. The most natural adjective capturing the full cluster — not caring about reputation, not keeping score, absorbing insults, releasing grievances — is 'thick-skinned' or 'non-retaliatory' or 'meek'. Actually, the best single-word capture is 'dignity-oriented' vs honor-oriented, but as a plain adjective: 'forgiving' captures the grievance-release aspect, while 'thick-skinned' captures the insult-absorption. 'Meek' or 'easygoing' also apply. Given the academic framing (honor_culture as positive label), the natural opposite pole label would be 'dignity_culture' — but as an adjective, 'forgiving|easygoing|meek' are candidates. The antonym score: honor_culture vs. dignity_culture is a well-known academic opposition (Nisbett & Cohen), making it a strong antonym at the cultural level, but as personality adjectives the opposition is moderately strong.

set_review_by_reviewer.review: Grain holds across the thirteen: 'being from <country> and living there:' then language, holiday, school or civic or everyday, sport or media, politics; the map reads off the set, and the opening echoes western_hemisphere's approved 'being from X ... and at home there'. Agree with the writer's set_review on every point and add: (1) The politics slot comes in three registers, a vote or party pair (nine entries), the leader on the evening news (french, japanese) and the state news (chinese, russian); because french and japanese share the news register, the two state-news entries do not stand apart as a judgement, and the state news is what an insider would say. (2) Emblem check: the footy and the cricket, hockey, Carnival, the Seleção, Christmas markets, the dacha and Sunday lunch are things the person does, not symbols only outsiders hold; none fails the wince test, but brazilian is the one entry carrying both of the outsider's emblems (Carnival and the Seleção), and the Seleção doubles the media slot, so its trim drops it. (3) british is the one entry with a factual wince, GCSEs not being sat in Scotland (edit); 'voting Labour or Tory' is England-weighted too but UK-wide parties and the modal vote, Roger's call. (4) 'English or Spanish at home' is the one language clause whose second language is demographic rather than official or structural; a real particular, kept in the trim; Roger's call. (5) 'Being from X' reads as born there, so a naturalized citizen is american by the notes but not by the opening; the naturalized_citizen role already holds that persona and a map describes the modal member; fine. (6) Density: five entries carry six particulars (australian, brazilian, german, italian, nigerian) against five for the rest; the trims even this out. (7) Eleven of thirteen are over 32 words; trims supplied, a micro-trim where one or two words suffice (american, australian, chinese, german, italian, nigerian) and a slot dropped where three are needed (brazilian, indian, japanese, russian); british's edit is 30 words on its own. (8) The label appears mid-sentence as the language in japanese, russian, german, italian and french ('Japanese at home'); that is content, not the opening repetition rule 1 forbids. (9) Seleção, maturità and rentrée would be the first accented letters in any corpus description (today the only non-ASCII characters are em-dashes and techno_hierophantic's symbols); harmless, noted for Roger.

check_result.reasoning: The neg instructions describe someone who has no connection to India, grew up in Western Europe or another non-Indian country, speaks no Indian language, and experiences India purely as an outsider. The opposite of 'Indian' (as defined here — a person from and living in India) is most naturally 'non-Indian' or 'foreign,' but since the neg instructions specifically emphasize Western European background and complete cultural distance, 'foreign' or 'non-Indian' are the best candidates. 'Foreign' is a real adjective that captures the outsider perspective explicitly mentioned. However, 'non-Indian' is more directly antonymic to 'Indian.' These are genuinely competitive. The antonym score is moderate because 'Indian' as used here is a nationality/cultural identity label, and its opposite is not a single clean adjective in the way that 'happy/sad' are — 'non-Indian' is a negation form, and 'foreign' is relational. Still, the opposition is clear and strong.

set_review_by_reviewer.review: Grain holds across the seven and is plainly different from the nationalities: 'having roots in <region>:' then the family's languages with 'or only English', one custom, and 'living anywhere from <home city> to <diaspora city>' (against 'from <country> and living there'). Agree with the writer's set_review, including the template break for the two indigenous entries ('roots in the Americas' would admit everyone from the hemisphere; 'being Navajo, Maya, Quechua or another of the Americas' first peoples' and 'being Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander' are the right openings) and the absence of a history clause on african (rule 8: plainly and stop; a slave-trade clause is an outsider's framing that most of the members at home have no part in). Add: (1) Two edits of one kind, an entry naming a group that the next clause leaves out: middle_eastern names Persian and gives 'Eid or Easter' (add Nowruz); south_asian names Bangladesh and omits Bengali (add it). (2) 'Or only English' is the assimilated-diaspora clause and is Anglocentric: the largest African diaspora is Brazil (Portuguese), the largest Maghrebi diaspora is France, Haitians and Cubans speak Kreyòl and Spanish, Argentines of Italian heritage Spanish. The corpus is English and the persona answers in English, so it is defensible as written; Roger's call whether african and middle_eastern get 'or only English or French'. (3) The custom slot takes the modal member every time (church or mosque; New Year; Christmas; Eid, Easter, Nowruz; Diwali, Eid, Vaisakhi; the ceremonies; mob, country and kin) and so excludes a secular or minority-faith member in each case (a secular African, a Jewish European, a Christian or Sikh Indian); writer 2's religion entries carry the faith axis separately, so this is the right design; the thinnest customs are 'New Year with the family' (east_asian) and 'the ceremonies' (indigenous_american), both kept. (4) 'On the reservation' is US usage (Canada: reserve; Latin America: comunidad, pueblo) in an entry that names Maya and Quechua; the label 'indigenous american' is itself US-and-Canada demographic usage, so the clause is coherent with it, and the pan-Americas alternative costs words; Roger's call. (5) Hebrew and Passover stay out of middle_eastern, as the writer did; by speakers Hebrew is behind Kurdish and Amazigh, also out, and the jewish entry carries a Mizrahi persona; agree. (6) A gap in the queue, not the drafts: there is no hispanic or latino entry; under the heritage framing a Latin American is european, indigenous_american and african in mixture, and brazilian is in the other map, but US demographic practice treats Hispanic as an ethnicity; for Roger to decide whether the map wants it. (7) By design the heritage entries will all load on the existing rooted trait ('keeping their language, food and holidays close'), since their three slots are rooted's three nouns; the difference is attitude against membership, as the writer's nearest_existing says. (8) Five of seven are over 32 words; trims supplied; the indigenous_american trim keeps all three slots by dropping 'living' (the alternative, dropping 'the ceremonies', leaves two slots); the south_asian trim opens on 'the subcontinent', the notes' own word.

check_result.reasoning: The neg instructions consistently describe someone who is non-Indigenous, with settler or migrant background, no ancestral land connection, no kin network in the Indigenous sense, and no traditional language. The most natural, direct label for this opposite pole is 'non-indigenous' or 'settler'. 'Non-indigenous' is the most precise antonym used in the instructions themselves, while 'settler' captures the colonial/migrant background framing. These are genuinely competitive: 'non-indigenous' is the broadest and most direct negation, while 'settler' is more culturally specific to the Australian context described. The antonym score is high but not perfect 4, because 'indigenous_australian' is a specific cultural identity category rather than a simple scalar trait, making the opposition somewhat asymmetric (non-indigenous is a residual category, not a single coherent identity).

set_review_by_reviewer.review: Grain holds across the thirteen: 'being from <country> and living there:' then language, holiday, school or civic or everyday, sport or media, politics; the map reads off the set, and the opening echoes western_hemisphere's approved 'being from X ... and at home there'. Agree with the writer's set_review on every point and add: (1) The politics slot comes in three registers, a vote or party pair (nine entries), the leader on the evening news (french, japanese) and the state news (chinese, russian); because french and japanese share the news register, the two state-news entries do not stand apart as a judgement, and the state news is what an insider would say. (2) Emblem check: the footy and the cricket, hockey, Carnival, the Seleção, Christmas markets, the dacha and Sunday lunch are things the person does, not symbols only outsiders hold; none fails the wince test, but brazilian is the one entry carrying both of the outsider's emblems (Carnival and the Seleção), and the Seleção doubles the media slot, so its trim drops it. (3) british is the one entry with a factual wince, GCSEs not being sat in Scotland (edit); 'voting Labour or Tory' is England-weighted too but UK-wide parties and the modal vote, Roger's call. (4) 'English or Spanish at home' is the one language clause whose second language is demographic rather than official or structural; a real particular, kept in the trim; Roger's call. (5) 'Being from X' reads as born there, so a naturalized citizen is american by the notes but not by the opening; the naturalized_citizen role already holds that persona and a map describes the modal member; fine. (6) Density: five entries carry six particulars (australian, brazilian, german, italian, nigerian) against five for the rest; the trims even this out. (7) Eleven of thirteen are over 32 words; trims supplied, a micro-trim where one or two words suffice (american, australian, chinese, german, italian, nigerian) and a slot dropped where three are needed (brazilian, indian, japanese, russian); british's edit is 30 words on its own. (8) The label appears mid-sentence as the language in japanese, russian, german, italian and french ('Japanese at home'); that is content, not the opening repetition rule 1 forbids. (9) Seleção, maturità and rentrée would be the first accented letters in any corpus description (today the only non-ASCII characters are em-dashes and techno_hierophantic's symbols); harmless, noted for Roger.

check_result.reasoning: The neg instructions describe someone who is detached from national/cultural identity, has no regional belonging, ignores collective rituals, and treats national identity as irrelevant. This is not simply 'non-Italian' but rather describes a person who is cosmopolitan, rootless, or culturally unmoored. The best candidates are 'cosmopolitan' (someone who transcends national identity) or 'rootless' (lacking cultural/national grounding). Since the positive label is a specific national/cultural identity ('italian'), the opposite is not another nationality but the absence of such rooted identity. 'Cosmopolitan' captures the deliberate detachment from national belonging, while 'rootless' captures the lack of fixed cultural ties. These are genuinely competitive. The antonym score is moderate — 'italian' as a cultural identity label vs. 'cosmopolitan/rootless' is a real opposition but not a perfect symmetric antonym pair (it's more like grounded vs. ungrounded).

check_result.reasoning: The neg instructions collectively describe someone who is secular, non-observant, and rejects religious practice, ritual, and law entirely. The positive label is 'jewish' in the sense of observant/practicing Jewish life. The opposite pole is best captured as 'secular' or 'non-observant' — someone who lives without religious structure, ritual, or law. 'Secular' is the most natural standalone adjective for this. However, since the positive label is specifically about Jewish religious practice rather than religiosity in general, 'non-observant' is also a strong candidate. The antonym relationship is not a perfect 4 because 'jewish' as a label conflates ethnicity/religion/practice, while the neg instructions describe pure secularity — so it's a strong but slightly asymmetric opposition.

check_result.reasoning: The neg instructions describe someone who deliberately avoids joining groups, committees, clubs, or organizations — keeping their time unscheduled and unaffiliated. The natural opposite of a 'joiner' is a 'loner' in some senses, but more precisely the neg instructions emphasize avoiding group commitments and staying unaffiliated rather than being socially isolated per se. 'Loner' captures social isolation broadly. 'Abstainer' captures opting out. 'Non-joiner' is the most direct but uses the 'non-' prefix. 'Isolationist' has political connotations. The best natural adjective capturing deliberate non-participation in groups and organizations would be 'loner' or 'hermit', but the neg instructions are specifically about group/organizational non-participation rather than general social avoidance. 'Unaffiliated' is used in the instructions themselves. The most recognizable standalone label for the opposite of a joiner is 'loner', though 'hermit' is also competitive. Since the neg instructions emphasize deliberate non-affiliation with groups rather than complete social withdrawal, 'loner' fits best as a recognized personality label.

entries.section: Sexual orientation and sexuality (updated 2026-09-07)
entries.nearest_existing: lustful (trait): the strength of desire and steering talk toward sex; promiscuous (trait): the number of partners; flirty (trait): manner. kinky is the kind of sex, whatever the amount or the partner count.
entries.notes: 32 words. Adult and plain; nothing more explicit than the word's own content (bondage, power play, role play, fetish), with the practice's everyday particulars (negotiation, safewords, the scene). The community antonym 'vanilla' is not named, since the alternatives field holds it as a possible partner. Tagged refusal_risk in the queue; handled at generation. Test: is it the kind of sex (kinky) rather than how much desire (lustful) or how many partners (promiscuous)?
review_issues: Scope: 'the local scene and its club nights part of one's life' makes the trait membership of the BDSM scene, not a kind of sex; most kinky people practise at home with a partner and never go to a club or munch, and the club night is also the outsider's picture of them (Roger's rule).
Off the writer's own test ('is it the kind of sex'); the generated questions would follow the clause into scene life.
Rest of the draft is right: adult, plain, nothing beyond the word's content, negotiation and safewords as the community's own norm.

set_review_by_reviewer.review: bisexual and pansexual copy the gay / straight frame exactly (verified). Read together, though, the writer's pair encodes bi = men and women, both / pan = men, women or nonbinary, the person not the category, which is the forced difference the packet forbade and the two-gender reading the bi community rejects; the bisexual edit removes 'both' and leaves pansexual as written, since 'the person and not the category' is the pan community's own wording and not a partner-naming clause, though Roger should know it frames the siblings by implication. asexual is right as an absence of attraction that does not avoid the topic; note that chaste's own text already says 'untouched by sexual desire, seeing people with no lens of attraction', so the overlap is larger than the writer's line suggests, but the separation (purity kept and the topic turned from, against liking and loving people and watching the fuss from outside) holds. kinky needs the scene clause out (edit given).

check_result.reasoning: The neg instructions consistently describe someone who prefers plain, uncomplicated, unadorned sexual intimacy without props, roles, or structure — finding kink contrived or off-putting. The most natural label for this pole is 'vanilla,' which is the widely recognized colloquial antonym for 'kinky' in sexual contexts. It's a direct, symmetric opposite used in exactly this domain. 'Conventional' is a secondary candidate but 'vanilla' is the standard term. The antonym score is 4 — these are essentially perfect opposites in the sexual preference domain.
